topic: ventilation_flow
claim: The safety margin assumed from still-air tests may not hold in most spacecraft, because ventilation flow strongly enhances flames.
quote: Microgravity experiments demonstrated that the assumed margin of safety of reduced flammability in microgravity, based on quiescent test results, may not be valid for most spacecraft environments where ventilation flow strongly enhances flames.
source_title: A Researcher's Guide to: Combustion Science

topic: ventilation_flow
claim: For flame spread over solid materials, a gas velocity on the order of 10 cm/s corresponds to a maximum in the flame spread rate.
quote: For flame spread across solid materials, the characteristic gas velocity of the minimum in the curve is on the order of 10 cm/s and also corresponds to a maximum in the flame spread rate.
source_title: A Researcher's Guide to: Combustion Science

topic: flame_spread
claim: In space, at low forced-flow velocities, a flame spreads upstream into the oncoming airflow, contrary to normal-gravity behavior.
quote: Completely contrary to normal-gravity behavior, the flame spreads upstream, into the oncoming airflow, in space when the forced-flow velocities are low
source_title: A Researcher's Guide to: Combustion Science

topic: flammability_limit
claim: BASS results indicate that NASA-STD-6001 Test 1 is not conservative: materials can burn at lower oxygen levels in microgravity than on Earth.
quote: Recent results from the BASS experiment currently running on the ISS indicate that NASA-STD-6001 Test 1 is not conservative, and materials can burn at lower oxygen levels in microgravity than on Earth.
source_title: A Researcher's Guide to: Combustion Science

topic: flammability_limit
claim: In low-flow conditions of microgravity or partial gravity, some materials are flammable at lower oxygen concentrations than in normal gravity.
quote: In the low-flow conditions of microgravity or partial gravity, some materials are flammable at lower oxygen concentrations than in normal gravity
source_title: A Researcher's Guide to: Combustion Science

topic: oxygen_enrichment
claim: In Saffire-V, elevated oxygen levels gave more energetic flames, which would have a larger impact on the vehicle.
quote: The elevated oxygen levels show more energetic flames, which would have a larger impact on the vehicle
source_title: Saffire Ignites New Discoveries in Space

topic: oxygen_enrichment
claim: Many commonly used ISS materials are flammable above 30% oxygen.
quote: Further, many commonly used ISS materials are flammable above 30% O2.
source_title: Impacts of Reduced Pressure Atmospheres on Environmental Control and Life Support Systems (ECLSS) Architectures

topic: data_gap
claim: NASA has flammability data for many materials at 30% oxygen, but limited data above that level.
quote: NASA has data for many materials in a 30% O2 environment, but limited material flammability data above this O2 limit.
source_title: Impacts of Reduced Pressure Atmospheres on Environmental Control and Life Support Systems (ECLSS) Architectures

topic: pressure
claim: Saffire found that reducing pressure slows down the flame spread.
quote: found that reducing pressure slows down the flame spread
source_title: Science in Space: Week of Sept. 29, 2023 - Fire Safety in Space

topic: partial_gravity
claim: Modeling, supported by parabolic-flight and ISS experiments, suggests that materials may burn at lower oxygen concentrations in lunar gravity than on Earth.
quote: Previous computational modeling, bolstered by experiments aboard parabolicflight aircraft and the ISS, suggest that materials may burn at lower oxygen concentrations in lunar gravity compared to Earth.
source_title: Flammability of Materials on the Moon (FM2)

topic: partial_gravity
claim: The challenge page states that PSI currently holds no partial-gravity combustion data.
quote: there is currently no partial-gravity combustion data available in PSI
source_title: Flame in Freefall (NASA Space Apps Challenge 2026, challenge page)

topic: partial_gravity
claim: The challenge page says microgravity and normal-gravity results could bound intermediate gravity levels; it does not say this is demonstrated.
quote: Microgravity and normal-gravity results could bound what occurs at intermediate gravity levels.
source_title: Flame in Freefall (NASA Space Apps Challenge 2026, challenge page)

topic: exploration_atmosphere
claim: Saffire samples were also burned at 8.2 psia and 34% oxygen to simulate the atmosphere of deep space exploration vehicles.
quote: In addition, the samples were burned at 8.2 psia and 34% oxygen levels to simulate atmosphere conditions for deep space exploration vehicles.
source_title: Spacecraft Fire Safety (Saffire)

topic: exploration_atmosphere
claim: The exploration atmosphere helps spacewalks but brings the challenge of fire management at higher-than-normal oxygen.
quote: Unfortunately, the benefits of EA in support of safe and efficient EVAs comes with the challenge of fire management in a higher-than-normal O
source_title: Moon to Mars (M2M): Exploration Atmosphere

topic: detector_response
claim: Spacecraft fire detection has to target the early phase of a fire: pyrolysis products rather than soot.
quote: Given the constrained space on any spacecraft, the target for the fire detection system is necessarily the early phase and not established flaming fires; consequently, the primary target for detection is pyrolysis products rather than soot.
source_title: Smoke Aerosol Measurement Experiment (SAME), NASA fact sheet

topic: smoke_particles
claim: In SAME, all samples produced many sub-micron particles, better detected by an ionization detector; a light-scattering detector would perform very well for most of the cases.
quote: All samples produced significant numbers of sub-micron particulate that are better detected using an ionization smoke detector, however a light scattering detector would perform very well for most of the cases.
source_title: Smoke Aerosol Measurement Experiment (SAME), NASA fact sheet

topic: detector_response
claim: ISS smoke detectors use near-infrared forward scattering and are most sensitive to particles larger than 1 µm.
quote: The International Space Station (ISS) smoke detectors use near-IR forward scattering, rendering them most sensitive to particles larger than 1 µm, outside of the range of sensitivity of the shuttle detector.
source_title: Smoke Aerosol Measurement Experiment (SAME), NASA fact sheet

topic: smoke_particles
claim: Smoke particles that form in microgravity can be larger than those formed on Earth.
quote: smoke particles that form in microgravity can be larger than those formed on Earth.
source_title: Dust and Aerosol Measurement Feasibility Test (DAFT), NASA fact sheet

topic: flame_shape
claim: On the space station, low-momentum flames tend to be rounded or even spherical.
quote: In microgravity, this flow doesn't occur and on the space station, low-momentum flames tend to be rounded or even spherical.
source_title: Studying Combustion and Fire Safety

topic: no_visible_flame
claim: FLEX led to the discovery of a cool flame: the fuel kept burning under certain conditions after the visible flame went out.
quote: FLEX, which analyzed the effectiveness of fire suppressants, led to the discovery of a type of cool flame, where the fuel continued "burning" under certain conditions after extinction of the visible flame.
source_title: Studying Combustion and Fire Safety

topic: no_visible_flame
claim: Cool flames produce carbon monoxide and formaldehyde, where typical flames produce carbon dioxide and water.
quote: Typical flames produce carbon dioxide and water, but cool flames produce carbon monoxide and formaldehyde.
source_title: Studying Combustion and Fire Safety

topic: suppressant_application
claim: On Earth, an extinguisher generally works best when it attacks the base of the flame.
quote: On Earth it is understood that the best results are generally obtained when the extinguisher "attacks" the base of the flame, which is both the stabilization point and the point where fresh air first enters the flame.
source_title: Burning and Suppression of Solids (BASS), NASA fact sheet

topic: suppressant_application
claim: A suppressant stream may be ineffective or may even make the flame worse by entraining oxygen.
quote: it is possible that the suppressant stream will be ineffective or might actually make the flame worse through the entrainment of oxygen
source_title: Burning and Suppression of Solids (BASS), NASA fact sheet

topic: suppressant_application
claim: Local application of suppressant is not adequate to extinguish the flame: the local jet entrains air and sustains the flame even with the ambient airflow off.
quote: Also, current findings show that local application of suppressant is not adequate for flame extinguishment. The local jet entrains air and sustains the flame even when the ambient airflow is turned off.
source_title: A Researcher's Guide to: Combustion Science

topic: suppressant_application
claim: Extinguishing methods used on the ground could be ineffective in space or even make the flame worse.
quote: Putting out fires in space must consider flame geometry, characteristics of the materials, and methods used to extinguish it, because methods used on the ground could be ineffective or even make the flame worse.
source_title: Studying Combustion and Fire Safety

topic: suppressant_agent
claim: Terrestrial standards for inert-gas suppressants do not offer the same margin of safety in low gravity as in normal gravity.
quote: The implication is that terrestrial standards for inert gas suppressants in low gravity do not offer the same margin of safety as in normal gravity.
source_title: A Researcher's Guide to: Combustion Science

topic: battery
claim: A battery in thermal runaway is a self-propagating combustion event; displacing oxygen is no longer enough to extinguish it.
quote: When a battery goes into thermal run-away, it becomes a self-propagating combustion event and displacing oxygen is no longer a sufficient means by which to extinguish the event.
source_title: Evolution of Hardware and Philosophy of Emergency Response Actions on the International Space Station and Future Spacecrafts

topic: comm_delay
claim: On a Mars mission the communication delay is up to 20 minutes one way.
quote: Facing a communication delay of up to 20 minutes one way
source_title: Hazard: Distance From Earth

topic: comm_delay
claim: On a Mars mission the round-trip communication delay is up to 40 minutes.
quote: On a mission to Mars, the crew will experience roundtrip communication delays up to 40 minutes
source_title: Effects of Communication Delay on Human Spaceflight Missions

topic: flame_spread
claim: Two Saffire-II silicone samples that burned completely in the 1-g test show a burn length of about 0 in microgravity.
source_title: Spacecraft Fire Experiment-II, PSI experimental table

topic: flame_spread
claim: The Saffire-II SIBAL sample burned 29 cm in microgravity; the 1-g test burned the whole sample.
source_title: Spacecraft Fire Experiment-II, PSI experimental table

topic: Inert gas choice changes cool-flame extinction: helium ends it early, xenon prolongs it
claim: ISS droplet tests found that diluent choice changes cool-flame behavior.
quote: Different diluents were observed to exert remarkably different influences on the cool-flame combustion of fuel droplets.
source_title: Effects of Ambient Inert Gas Properties on Cool-Flame Combustion of Normal-Alkane Droplets in Microgravity

topic: 75% helium: hot flame died in a fraction of a second, brief cool flame followed
claim: In FLEX-2 test R707, a brief cool flame followed hot-flame extinction.
quote: The hot flame that formed during the ignition dies within a fraction of a second and the cool flame burning commences immediately which also ends quickly leaving the droplet to evaporate.
source_title: Cool-flame Extinction During N-Alkane Droplet Combustion in Microgravity

topic: hot material keeps releasing fuel vapor after extinction
claim: Hot PMMA can keep supplying fuel after flame extinction.
quote: After extinction, the hot material can continue to produce fuel for some time until it cools.
source_title: Burning and Suppression of Solids-II (BASS-II) Summary Report, NASA/TM-20210011385

topic: burning without airflow
claim: Preliminary BRE results describe quasi-steady emulated burning corresponding to materials such as PMMA and Nylon in microgravity without air flow, with continued burning in elevated oxygen and short-time self-extinction at 21% oxygen.
quote: Quasi-steady burning corresponding to various condensed-phase materials (such as PMMA and Nylon) was observed in microgravity despite the absence of air flow, where the cessation of ventilation is an established step in putting out spacecraft fires. The ongoing combustion without air flow was notably seen in elevated-oxygen atmospheres which are being considered for use in future spacecraft, whereas such flames in a normal atmosphere of 21% oxygen self-extinguished in a short time. While BRE’s results are still preliminary, they suggest that NASA may want to increase use of its alternative flammability Test 2, with the cone calorimeter, where that test can measure material properties corresponding to the microgravity flames observed with the BRE burner.
source_title: ACME/BRE Final Report (2022)

topic: oxygen limit in still atmosphere
claim: In BRE, low-momentum microgravity flames could burn for minutes without air flow, but self-extinguished below about 25% oxygen by volume. At elevated oxygen, larger flames generally self-extinguished within 1.5 minutes, and methane flames within a minute, while smaller or ethylene flames could burn for minutes.
quote: Low-momentum microgravity flames can burn for minutes in the absence of an air flow or flame spread. While the flames can burn for minutes in elevated oxygen concentrations, like those being considered for future spacecraft, they were found to self-extinguish in concentrations below ~25% (by volume). While smaller flames can burn for minutes at elevated oxygen concentrations, larger flames were generally seen to self-extinguish within 1.5 minutes. While ethylene flames at elevated oxygen concentrations can burn for minutes, methane flames were seen to self-extinguish within a minute.
source_title: Recent Research on Flames of Gaseous Fuel Aboard the International Space Station

topic: normal atmosphere versus elevated oxygen
claim: BRE reports continued combustion without air flow in elevated-oxygen atmospheres, versus short-time self-extinction at 21% oxygen; the source explicitly calls the results preliminary.
quote: The ongoing combustion without air flow was notably seen in elevated-oxygen atmospheres which are being considered for use in future spacecraft, whereas such flames in a normal atmosphere of 21% oxygen self-extinguished in a short time. While BRE’s results are still preliminary, they suggest that NASA may want to increase use of its alternative flammability Test 2, with the cone calorimeter, where that test can measure material properties corresponding to the microgravity flames observed with the BRE burner.
source_title: ACME/BRE Final Report (2022)

topic: oxygen limit in still atmosphere
claim: All BRE flames ignited in a normal atmosphere self-extinguished within 40 s, while oxygen mole fractions of 0.265 and above gave quasi-steady flames.
quote: All flames ignited in normal atmosphere self-extinguished within 40 s. In contrast, oxygen mole fractions of 0.265 and above resulted in quasi-steady flames.
source_title: ACME/BRE Final Report (2022)

topic: oxygen as the dominant factor
claim: Quasi-steady burning on a flat surface can exist in microgravity, and ambient oxygen mole fraction plays the most significant role in whether it does.
quote: It is found out that quasi-steady burning on a flat surface, representing a pool fire, can exist in microgravity. Ambient oxygen mole fraction plays the most significant role in this regard.
source_title: ACME/BRE Final Report (2022)

topic: exploration atmosphere 34% oxygen at 8.2 psia
claim: In a NASA proposed nominal atmosphere of 34% oxygen and 0.56 atm, a BRE flame appeared to be steady after about 100 s.
quote: Figure 9. Flame growth from ignition to steady state in test 19070D1. The conditions are ethylene/N2, hc = 24 kJ/g, 4.95 g/m2s, 34% O2, 8.2 psia, L = 2.42 kJ/g, steady. Figure 9 shows steady results for a NASA proposed nominal atmosphere of 34% oxygen and 0.56 atm. After about 100 s the flame appears to be steady.
source_title: ACME/BRE Final Report (2022)

topic: exploration atmosphere 26.5% oxygen at 10.2 psia
claim: Test 19070K1, with ethylene/nitrogen at 26.5% oxygen, 10.2 psia and 2.3 g/m2s, grew from ignition to a steady state.
quote: Figure 7. Flame growth from ignition to steady state in test 19070K1. The conditions are ethylene/N2, hc = 24 kJ/g, 2.3 g/m2s, 26.5% O2, 10.2 psia, L = 3.0 kJ/g, steady.
source_title: ACME/BRE Final Report (2022)

topic: self-extinction case at 10.2 psia
claim: Test 19056F1, with ethylene/nitrogen at 27% oxygen, 10.2 psia and 4.55 g/m2s, went from ignition to self-extinction at 45 s.
quote: Figure 6. Flame growth from ignition to self-extinction in test 19056F1. The conditions are ethylene/N2, hc = 24 kJ/g, 4.55 g/m2s, 27% O2, 10.2 psia, L = 0.66 kJ/g, extinction at 45 s.
source_title: ACME/BRE Final Report (2022)

topic: common plastic in exploration atmospheres
claim: The BRE report interprets an emulation with heat of combustion about 24 kJ/g and heat of gasification about 3 kJ/g as potentially representing PMMA, suggesting that a common plastic could burn steadily under the proposed atmospheres discussed there.
quote: This emulation corresponds to a material with a heat of combustion of about 24 kJ/g and a heat of gasification of about 3 kJ/g. As such it could represent PMMA as a material solid. This is a profound result indicating a common plastic could steadily burn under these NASA proposed atmospheric conditions.
source_title: ACME/BRE Final Report (2022)

topic: material property range that burns
claim: From its emulation findings, the BRE report infers that solid materials with heats of combustion from 23.6 to 47.2 kJ/g and heats of gasification from about 1 to 10 kJ/g can burn in microgravity.
quote: One important fire safety consideration, based on the findings of this study, is that solid materials with heats of combustion in the range 23.6 to 47.2 kJ/g and heats of gasification from about 1 to 10 kJ/g can burn in microgravity.
source_title: ACME/BRE Final Report (2022)

topic: burning rates of named plastics
claim: The BRE flammability map suggests polyethylene and polypropylene would burn in microgravity at about 3 g/m2s, Nylon and PMMA at about 2.5 g/m2s, and a phenolic glass fiber composite at about 1 g/m2s.
quote: Figure 14 would suggest that polyethylene (PE) and polypropylene (PP) would burn in microgravity at about 3 g/m2s. Nylon and PMMA would burn at about 2.5 g/m2s, and the phenolic glass fiber composite would burn at about 1 g/m2s.
source_title: ACME/BRE Final Report (2022)

topic: fuel chemistry and burn time
claim: Methane/nitrogen BRE flames self-extinguished within a minute in every ambient condition tested, which indicates that burn time depends on fuel chemistry.
quote: Methane nitrogen-generated flames self-extinguished within a minute for all ambient conditions. That indicates that the burn time depends on the fuel chemistry.
source_title: ACME/BRE Final Report (2022)

topic: flame size and self-extinction
claim: At elevated oxygen concentrations smaller BRE flames could burn for minutes, while larger flames generally self-extinguished within 1.5 minutes.
quote: While smaller flames can burn for minutes at elevated oxygen concentrations, larger flames were generally seen to self-extinguish within 1.5 minutes.
source_title: Recent Research on Flames of Gaseous Fuel Aboard the International Space Station

topic: two extinction limits
claim: Large BRE flames extinguished because of radiative heat loss, while small flames quenched at a second limit.
quote: Large flames extinguished due to radiative heat loss, while small flames quenched at a second limit.
source_title: ACME/BRE Final Report (2022)

topic: extinction temperature
claim: Thin filament pyrometry of four BRE flames gave a critical temperature range for extinction of 1100 to 1200 K.
quote: TFP measurements of four flames confirmed that critical temperature range for extinction is 1100 to 1200 K. This is confirmed by numerical simulations.
source_title: ACME/BRE Final Report (2022)

topic: radiative heat loss
claim: The radiative loss fraction of the microgravity BRE flames can reach about 60%, compared with 30% for normal-gravity flames.
quote: Radiative loss fraction for the flames in microgravity can reach about 60% compared to 30% for the normal gravity flames.
source_title: ACME/BRE Final Report (2022)

topic: soot-free dim flames
claim: Ethylene flames, which tend to soot in normal gravity, did not soot in microgravity on the BRE burner: soot appeared only at ignition and disappeared quickly.
quote: Ethylene flames, which tend to soot under normal gravity conditions, did not soot under microgravity conditions. Sooting only occurred upon ignition and disappeared quickly after ignition.
source_title: ACME/BRE Final Report (2022)

topic: dim blue flame
claim: In a BRE test video the soot seen at ignition quickly fades away and leaves a dim blue flame.
quote: Initially, the flame behavior is similar to previous BRE tests. The flame is very sooty at ignition, due to ethylene's double bond, where you can see the glowing soot particles pass through the flame. But the soot quickly fades away leaving a dim blue flame, where blue is the natural color of hydrocarbon flames.
source_title: ACME/BRE Final Report (2022)

topic: flame hole and re-establishment
claim: In the described BRE test, a thickening cloud of carbon dioxide and water vapor inhibited oxygen diffusion; radiative heat loss opened a hole in the weakened flame, after which oxygen mixed with fuel and the flame reestablished.
quote: Meanwhile, the flame is blanketed by a thickening cloud of carbon dioxide and water vapor inhibiting the oxygen's diffusion to the flame. With the poor oxygen transport, the flame weakens, and radiative heat loss leaves a hole in the flame. But oxygen then mixes with the fuel, causing the flame to quickly reestablish and the hole closes.
source_title: ACME/BRE Final Report (2022)

topic: pressure effect
claim: Ambient pressure had a weak effect on the quality of burning in BRE, but it affects radiative heat loss by changing the partial pressures of the radiating species H2O and CO2.
quote: Although ambient pressure has a weak effect on the quality of burning, it affects radiative heat loss by changing the partial pressures of radiating species, i.e., H2O and CO2.
source_title: ACME/BRE Final Report (2022)

topic: pressure and oxygen in the theoretical map
claim: The BRE theoretical flammability map indicates that lower pressure and higher oxygen concentration are favorable conditions for long-duration burning.
quote: Moreover, the flammability map based on our theoretical analysis is shown in Figure 17. It shows similar asymptotic trend and clearly indicates lower pressure and higher oxygen concentration as favorable conditions for long duration burning.
source_title: ACME/BRE Final Report (2022)

topic: carbon dioxide atmospheres not tested
claim: Burning in O2/CO2 ambients, a desired BRE objective, is named as a good candidate for a follow-on experiment because CO2 is used in spacecraft fire extinguishers.
quote: A study of the burning behavior in an ambient of O2/CO2 (the desired objective) is a good candidate for a follow-on experiment because of the utility of CO2 in spacecraft fire extinguishers.
source_title: ACME/BRE Final Report (2022)

topic: flammability test methods
claim: The preliminary BRE results suggest NASA may want to make more use of its alternative flammability Test 2, the cone calorimeter, which can measure material properties corresponding to the microgravity flames seen with the BRE burner.
quote: While BRE’s results are still preliminary, they suggest that NASA may want to increase use of its alternative flammability Test 2, with the cone calorimeter, where that test can measure material properties corresponding to the microgravity flames observed with the BRE burner.
source_title: ACME/BRE Final Report (2022)

topic: limits of current material tests
claim: The BRE science requirements say Test 1 and Test 2 cannot directly predict spacecraft material fire hazards, while also stating that Test 2 can measure heats of combustion and gasification and surface reradiation.
quote: Currently NASA Test 1 and Test 2 are incapable of directly analyzing material fire hazards in spacecraft. There is no predictive methodology to extrapolate from these tests. However, NASA Test 2, the Cone Calorimeter, is capable of determining heats of combustion and gasification, and surface reradiation in burning.
source_title: ACME/BRE Final Report (2022)

topic: time needed to reach quasi-steady burning
claim: The cited BRE assessment says limited drop-facility testing cannot establish quasi-steady conditions because characteristic response times are about 20 s for the gas phase and about 40 s for burner surface temperature.
quote: While limited testing is possible in drop facilities, the characteristic times for the gas phase (approximately 20 s) and the burner surface temperature (approximately 40 s) preclude consideration of quasi-steady conditions.
source_title: ACME/BRE Final Report (2022)

topic: drop tower flames not steady
claim: A transient analysis compared with a 5 s BRE drop test estimated the flame height at about 37% of steady state after 5 seconds for the illustrated case.
quote: For the particular case shown in Figure 2a, the flame height reaches only about 37% of steady state after 5 seconds.
source_title: Emulation of Condensed Fuel Flames Using a Burning Rate Emulator (BRE) in Microgravity

topic: soot production in microgravity
claim: Soot volume fraction measurements indicate that microgravity coflow flames contain five to eight times more soot than the equivalent normal-gravity flames.
quote: Soot volume fraction measurements indicate that microgravity ﬂames contain ﬁve to eight times more soot than the equivalent normal gravity ﬂames.
source_title: Advanced Combustion via Microgravity Experiments (ACME) fact sheet

topic: flame shape and temperature
claim: For sooty flames, microgravity coflow flames are taller, wider, cooler and far sootier than in normal gravity.
quote: For sooty ﬂames, results show that the absence of gravity can have a major eﬀect. Flames are taller, wider, cooler, and far sootier in microgravity as compared to normal gravity.
source_title: Advanced Combustion via Microgravity Experiments (ACME) fact sheet

topic: dilution limits extended
claim: Dilution limits for both methane and ethylene coflow flames were extended in microgravity: the flames are more stable and stay lifted at lower fuel concentrations.
quote: Meanwhile, dilution limits for both methane and ethylene flames were extended in microgravity, where the microgravity flames are more stable, allowing for lifted flames at lower fuel concentrations.
source_title: Recent Research on Flames of Gaseous Fuel Aboard the International Space Station

topic: faint diluted flames
claim: When the fuel is diluted with nitrogen the soot disappears and the flame can lift off the burner and appear as a faint blue cone; with more dilution it becomes a flat disk and finally extinguishes.
quote: When the fuel is diluted with an inert gas (nitrogen in our case), the soot disappears and the ﬂame can lift oﬀ the burner surface and appear as a faint blue cone. With increased dilution, the ﬂame becomes a ﬂat disk, and ﬁnally extinguishes.
source_title: Advanced Combustion via Microgravity Experiments (ACME) fact sheet

topic: no buoyant rise
claim: Comparing coflow flames in normal gravity and microgravity shows a striking difference: without buoyancy, hot gases no longer rise.
quote: However, comparison of the ﬂames under normal gravity and microgravity conditions shows a striking diﬀerence (in microgravity, the absence of buoyancy means hot gases no longer rise).
source_title: Advanced Combustion via Microgravity Experiments (ACME) fact sheet

topic: SLICE precursor: flame length
claim: In SLICE, the ISS precursor to CLD Flame, computed and measured nonbuoyant methane flames were noticeably longer than their 1g counterparts, and flame length was proportional to the fuel mass flow rate.
quote: Buoyant and nonbuoyant luminous flame lengths are proportional to the mass flow rate of the fuel mixture; computed and measured nonbuoyant flames are noticeably longer than their 1g counterparts; the effect of fuel dilution on flame shape (i.e., flame length and flame radius) is negligible when the flame shape is normalized by the methane flow rate.
source_title: A Computational and Experimental Study of Coflow Laminar Methane/Air Diffusion Flames: Effects of Fuel Dilution, Inlet Velocity, and Gravity

topic: weak flames stabilized by small electric fields
claim: Very weak, low fuel concentration flames were stabilized at ignition with very small electric fields; without the fields they would quickly quench.
quote: The very weak low fuel concentration flames were stabilized at ignition with very small electric fields, where without the fields the flames would quickly quench. This stabilizing feature of electric fields for weak zero gravity flames was a surprise, and it suggests that electric fields may be a good tool for approximating buoyancy body forces at partial gravity.
source_title: ACME/E-FIELD Flames Final Report (2019), dated 10 April 2021

topic: electric field as a stand-in for partial gravity
claim: The stabilizing effect of electric fields on weak zero-gravity flames suggests that electric fields may be a good tool for approximating buoyancy body forces at partial gravity.
quote: This stabilizing feature of electric fields for weak zero gravity flames was a surprise, and it suggests that electric fields may be a good tool for approximating buoyancy body forces at partial gravity.
source_title: ACME/E-FIELD Flames Final Report (2019), dated 10 April 2021

topic: stabilization at high dilution without coflow
claim: The electric field can stabilize the microgravity diffusion flame at very high dilution, especially when there is no coflowing air.
quote: Among other effects, the results show that the electric field can stabilize the microgravity diffusion flame at very high dilution conditions, especially when there is no coflowing air.
source_title: ACME/E-FIELD Flames Final Report (2019), dated 10 April 2021

topic: blow out by electric field
claim: Under some conditions the electric field was able to blow out flames.
quote: The electric field was also able to blow out flames under some conditions.
source_title: ACME/E-FIELD Flames Final Report (2019), dated 10 April 2021

topic: soot in microgravity
claim: Sooting is far more significant in microgravity flames than in similar conditions with 1-g flames.
quote: Sooting is far more significant in flames in microgravity than is seen in similar conditions with 1-g flames.
source_title: ACME/E-FIELD Flames Final Report (2019), dated 10 April 2021

topic: unpredictable sooty flames in a field
claim: In the E-FIELD Flames results, electric fields acting on sooty flames produced unpredictable behavior, including soot elimination apparently through enhanced mixing, luminous particles likely to be incandescent soot agglomerates, and unstable dancing flames.
quote: When soot is present in a flame, electric fields create a wide range of unpredictable behaviors that include elimination of the soot through what appears to be enhanced mixing for combustion, showers of luminous particles that are likely to be incandescent soot agglomerates, and unstable dancing flames.
source_title: ACME/E-FIELD Flames Final Report (2019), dated 10 April 2021

topic: corona and arc discharge
claim: Jet flames were unstable at high field strengths and experienced corona and then arc discharges because of the large field concentration near the jet burner tip.
quote: Jet flames under the influence of the electric field were unstable at high field strengths, and these flames experienced corona and then arc discharges due to the large field concentration near the jet burner tip. The flame behavior was dramatic but difficult to characterize, suggesting a spatially- and time-varying field/flame interaction.
source_title: ACME/E-FIELD Flames Final Report (2019), dated 10 April 2021

topic: ion current as a flame signal
claim: In microgravity the voltage-current curve shows no distinctive saturation plateau; the flames show a distinct peak ion current that corresponds to the most compact flame.
quote: The behavior of the V-I curve is distinctly different in microgravity as compared to 1-g flames, where in microgravity there is not a distinctive saturation ion current plateau but rather the flames exhibit a distinct peak ion current that corresponds to the most compact flame.
source_title: ACME/E-FIELD Flames Final Report (2019), dated 10 April 2021

topic: ion current tracks combustion intensity
claim: The E-FIELD Flames report finds correlations between luminosity, combustion intensity and ion current, and suggests that the most robust burning produces the highest ion current even when the flame is most compact.
quote: There are clear correlations between flame luminosity, combustion intensity, and ion current. The results suggest that the most robust burning also produces the highest ion current, even though the flame is most compact.
source_title: ACME/E-FIELD Flames Final Report (2019), dated 10 April 2021

topic: field strength that removes soot
claim: Soot decreased as the negative field strength increased and disappeared at 0.80 kV/cm.
quote: The soot reduces with increasing negative field strength, and it disappears at 0.80 kV/cm (Fig. 19) along the parabolic decay line after passing the ion current peak.
source_title: ACME/E-FIELD Flames Final Report (2019), dated 10 April 2021

topic: critical extinction temperature and mass flux
claim: For the ISS flames in its reported extinction analysis, Flame Design gives a critical extinction temperature of 1130 K, with fuel mass flux of 0.2 g/m2-s for normal flames and oxygen mass flux of 0.68 g/m2-s for inverse flames.
quote: All the ISS flames observed by this project extinguish at a critical extinction temperature of 1130 K, and at a fuel mass flux of 0.2 g/m2-s for normal flames, and at an oxygen mass flux of 0.68 g/m2-s for inverse flames.
source_title: ACME/Flame Design Final Report (2023)

topic: steady flames despite radiative loss
claim: Steady-state gaseous microgravity spherical diffusion flames can exist despite radiation heat loss, provided the steady-state flame is smaller than the size for radiative extinction and it develops fast enough that its temperature does not drop below 1130 K.
quote: It is found that steady- state gaseous microgravity spherical diffusion flames can exist in the presence of radiation heat loss, provided that the steady-state flame size is less than the flame size for radiative extinction, and the flame develops fast enough that radiation heat loss does not drop the flame temperature below the critical temperature for radiative extinction (1130 K).
source_title: ACME/Flame Design Final Report (2023)

topic: longest steady flame
claim: Flames showing steady-state behavior were observed aboard the ISS for up to 870 s.
quote: Despite a narrow range of attainable conditions, flames that exhibit steady-state behavior are observed aboard the ISS for up to 870 s, even with the constraint of a finite boundary.
source_title: ACME/Flame Design Final Report (2023)

topic: oscillation before extinction
claim: Before complete extinction a spherical flame may enter an oscillatory mode in which part of the flame extinguishes and then reforms, with oscillations growing until complete extinction.
quote: Before a flame experiences complete extinction, it may enter an oscillatory mode in which part of the flame partially extinguishes and then reforms. The oscillations grow in magnitude until complete extinction.
source_title: ACME/Flame Design Final Report (2023)

topic: radiative extinction mechanism
claim: Radiative extinction is observed when, at constant reactant flow rate, the flame expands until radiation heat loss approaches the chemical heat release.
quote: Radiative extinction is observed when, at constant reactant flow rate, a flame expands until radiation heat loss approaches the chemical heat release.
source_title: ACME/Flame Design Final Report (2023)

topic: flame size versus flow and oxygen
claim: In the normal-flame ISS tests, flame size increased with reactant flow rate and decreased with ambient oxygen concentration.
quote: As expected in the normal-flame ISS testing, the flame size increases with reactant flow rate and decreases with ambient oxygen concentration.
source_title: Recent Research on Flames of Gaseous Fuel Aboard the International Space Station

topic: burn times and flame growth
claim: In the reported Flame Design study, burn times ranged from 28 to 336 s, all flames grew monotonically after ignition, and peak gas temperature generally decreased with time.
quote: Burn times range from 28 –336 s. All flames grow monotonically after ignition. Peak gas temperature generally decreases with time.
source_title: ACME/Flame Design Final Report (2023)

topic: time to reach steady state
claim: In the spherical, infinite-domain configuration, the characteristic time for the diffusion-controlled system to effectively reach steady state is on the order of 100,000 s.
quote: In the spherical, infinite domain configuration, the characteristic time for the diffusion- controlled system to effectively reach steady-state is found to be on the order of 100,000 s.
source_title: ACME/Flame Design Final Report (2023)

topic: oxygen range tested
claim: For safety reasons the oxygen mole fraction limit for normal-flame tests was 40% and the ethylene mole fraction limit for inverse flames was 65%.
quote: In particular, for safety reasons, the O2 mole fraction limit for normal tests was 40% and the C2H4 mole fraction limit for inverse flames was 65%.
source_title: ACME/Flame Design Final Report (2023)

topic: soot and flame structure (drop tower precursor)
claim: In the DESI precursor tests described in the source, four spherical ethylene flames burned at 1.5 mg/sec in a still ambient at 1 atm; soot was suppressed entirely when nitrogen was supplied with the fuel, with convection direction having a smaller influence.
quote: These four flames burn ethylene (C2H4) at a rate of 1.5 mg/sec in a still ambient at a pressure of 1 atm. Several salient features of these flames are summarized in the table. In these flames, structure has a defining influence on soot production, with soot suppressed entirely when nitrogen is supplied with the fuel. Convection direction has a smaller influence, suppressing soot when convection is directed toward the oxidizer.
source_title: Flame Design: A Novel Approach Developed to Produce Clean, Efficient Diffusion Flames

topic: two extinction modes
claim: Nitrogen-diluted methane and ethylene spherical flames in air seem to show kinetic extinction at low flow rates and radiative extinction at high flow rates.
quote: Nitrogen-diluted methane and ethylene flames in air seem to demonstrate kinetic extinction at low flow rates (low system Da) and radiative extinction at high flow rates (high system Da). Such phenomena were not observed in our ground-based research, given the limited microgravity durations. Nevertheless, comparisons with computational simulations are needed to assess better the extinction behavior.
source_title: ACME/s-Flame Final Report (2021)

topic: flow window for a spherical ethylene flame
claim: For mixtures with 20-30% ethylene, spherical non-sooty flames established at 3 cc/s underwent kinetic extinction on ramp down before reaching 1 cc/s and radiative extinction on ramp up before reaching 8 cc/s.
quote: For mixtures with 20-30% C2H4 content, spherical non-sooty flames are established at 3 cc/s; and kinetic extinctions are observed during ramp down before reaching 1 cc/s. For the same mixtures, radiative extinctions are observed when the non-sooty flames are established at 3 cc/s and the flow rates are ramped up before reaching 8 cc/s.
source_title: ACME/s-Flame Final Report (2021)

topic: radiative extinction is common
claim: Radiative extinction was found to be a common event in s-Flame ISS testing; it had been predicted computationally but not observed before for these flame conditions.
quote: Surprisingly, radiative extinction has been found to be a common event in ISS testing, which was predicted computationally, but not observed previously for our flame conditions.
source_title: ACME/s-Flame Final Report (2021)

topic: no soot from ethylene flames
claim: Ethylene flames, which tend to soot in normal gravity, did not soot in microgravity in s-Flame; soot appeared only during forced ignition from the hot wire and soon dissipated.
quote: Ethylene flames which tend to soot under normal gravity conditions did not soot under microgravity conditions. Sooting only occurred during forced ignition from the hotwire, but soon dissipated.
source_title: ACME/s-Flame Final Report (2021)

topic: brightness is not strength
claim: Flame luminosity does not necessarily correspond with flame strength or combustion intensity.
quote: Flame luminosity does not necessarily correspond with flame strength (or combustion intensity).
source_title: ACME/s-Flame Final Report (2021)

topic: barely visible hydrogen flames
claim: Nitrogen-diluted hydrogen flames were very faint and barely visible, but thermocouples, radiometers and photomultiplier tubes made their presence obvious.
quote: These tests were conducted with nitrogen-diluted hydrogen fuel making the flames very faint. Even though the flames were barely visible, their presence was obvious due to the measurements of various instrumentation, including thermocouples, radiometers, and photomultiplier tubes.
source_title: ACME/s-Flame Final Report (2021)

topic: hydrogen flames missed by cameras
claim: Pure and diluted hydrogen flames were not apparent or hardly visible to the main data camera and the analog operations camera.
quote: A critical challenge for s-Flame was in imaging the pure hydrogen and diluted hydrogen flames, which were not apparent or hardly visible to the DataCam and analog operations camera.
source_title: ACME/s-Flame Final Report (2021)

topic: hydrogen flames did not self-extinguish
claim: Nitrogen-diluted hydrogen flames seemed to require very large sizes to self-extinguish; radiative extinction was not observed in the cases run despite lower hydrogen concentration, although kinetic extinction appeared during ramp down.
quote: Nitrogen-diluted hydrogen flames seem to need to be at very large characteristic sizes to self- extinguish. As such, radiative extinction was not observed for the cases run, despite lowering the H2 concentration. However, kinetic extinction during ramp down seem to be exhibited for hydrogen flames.
source_title: ACME/s-Flame Final Report (2021)

topic: flash and re-ignition before extinction
claim: In s-Flame test day 20132, with 25% hydrogen / 20% methane / 55% helium issuing into 21% oxygen / 79% helium, flames at 5-10 cc/s seemed to disappear and re-ignite with a flash before final extinction; the phenomenon was still under investigation.
quote: Test day 20132 examines helium-diluted fuel mixture of 25% H2 / 20% CH4 / 55% He issuing into an ambient of 21% O2 / 79% He. The high thermal conductivity of He drastically shifts the ignition parameters from that using N2 as inert in Round 1. The tests produced flames at 3-10 cc/s that expand outwardly quickly and extinguish. For 5-10 cc/s, the flames seemed to disappear and 're- ignite' with a "flash" before final extinction. We are currently investigating the flash phenomenon.
source_title: ACME/s-Flame Final Report (2021)

topic: elevated oxygen and ignition
claim: For the reported 30% hydrogen / 15% methane / 55% helium blend issuing into 30% oxygen / 70% helium, elevated oxygen facilitated ignition and reduced characteristic flame size; the 5-16.5 cc/s flames expanded to oscillatory radiative extinction.
quote: Test day 20142 investigates the fuel blend 30% H2 / 15% CH4 / 55% He issuing into 30% O2/ 70% He. Elevated oxygen ambient facilitates ignition and results in smaller characteristic flame size. For 5-16.5 cc/s flow rates, flames expand to wavy/oscillatory radiative extinction. Ramp down cases did not allow for assessment of kinetic extinction.
source_title: ACME/s-Flame Final Report (2021)

topic: dilution limit for methane at 30% oxygen
claim: Flames of 15% methane / 85% nitrogen ignited but extinguished soon after.
quote: For 15% CH4 / 85% N2, flames are ignited, but extinguish soon after.
source_title: ACME/s-Flame Final Report (2021)

topic: helium dilution
claim: Helium-diluted cases had shifted extinction limits compared with nitrogen-diluted cases, and ignition was severely affected by using helium as the diluent.
quote: Helium-diluted cases had shifted extinction limits with respect to the nitrogen-diluted cases. In general, kinetic extinction was difficult to observe for the conditions examined. Ignition was also severely affected by using He as diluent. More analyses are needed to assess instability near the flame limits, which was predicted to occur computationally.
source_title: ACME/s-Flame Final Report (2021)

topic: no ignition in 21% oxygen with helium
claim: In the reported s-Flame test-day-20164 case, ignition was not achieved in the 21% oxygen / 79% helium atmosphere for the ignition parameters used.
quote: Ignition is not achieved for tests conducted with 21% O2 / 79% He atmosphere, for the ignition parameters utilized.
source_title: ACME/s-Flame Final Report (2021)

topic: first spherical cool flames of gaseous fuel
claim: CFI-G observed spherical non-premixed cool flames burning gaseous fuels for the first time.
quote: New research conducted aboard the orbiting laboratory in June 2021 has now achieved another first for microgravity flame research. Data from tests conducted for the Cool Flames Investigation with Gases (CFI-G), sponsored by the ISS U.S. National Lab and National Science Foundation, show the presence of cool flames. While the flames created aboard station in 2012 burned liquid fuel, these new cool flames burned gaseous fuels. This was the first time spherical non-premixed cool flames have been observed burning gaseous fuels.
source_title: Cool Flames Created During a First for International Space Station Research

topic: conditions that gave cool flames
claim: Cool diffusion flames were not readily produced: they were obtained only for normal n-butane flames at 2 bar with an ambient oxygen mole fraction of 0.39.
quote: However, these CDFs were not readily produced and were only obtained for normal n-butane flames at 2 bar with an ambient oxygen mole fraction of 0.39.
source_title: ACME/CFI-G Final Report (2022)

topic: cool flames too faint to see
claim: Because cool flames give off little heat or light, they were too faint to be visible in real time during station testing; three cool flames were found afterwards in the thermal radiation and burner temperature data.
quote: Since cool flames give off little heat or light, they were too faint to be visible in real time during space station testing. The research team uncovered the presence of three cool flames in the data on thermal radiation and burner temperature measurements after the hot flames were quenched.
source_title: Cool Flames Created During a First for International Space Station Research

topic: cool flame after hot flame quenches
claim: In CFI-G imaging, the hot flame quenched, a comparatively dark period of roughly a second followed, and then a cool flame became evident.
quote: An intensified camera filtered to look for the very faint emissions of a cool flame produced the flame images above. As expected, the cool flame was much smaller than the hot flame. The sequence shows the quenching of the hot flame, followed by a comparatively dark period lasting roughly a second, after which the cool flame becomes evident.
source_title: Cool Flames Created During a First for International Space Station Research

topic: cool flame size
claim: The hot flames that spawned the cool diffusion flames were 2.6 times as large as the cool flames.
quote: However, these CDFs were not readily produced and were only obtained for normal n-butane flames at 2 bar with an ambient oxygen mole fraction of 0.39. The hot flames that spawned the CDFs were 2.6 times as large.
source_title: ACME/CFI-G Final Report (2022)

topic: cool flame temperature
claim: Cool diffusion flames have peak temperatures of 500 to 1000 K.
quote: Research into cool diffusion flames (whose peak temperatures are 500 – 1000 K) has grown exponentially since they were discovered in 2012.
source_title: ACME/CFI-G Final Report (2022)

topic: hot-flame reignition from a cool flame
claim: In the reported CFI-G tests, hot-flame reignition from cool flames was attributed to catalysis by platinum in the exposed type-B thermocouple closest to the burner.
quote: Unfortunately, an unwanted outcome was hot-flame reignition (from the cool flames) caused by catalysis from the platinum in the exposed type-B thermocouple closest to the burner. While temperature measurements were made, the cool flames on that additional day of testing were regrettably short-lived.
source_title: ACME/CFI-G Final Report (2022)

topic: repeated hot-to-cool transitions in one test
claim: PSI records normal-flame test 21291 C1 (30% butane, about 2.03 bar, oxygen mole fraction about 0.39) as having 5 transitions from hot to cool, with 6 hot and 5 cool flames in a 246 s burn.
quote: Normal,11,30% butane,21291 C1,"yes, PCI-F",0.394233062,0.389271344,2.0266,0.3,1,No,2652.186558,0.202014347,Yes,246,FT,435,"5 transitions from hot to cool, 6 hot and 5 cool flames"
source_title: PSI-159 Experimental table: PSI-159_Experimental table_CFI-G_Normal Flames.csv

topic: highest-oxygen tests (inverse flames)
claim: In CFI-G inverse-flame test 21222 A3, the table records propane, approximate pressure 3.3099 bar, burner oxidizer oxygen mole fraction 0.85, burn time 18 s and self-extinction (SE).
source_title: PSI-159 Experimental table: PSI-159_Experimental table_CFI-G_Inverse Flames.csv

topic: inverse flames are inside out
claim: The CFI-G inverse flames were run with the chamber filled with nitrogen and gaseous fuel while an oxygen/nitrogen mixture flowed from the burner, so the flames were effectively inside out, with soot forming outside the flame.
quote: The ISS operations for CFI-G were conducted from March to Oct. 2021 in two sequential rounds of testing. The two rounds occurred during Increments 64-65 and 65-66 and respectively featured normal and inverse flames. The inverse flame tests were conducted with the chamber filled with a mixture of nitrogen and gaseous fuel while an oxygen/nitrogen mixture flowed from the burner. As a result, the inverse flames were effectively inside out, e.g., where the soot formed outside rather than inside of the flames.
source_title: ACME/CFI-G Final Report (2022)

topic: what a spacecraft detector must look for
claim: On a spacecraft the fire detection system has to target the early phase of a fire, so the primary thing to detect is pyrolysis products, not soot.
quote: Given the constrained space on any spacecraft, the target for the fire detection system is necessarily the early phase and not established flaming fires; consequently, the primary target for detection is the pyrolysis products and not the soot.
source_title: Smoke Aerosol Measurement Experiment (SAME), Final Report, March 15, 2010 (PSI-102, Reports folder)

topic: Space Shuttle smoke detector alarm setting
claim: The Space Shuttle (STS) smoke detector as built was designed to alarm at a particle loading of 2 mg/m3 held for 5 seconds (based on 1 micron particles) or a rise of 0.022 mg/m3 per second held for 20 seconds.
quote: The STS detector as built was designed to alarm at a particle loading of 2 mg/m3 for 5 seconds (based on 1 micron particles) or a 0.022 mg/m3/s rise in concentration for 20 seconds
source_title: Smoke Aerosol Measurement Experiment (SAME), Final Report, March 15, 2010 (PSI-102, Reports folder)

topic: Space Shuttle detector rejects large particles
claim: The Shuttle detector used a pump and a particle separator that rejected particulate larger than 1 micrometer; its design assumed incipient fires show up as particulate in the 0.4 to 0.7 micrometer range.
quote: based their design on data that suggested incipient fires could be discriminated by looking for particulate in the 0.4 μm to 0.7 μm range.8 The use of a pump provided the opportunity to use a particle separator that rejected particulate larger than 1μm.
source_title: Smoke Aerosol Measurement Experiment (SAME), Final Report, March 15, 2010 (PSI-102, Reports folder)

topic: ISS smoke detector size sensitivity
claim: ISS smoke detectors are laser-diode forward-scattering detectors; their sensitivity extends down to 0.3 micrometer but is greatest for particles larger than 1 micrometer.
quote: The ISS detectors (Fig. 2) are laser-diode, forward-scattering, smoke or particulate detectors. The sensitivity extends down to 0.3 μm but is greatest for particles larger than 1 μm.
source_title: Smoke Aerosol Measurement Experiment (SAME), Final Report, March 15, 2010 (PSI-102, Reports folder)

topic: ISS smoke detector alarm setting
claim: The ISS detector was designed to alarm at 1% obscuration per foot.
quote: The ISS detector was designed to alarm at 1% obscuration per foot
source_title: Smoke Aerosol Measurement Experiment (SAME), Final Report, March 15, 2010 (PSI-102, Reports folder)

topic: ISS and Shuttle detectors see different particle sizes
claim: Because of their designs, the ISS detector and the Shuttle Orbiter detector have particle sensitivities that do not overlap.
quote: As a result of these design decisions, the ISS and the Orbiter detectors have particle sensitivities that do not overlap.
source_title: Smoke Aerosol Measurement Experiment (SAME), Final Report, March 15, 2010 (PSI-102, Reports folder)

topic: smoke particle sizes by material, fresh and aged
claim: SAME flight results (geometric mean diameter / arithmetic mean diameter / diameter of average mass, nm; geometric standard deviation). Unaged: Kapton 80/105/179 (2.08), lamp wick 186/227/341 (1.89), silicone 189/257/472 (2.18), Teflon 170/205/297 (1.84). Aged: Kapton 155/186/267 (1.82), lamp wick 258/308/438 (1.81), silicone 352/422/606 (1.83), Teflon 228/273/392 (1.82).
quote: Kapton 80 105 179 2.08 Kapton aged 155 186 267 1.82 Lamp wick 186 227 341 1.89 Lamp wick aged 258 308 438 1.81 Silicone 189 257 472 2.18 Silicone aged 352 422 606 1.83 Teflon 170 205 297 1.84 Teflon aged 228 273 392 1.82
source_title: Smoke Aerosol Measurement Experiment (SAME), Final Report, March 15, 2010 (PSI-102, Reports folder)

topic: a substantial portion of smoke particles is below 500 nm
claim: For the materials tested in SAME, a substantial portion of the smoke particles are below 500 nm in diameter.
quote: The experimental results show that, for the materials tested, a substantial portion of the smoke particles are below 500 nm in diameter.
source_title: Smoke Aerosol Measurement Experiment (SAME), Final Report, March 15, 2010 (PSI-102, Reports folder)

topic: silicone rubber smoke: small count mean, mass in large particles
claim: The report states that although the count mean diameter (CMD) for silicone rubber smoke is 189 nm, almost half of the particle mass is in particles larger than 1 micrometer, as shown by the ratio of the two DustTrak instruments; lamp wick behaves similarly. (Table 1 of the same report lists 189 nm as the geometric mean diameter of silicone smoke and 257 nm as its arithmetic mean.)
quote: Consequently, although the CMD for silicone rubber is 189 nm, almost half the particle mass is larger than 1 m, as evidenced by the ratio of the DustTrak instruments. The lamp wick shows similar behavior.
source_title: Smoke Aerosol Measurement Experiment (SAME), Final Report, March 15, 2010 (PSI-102, Reports folder)

topic: Teflon and Kapton smoke is hard for light scattering
claim: Kapton and Teflon gave small particles, which makes this smoke challenging for light-scattering devices, while lamp wick and silicone gave large particles and very large light-scattering signals; the report concludes that detecting all of these against the background needs a system that measures more than one moment of the size distribution.
quote: The small diameters for the Kapton and Teflon will make detection of this smoke challenging for light scattering devices, on the other hand the large sizes seen with the lamp wick and silicone would generate very large signals on a light scattering system, suggesting that detection of these particles against the background environment will require a detection system capable of measuring more than one moment of the particle size distribution.
source_title: Smoke Aerosol Measurement Experiment (SAME), Final Report, March 15, 2010 (PSI-102, Reports folder)

topic: ISS detector signal erratic for Teflon smoke
claim: In the Teflon run of figure 12 the Shuttle (STS) detector gave a strong signal while the ISS detector signal was more erratic, because Teflon smoke is mostly particles under 1 micrometer; the report takes this as showing that the two detectors respond to different particle size ranges.
quote: In figure 12, the STS detector provided a strong signal, whereas the signal from the ISS detector was more erratic, because the Teflon smoke is comprised primarily of particles having diameters less than 1 m, as mentioned above. This shows that the smoke detectors used in STS and ISS have different response to particle size range.
source_title: Smoke Aerosol Measurement Experiment (SAME), Final Report, March 15, 2010 (PSI-102, Reports folder)

topic: silicone rubber smoke triggers both detectors
claim: For silicone rubber smoke both the ISS detector and the STS detector showed strong signals.
quote: It is also interesting to compare the response of the ISS and STS detectors for silicone rubber and Teflon. In figure 11, both the ISS detector and the STS detectors show strong signals.
source_title: Smoke Aerosol Measurement Experiment (SAME), Final Report, March 15, 2010 (PSI-102, Reports folder)

topic: ionization detector responded in every SAME test
claim: Every test in the SAME series gave a strong signal on the Space Shuttle (ionization) detector, even for the larger particle size distributions of lamp wick (cellulose) and silicone rubber.
quote: All of the tests conducted in this series of experiments show strong signals on the Space Shuttle detector (ionization) despite the larger particle size distributions seen for the lamp wick (cellulose) and silicone rubber.
source_title: Smoke Aerosol Measurement Experiment (SAME), Final Report, March 15, 2010 (PSI-102, Reports folder)

topic: earlier CSD flight: ionization detector missed large-particle smoke
claim: The earlier Comparative Soot Diagnostics (CSD) experiment reported poor detection by the Space Shuttle detector for non-flaming overheating of cellulose and silicone rubber; the SAME report reads this as a sign that under some reasonable pre-fire conditions smoke can grow larger than the sizes seen in SAME.
quote: The CSD experiment5 reported poor detection by the Space Shuttle detector for non-flaming overheat of cellulose and silicone rubber (indicating larger particle sizes). The reduced signal on the Space Shuttle detector for CSD suggests that under some reasonable pre-fire conditions the smoke size distribution can extend to diameters beyond those seen in the SAME experiment.
source_title: Smoke Aerosol Measurement Experiment (SAME), Final Report, March 15, 2010 (PSI-102, Reports folder)

topic: aging: number falls, mass stays
claim: In a smoke aging run for silicone rubber the overall number count dropped substantially while the mass concentrations stayed relatively steady, consistent with particle coagulation with limited wall loss.
quote: Figure 13. Instrument traces for a typical smoke aging run for silicone rubber. Base levels are at the beginning and end of the trace. The first sampling interval is between 5200 and 5250 seconds and the post aging sampling interval is between 6000 and 6050 seconds. Consistent with particle coagulation with limited wall loss, the overall number count (Ptrak) decreases substantially while the mass concentrations (DustTraks) remain relatively steady.
source_title: Smoke Aerosol Measurement Experiment (SAME), Final Report, March 15, 2010 (PSI-102, Reports folder)

topic: size discrimination needed to reject dust
claim: Combining SAME with the earlier CSD experiment, the report concludes that detecting smoke across the observed size range while still discriminating against dust (which tends to be large) will probably require a detection system that can discriminate the particle size distribution at least to a limited degree.
quote: the detection of smoke across the size range seen in SAME and CSD, while still discriminating against dust (which tends to be large), will probably require a detection system that can discriminate the particle size distribution to at least a limited degree.
source_title: Smoke Aerosol Measurement Experiment (SAME), Final Report, March 15, 2010 (PSI-102, Reports folder)

topic: low-gravity smoke about 50% larger than normal gravity
claim: In the first SAME results, smoke particulate produced in low gravity was typically 50% larger in count mean diameter than under similar conditions in normal gravity, and all the resulting sizes were below 300 nm.
quote: Smoke particulate produced in low-gravity was found to be typically 50% large in count mean diameter than similar conditions in normal gravity. The resultant sizes were all below 300 nm
source_title: Smoke Aerosol Measurement Experiment (SAME), Final Report, March 15, 2010 (PSI-102, Reports folder)

topic: smoke transport in the cabin: mixing, longer detection lag
claim: The smoke transport model run for SAME showed that mixing dominates smoke transport, and that detection time lags are therefore longer than in normal gravity.
quote: The smoke transport model demonstrated that mixing dominates the smoke transport and that consequently detection time lags are longer than in normal gravity.
source_title: Smoke Aerosol Measurement Experiment (SAME), Final Report, March 15, 2010 (PSI-102, Reports folder)

topic: no ceiling layer: smoke mixes through the module
claim: In the zero-gravity simulation of the ISS US Lab, apart from a high-concentration zone near the source the smoke was fairly well mixed through the unobstructed region; in normal gravity smoke instead concentrates near the ceiling with less complete mixing.
quote: It is notable that other than the high concentration zone near the source, the smoke is fairly well mixed throughout the region without obstructions. The region with obstructions has lower smoke levels than the rest of the module. This scenario is substantially different from that seen in normal gravity where the smoke concentrates near the ceiling and mixing is generally not as complete as seen in Fig. 6.
source_title: Smoke Aerosol Measurement Experiment (SAME), Final Report, March 15, 2010 (PSI-102, Reports folder)

topic: ISS detector alarm point used in the model
claim: The transport model took the alarm point of the ISS detector to be on the order of 0.5 mg/m3.
quote: The alarm point for the ISS detector is on the order of 0.5 mg/m3.
source_title: Smoke Aerosol Measurement Experiment (SAME), Final Report, March 15, 2010 (PSI-102, Reports folder)

topic: obstructions lengthen smoke transit to the detector
claim: In the US Lab simulation, for smoke sources on the starboard side or zenith the obstructions had a strong impact, because the smoke took longer to reach the detector.
quote: For cases on the starboard or zenith, the obstructions had a strong impact due to the longer transit time of the smoke to the detector.
source_title: Smoke Aerosol Measurement Experiment (SAME), Final Report, March 15, 2010 (PSI-102, Reports folder)

topic: a weak smoke source may never trip an area detector
claim: In the US Lab smoke transport simulation a did-not-alarm condition occurred at 0.05 soot yield for two cases: a source at section LA1 on the N1 wall (detector at return register LAS5RR) and a source at LA3 on the S3 wall (detector at LAP1RR).
quote: Note that a DNA (did not alarm) condition occurred for LA1 for the 0.05 soot yield on the N1 wall for LAS5RR and for LA3 0.05 soot yield on the S3 wall for LAP1RR.
source_title: Smoke Aerosol Measurement Experiment (SAME), Final Report, March 15, 2010 (PSI-102, Reports folder)

topic: detection time depends on location
claim: Numerical modelling of smoke transport in the ISS US Lab predicted that actual detection times can be quite long and strongly dependent on location.
quote: modeling of smoke transport in the US Lab Module of the ISS predicted that actual detection times can be quite long and strongly dependent on location
source_title: Smoke Aerosol Measurement Experiment (SAME), Final Report, March 15, 2010 (PSI-102, Reports folder)

topic: gravity is not the main driver of smoke particle size
claim: Looking back at the SAME results, particle size depended strongly on material, flow conditions, gravity level, aging time at high concentration and heating rate; gravity was not the dominant cause of size variation, which allowed ground-based testing to supply most of the design data for smoke detection.
quote: The particle size distribution was a strong function of the overheated material composition; the flow conditions; gravity level; how long the smoke aged at high concentration, and the heating rate. Given the change in size due to the other parameters, the influence of gravity was not the dominant cause of size variation. This important result enabled the future use of ground-based testing to establish the bulk of the design data for smoke detection.
source_title: Fire Detection Tradeoffs as a Function of Vehicle Parameters (NTRS 20170000248, full text)

topic: diameter of average mass ranges by material
claim: In the SAME results, plastics such as Teflon and Kapton produced very small particles (100 to 250 nm diameter of average mass), which are harder to detect by light scattering, while silicone rubber and cellulose produced larger particles (250 to 620 nm diameter of average mass).
quote: plastics such as Teflon and Kapton produced very small particles (100- 250 nm diameter of average mass) which are more challenging to detect with light scattering systems whereas silicone rubber and cellulose (representing paper and clothing) produced substantially larger particles (250- 620 nm diameter of average mass).
source_title: Fire Detection Tradeoffs as a Function of Vehicle Parameters (NTRS 20170000248, full text)

topic: detector signal versus particle size
claim: Both current detection methods give more signal for larger particles: roughly linearly with size for ionization (Space Shuttle) and to the third power for light scattering (ISS).
quote: The current detection methods (ionization and light scattering) both show increased signal with increasing particle size with the increase roughly linear for ionization (Space Shuttle) and to the third power for light scattering (ISS).
source_title: Fire Detection Tradeoffs as a Function of Vehicle Parameters (NTRS 20170000248, full text)

topic: the hard part is small smoke without false alarms from large dust
claim: With smoke particle size varying by a factor of 6 and a varying dust background, the difficulty is not detecting the smallest particles but doing so without making the detector so sensitive to larger particles that the false alarm rate becomes unacceptable.
quote: This sensitivity to size change and the broad variation in smoke particle size (a factor of 6) coupled with a potentially widely varying background aerosol (e.g. dust) all contribute to challenging detector design criteria. The challenge lies not in detecting the smallest particles but rather in detecting them without making the detector so sensitive to larger particles that the false alarm rate is unacceptable.
source_title: Fire Detection Tradeoffs as a Function of Vehicle Parameters (NTRS 20170000248, full text)

topic: toxic gas can build up before the smoke alarm
claim: Results of a vehicle-level fire detection analysis suggest that hazardous gas species could accumulate to dangerous levels before a smoke alarm is triggered.
quote: These results suggest that hazardous gas species could accumulate to dangerous levels before a smoke alarm is triggered.
source_title: Fire Detection Tradeoffs as a Function of Vehicle Parameters (NTRS 20170000248, full text)

topic: HEPA filtration raises the smoke needed to alarm
claim: Because spacecraft life support often includes HEPA filtration that removes virtually all smoke particles, a relatively higher total amount of smoke must be released to reach alarm for a given smoke release rate.
quote: High Efficiency Particulate Air (HEPA) filtration which removes virtually all of the smoke particles. Given the existence of HEPA filtration systems, a relatively higher total amount of smoke must be released to achieve alarm for a given smoke release rate.
source_title: Fire Detection Tradeoffs as a Function of Vehicle Parameters (NTRS 20170000248, full text)

topic: thresholds must be vehicle specific
claim: The analysis concludes that spacecraft fire detection thresholds should not be based on terrestrial levels or on other spacecraft, but selected for the volume of the vehicle and its air filtration and ventilation systems.
quote: These results strongly suggest that spacecraft fire detection thresholds should not be based on terrestrial levels or on other spacecraft, but instead, need to be specifically selected based on the volume of the vehicle and the anticipated life support (air filtration and ventilation) systems.
source_title: Fire Detection Tradeoffs as a Function of Vehicle Parameters (NTRS 20170000248, full text)

topic: alarm time follows the airflow, not the distance
claim: NASA overview of detection challenges, citing a model of ventilation flow and detector response in ISS Destiny (Brooker et al. 2007): the proximity of the smoke source to the detector was an unreliable predictor of alarm time; alarm times were dictated by air flow patterns.
quote: Proximity of smoke source to detector was unreliable predictor of alarm time • Alarm times dictated by air flow patterns
source_title: An Overview of Smoke Detection and Spacecraft Fire Safety in Low Gravity (NTRS 20205008167, slides)

topic: ISS detector weak on Kapton and Teflon smoke
claim: A NASA summary of SAME key findings: the ISS forward light scattering detector had a diminished response to the smallest particles (Kapton and Teflon, under 300 nm).
quote: ISS forward light scattering detector had diminished response to smallest particles (Kapton and Teflon, <300 nm)
source_title: An Overview of Smoke Detection and Spacecraft Fire Safety in Low Gravity (NTRS 20205008167, slides)

topic: ionization detector slightly better on the smallest particles
claim: A NASA summary of SAME key findings: the ionization detector had a slightly better response to the smallest particles.
quote: Ionization detector had slightly better response to smallest particles
source_title: An Overview of Smoke Detection and Spacecraft Fire Safety in Low Gravity (NTRS 20205008167, slides)

topic: all tested materials made sub-micrometer smoke
claim: A NASA summary of SAME key findings: all tested fuels produced substantial PM1, and particle dynamics were dominated by factors other than gravity, for example changes in air flow altering coagulation rates.
quote: All tested fuels produced substantial PM1 • Particle dynamics predominated by factors other than gravity (e.g., changes in air flow alters coagulation rates)
source_title: An Overview of Smoke Detection and Spacecraft Fire Safety in Low Gravity (NTRS 20205008167, slides)

topic: smoke does not rise to the detector
claim: NASA lists as microgravity smoke detection challenges: detector placement (with no buoyancy smoke does not rise), plume dilution and slower propagation through the volume, which gives a fire the chance to grow before detection, and false alarms from background particles that do not settle.
quote: Challenges with detector placement (no buoyancy → smoke does not rise) • Plume dilution and slower propagation through volume→ opportunity for fire to grow prior to detection • False alarms from background particles (no gravitational settling)
source_title: An Overview of Smoke Detection and Spacecraft Fire Safety in Low Gravity (NTRS 20205008167, slides)

topic: lunar dust overlaps smoke sizes
claim: For lunar missions, NASA notes that Apollo lunar dust samples have a lognormal size distribution with modes of 100 to 200 nm, so telling smoke from dust by particle size could be challenging.
quote: lunar dust samples from Apollo missions have lognormal distribution, with modes 100-200 nm • Distinguishing smoke and dust particles for smoke detection based on size could be challenging
source_title: An Overview of Smoke Detection and Spacecraft Fire Safety in Low Gravity (NTRS 20205008167, slides)

topic: typical smoke particle size 200 to 400 nm
claim: In ISS tests of five spacecraft materials heated below the ignition point (the publication is listed in the PSI-101 SAME-R record), most of the average smoke particle sizes were in the 200 to 400 nanometer range; quiescent cases and cases with longer transport time typically gave substantially larger particles.
quote: Overall the majority of the average smoke particle sizes were found to be in the 200 to 400 nanometer range with the quiescent cases and the cases with increased transport time typically producing with substantially larger particles.
source_title: Evaluation of Low-Gravity Smoke Particulate for Spacecraft Fire Detection

topic: low-gravity smoke about twice the size of normal-gravity smoke
claim: Results varied between materials, but smoke particles produced in low gravity were typically twice the size of particles produced in normal gravity.
quote: The results varied between materials but the smoke particles produced in low gravity were typically twice the size of particles produced in normal gravity.
source_title: Evaluation of Low-Gravity Smoke Particulate for Spacecraft Fire Detection

topic: baseline particle diameters by material, fresh and aged 720 s
claim: SAME-R baseline runs (geometric mean / count mean / diameter of average mass, micrometers; geometric standard deviation). Unaged: Kapton 0.047/0.062/0.106 (2.072), lampwick 0.103/0.142/0.271 (2.232), silicone 0.152/0.221/0.468 (2.382), Teflon 0.093/0.111/0.173 (2.081), Pyrell 0.177/0.227/0.377 (2.032). Aged 720 s: Kapton 0.102/0.121/0.169 (1.790), lampwick 0.269/0.308/0.401 (1.673), silicone 0.320/0.400/0.628 (1.956), Teflon 0.080/0.115/0.237 (2.342), Pyrell 0.348/0.400/0.529 (1.697).
source_title: Smoke Aerosol Measurement Experiment Re-flight (SAMER), Final Report, June 2, 2014 (PSI-101, Reports folder)

topic: slow airflow gives larger smoke particles
claim: For Teflon, Kapton and lampwick, particle size plotted against duct velocity shows a strong trend of larger particles at low flow rates; the report concludes that smoke trapped in an avionics enclosure can be expected to be substantially larger than smoke released in ventilated areas.
quote: The results for Teflon, Kapton and lampwick are plotted versus duct velocity in figures 6, 7 and 8. These figures show a strong trend of increased particle size at low flow rates. This indicates that smoke trapped in an avionics enclosure can be expected to be substantially larger than smoke released in ventilated areas.
source_title: Smoke Aerosol Measurement Experiment Re-flight (SAMER), Final Report, June 2, 2014 (PSI-101, Reports folder)

topic: no airflow: diameter of average mass 30 to 40% larger
claim: For all materials the diameter of average mass was 30% to 40% larger in the zero-flow tests than in the tests with flow.
quote: It is found for all of the materials the diameter of average mass is 30 % to 40 % larger for the zero-flow tests compared to the flow tests.
source_title: Smoke Aerosol Measurement Experiment Re-flight (SAMER), Final Report, June 2, 2014 (PSI-101, Reports folder)

topic: no airflow: particles 2 to 3 times larger (report conclusions)
claim: The conclusions of the SAME-R final report state that the zero-flow conditions produced smoke particles 2 to 3 times larger than those produced at the nominal 8 cm/s flow rate.
quote: The zero flow conditions produced smoke particles that were 2 to 3 times larger than those produced at the nominal 8 cm/s flow rate.
source_title: Smoke Aerosol Measurement Experiment Re-flight (SAMER), Final Report, June 2, 2014 (PSI-101, Reports folder)

topic: still air in low gravity confines smoke near the source
claim: The report estimates that with zero flow in microgravity, transport is by molecular diffusion and thermal expansion: in 60 seconds the gases would diffuse on the order of 4 cm, which (assuming a cubical geometry) confines the smoke to about 64 cm3 instead of diluting it in the 6000 cm3 piston, so that, if the same number of particles is generated, the initial concentration is on the order of 50 times higher than with flow.
quote: The transport for the zero-flow case in μ-g is controlled by molecular diffusion and thermal expansion. Over a period of 60 seconds, the gases would diffuse a distance on the order of 4 cm. Assuming a cubical geometry this would correspond to the smoke being confined to a volume of about 64 cm3 rather than being diluted in the 6000 cm3 piston. If the same number of particles is generated as for the flow case, the initial concentration will be on the order of 50 times higher for the zero-flow case.
source_title: Smoke Aerosol Measurement Experiment Re-flight (SAMER), Final Report, June 2, 2014 (PSI-101, Reports folder)

topic: the stagnant large-particle case is unique to low gravity
claim: The report stresses that the zero-flow condition is unique to low gravity: at 1-g the buoyancy of the rising gases would greatly increase the mixing zone, so the larger particles seen at zero flow matter for the design of fire detection equipment for space vehicles.
quote: It is important to recognize that this condition is unique to low-gravity scenarios. If one performed the same experiment at 1-g, the buoyancy of the rising gases would greatly increase the mixing zone. So the larger particle diameters observed in these zero-flow conditions are important to consider in the development of improved fire detection equipment for space vehicles.
source_title: Smoke Aerosol Measurement Experiment Re-flight (SAMER), Final Report, June 2, 2014 (PSI-101, Reports folder)

topic: no airflow changes smoke morphology (Pyrell)
