claim: Pyrell smoke changed from fractal-like clusters of up to 30 primary spheres at 8 cm/s air flow to spherical particles at zero flow.
quote: the change in the morphology of the Pyrell smoke from fractal-like clusters with up to 30 primary spheres for the case with a flow of 8 cm/s to spherical particles for the zero-flow condition
source_title: Smoke Aerosol Measurement Experiment Re-flight (SAMER), Final Report, June 2, 2014 (PSI-101, Reports folder)

topic: sub-micrometer smoke suits ionization, aged smoke suits light scattering
claim: All samples produced significant numbers of sub-micron particles that are readily detected by an ionization smoke detector, but the aging results suggest that some materials, such as silicone rubber, can produce smoke that reaches sizes better detected by light scattering.
quote: all samples produced significant numbers of sub-micron particulate that are readily detected using an ionization smoke detector. However, the aging results suggest that some materials such as silicone rubber can produce smoke that can reach sizes better detected by light scattering techniques.
source_title: Smoke Aerosol Measurement Experiment Re-flight (SAMER), Final Report, June 2, 2014 (PSI-101, Reports folder)

topic: multi-moment detection recommended
claim: The SAME-R conclusions suggest that detection methods measuring more than one moment of the size distribution may detect better and reject false alarms better than single-moment detectors.
quote: These results suggest that detection methods that can measure more than one moment of the size distribution may show more successful detection and false alarm rejection than single moment detectors.
source_title: Smoke Aerosol Measurement Experiment Re-flight (SAMER), Final Report, June 2, 2014 (PSI-101, Reports folder)

topic: two-moment prototype (MPASS) separates smoke from dust
claim: By combining two moments, the MPASS prototype can tell a strong signal from a high smoke concentration apart from a strong signal from a lower concentration of very large dust particles, which can minimize false smoke detector alarms.
quote: The MPASS therefore has the ability to discern the difference between a strong signal from a high smoke concentration and a strong signal from a lower concentration of very large dust particles, a feature which can minimize false smoke detector alarms.
source_title: Smoke Aerosol Measurement Experiment Re-flight (SAMER), Final Report, June 2, 2014 (PSI-101, Reports folder)

topic: two-moment correlation halves response scatter
claim: Using a correlation of two measured moments reduced the relative variance of the MPASS response by roughly a factor of at least 2 compared with a conventional single-output sensor.
quote: Both figures show that the correlation decreases the relative variance by roughly a factor of at least 2 relative to that provided by a conventional single-output sensor.
source_title: Smoke Aerosol Measurement Experiment Re-flight (SAMER), Final Report, June 2, 2014 (PSI-101, Reports folder)

topic: silicone rubber smoke is liquid droplets that vanish before imaging
claim: Silicone rubber smoke left no particles visible by TEM, presumably because the particles were condensed liquid that evaporated before they could be imaged.
quote: Overall, silicone rubber presented no particles that were visible via TEM, presumably because the particles were condensed liquid that evaporated before they could be imaged in the TEM.
source_title: Smoke Aerosol Measurement Experiment Re-flight (SAMER), Final Report, June 2, 2014 (PSI-101, Reports folder)

topic: coagulation lasts up to a thousand seconds; liquid smokes coalesce
claim: The report describes coagulation as continuing for time scales of up to a thousand seconds and states that liquid particles coalesce into larger droplets, which is the case for the lampwick, silicone rubber and Kapton smokes (Fig. 11).
quote: This process may continue for time scales of up to thousand seconds. If the particles are liquid, the colliding particles will coalesce and form larger droplets. This is the case for the lampwick, silicone rubber, and Kapton smokes (Fig. 11).
source_title: Smoke Aerosol Measurement Experiment Re-flight (SAMER), Final Report, June 2, 2014 (PSI-101, Reports folder)

topic: same heater setting, different temperature
claim: For the same heater setting (wire resistance ratio Rt/R0) the actual sample heating temperature differed by as much as 30 degrees Celsius between tests.
quote: for the same Rt/R0, the actual heating temperature difference can be as large as 30 degrees Celsius
source_title: Smoke Aerosol Measurement Experiment Re-flight (SAMER), Final Report, June 2, 2014 (PSI-101, Reports folder)

topic: lognormal assumption checked on the ground
claim: Ground tests with a reference particle sizer showed a better lognormal fit for Kapton and lamp wick smoke and a less valid lognormal fit for silicone smoke.
quote: In general, the spread of the residuals is more compact for Kapton and lamp wick, indicating a better lognormal fit for these materials. Note that the Kapton residuals are mostly positive up to 70 nm, which indicates that the data are less steep than the lognormal fit. The lamp wick residual plot (Fig. 16) also shows a small but systematic deviation from the lognormal fit, which is evident by the change in sign of the unaged data residuals between 500 and 600 nm. Silicone residual plots (Fig. 17) show the least randomness, which indicates that the lognormal fit is less valid.
source_title: Smoke Aerosol Measurement Experiment Re-flight (SAMER), Final Report, June 2, 2014 (PSI-101, Reports folder)

topic: Kapton and lamp wick smoke is spherical, better suited to the moment method
claim: Morphology results show that only Kapton and lamp wick are spherical aerosols, so they are better suited to the moment method.
quote: Morphology results show that only Kapton and lamp wick are spherical aerosols so they are better suited to the moment method.
source_title: Smoke Aerosol Measurement Experiment Re-flight (SAMER), Final Report, June 2, 2014 (PSI-101, Reports folder)

topic: moment method validated
claim: From the SAME-R flight and ground tests the team concluded that the moment method, together with the lognormal distribution assumption, is a valid and effective way to characterize aerosols encountered in space vehicles.
quote: it is concluded that the moment method in conjunction the lognormal distribution assumption is a valid and effective approach to characterization of the aerosol encountered in space vehicles.
source_title: Smoke Aerosol Measurement Experiment Re-flight (SAMER), Final Report, June 2, 2014 (PSI-101, Reports folder)

topic: ISS cabin air: very low particle counts
claim: In the first DAFT session on ISS the P-Trak readings were low (2 to 5 pt/cc); the report calls the readings almost an order of magnitude below those of a typical laboratory (about 4,000 to 6,000 pt/cc for the P-Trak) and attributes this to the HEPA filter on the ISS air handling system.
quote: Those readings were low (2 – 5 pt/cc). The data for that test point can be seen in Section III C. Figures 1 and 2. A review of that data shows that the readings on both devices were very low for the entire test time, but that upon initial startup, the addition and removal of the HEPA filter (zero check) is clearly indicated in the P-Trak data, and there appears to be some residual dust in the sampling tube that is drawn out during the test point. For the remainder of the point, some small variations can be seen, the DustTrak especially gave low readings. Overall, these readings are almost an order of magnitude below those that would normally be seen in a typical laboratory environment ( ~ 4,000 – 6,000 pt/cc for P-Trak), but were not totally unexpected, due to the presence of a HEPA filter on the ISS air handling system.
source_title: Dust and Aerosol measurement Feasibility Test (DAFT), 30 Day Report (PSI-47, Reports folder)

topic: ISS background particulate: mass and number
claim: The three DAFT tests of undisturbed ISS air averaged fewer than 0.005 mg/m3 on the DustTrak and fewer than 15 particles/cm3 on the P-Trak.
quote: The three tests that sampled the undisturbed environment in the ISS showed very low levels of airborne particulates, averaging fewer than 0.005 mg/m3 from the DustTrak® and fewer than 15 particles/cm3 from the P-Trak
source_title: Dust and Aerosol Measurement Feasibility Test (DAFT) fact sheet, NASA Glenn Research Center (PSI-47, Presentations folder)

topic: ISS cleaner than the Space Shuttle
claim: ISS particulate levels were dramatically lower than the roughly 0.050 mg/m3 recorded on the Space Shuttle, as expected because the ISS US Lab has HEPA filtration of cabin air while the shuttle air handler had only a fine screen.
quote: These numbers are dramatically lower than the values recorded in the Space Shuttle in an earlier experiment (~ .050 mg/m3). Lower levels are to be expected because the ISS US Lab has HEPA ﬁltration for the cabin air as compared to merely a ﬁne screen on the shuttle air handler.
source_title: Dust and Aerosol Measurement Feasibility Test (DAFT) fact sheet, NASA Glenn Research Center (PSI-47, Presentations folder)

topic: low background is an opportunity for detection
claim: ISS particle counts measured by DAFT in the US Lab on Increment 10 were at the noise level of the instrument (less than 5 particles/cm3); the SAME report reads the low particle levels in the under-2.5-micrometer bin on the Shuttle and the low overall numbers on the ISS as a zone of opportunity for spacecraft fire detection, since typical normal-gravity fires produce substantial particulate in this size range.
quote: The measurements were made in the US Lab on Increment 10 and the particle count levels were at the noise level for the instrument (less than 5 particles/cm3). The low particle levels in the < 2.5 μm bin for the STS and the low overall numbers for the ISS suggest a zone of opportunity for spacecraft fire detection since typical normal gravity fires produce substantial particulate in this size range
source_title: Smoke Aerosol Measurement Experiment (SAME), Final Report, March 15, 2010 (PSI-102, Reports folder)

topic: ISS cabin very clean (NTRS summary)
claim: DAFT gave the first measurement of background smoke particulate levels on the ISS: the cabin was a very clean environment, with particulate levels substantially below the space shuttle and typical ground-based environments.
quote: provided the first measurement of the background smoke particulate levels on the ISS. These background levels are critical to the design of future smoke detectors. The ISS cabin was found to be a very clean environment with particulate levels substantially below the space shuttle and typical ground-based environments.
source_title: Particle and Smoke Detection on ISS for Next Generation Smoke Detectors

topic: crew activity makes particle bursts (Velcro)
claim: In test point 2 the P-Trak responded to Velcro dust with several readings above the 30,000 pt/cc mark.
quote: Test point #2 data (Figures 3 and 4) shows that the P-Trak responded to the Velcro dust quite well, with several readings above the 30,000 pt/cc mark
source_title: Dust and Aerosol measurement Feasibility Test (DAFT), 30 Day Report (PSI-47, Reports folder)

topic: large particles stay airborne without settling
claim: On orbit the count/mass ratio of the dust sample aerosol was lower than determined in ground testing, meaning the average particle counted on orbit was heavier; the report explains that without gravity to drive settling more of the larger dust particles remain entrained.
quote: The data points are clustered to the left of the line (area), in a region where the count/mass ratio is lower than what was determined from ground testing. This indicates then, that the mass of the average particle counted on orbit is higher than that determined on Earth. This observation makes sense since, on-orbit, without gravity to drive settling, more of the larger particles from the dust sample should remain entrained.
source_title: Dust and Aerosol measurement Feasibility Test (DAFT), 30 Day Report (PSI-47, Reports folder)

topic: average dust particle size measured on orbit
claim: For the particulates sampled from the DAFT bags the average particle mass was 2.5 E-12 grams (assuming the density of water) and the calculated average diameter 1.65 micron (range 1.56 to 1.7 micron).
quote: shows a good uniformity between the particulates sampled from the various bags. The average mass (assuming a material density of water) is 2.5 E-12 grams, with a range from 2 – 3 E-12. The calculated average diameter is 1.65 micron, ranging from 1.56 – 1.7 micron.
source_title: Dust and Aerosol measurement Feasibility Test (DAFT), 30 Day Report (PSI-47, Reports folder)

topic: particles on orbit larger than on Earth (NASA summary)
claim: NASA summary of DAFT: average particle sizes are larger on orbit than on Earth, perhaps because of the inefficiency of the spacecraft filter.
quote: Results show average particle sizes are larger on orbit than on Earth, perhaps due to inefficiency of the spacecraft’s ﬁlter.
source_title: Dust and Aerosol Measurement Feasibility Test (DAFT), NASA fact sheet (PDF)

topic: gravity-dependent instrument modified to work in microgravity
claim: The P-Trak particle counter relies on a downward-sloping condenser to return alcohol to its evaporator; for microgravity the cooling tube was modified so that capillary action moves the liquid alcohol back upstream.
quote: The condenser in the COTS device slopes down, enabling the alcohol from the droplets that adhere to the tube wall to be recycled back to the evaporator. In conjunction with fluid physics researchers at GRC, a modification to the cooling tube was developed that effectively moves liquid alcohol from the tip of the tube back upstream to the evaporator due to capillary action.
source_title: Dust and Aerosol measurement Feasibility Test (DAFT), 30 Day Report (PSI-47, Reports folder)

topic: modified particle counter worked in microgravity
claim: The DAFT data show that the instruments operated in microgravity for an extended period with no apparent failure; the feared build-up of alcohol in the P-Trak optics chamber did not happen.
quote: The data shows that the devices were able to operate in microgravity for an extended period of time with no apparent failure. One of the major concerns was that the P-Trak would accumulate alcohol in the optics chamber and obscure them, causing the unit to either read ‘0’ or display and error code. This did not happen.
source_title: Dust and Aerosol measurement Feasibility Test (DAFT), 30 Day Report (PSI-47, Reports folder)

topic: what the particle counter can see
claim: The P-Trak can count individual particles as small as 20 nm in diameter in an aerosol stream.
quote: The P-Trak, a hand-held instrument, can count individual particles as small as 20 nm in diameter in an aerosol stream.
source_title: Fundamental Research Applied To Enable Hardware Performance in Microgravity

topic: simulated microgravity smoke has larger particles than terrestrial smoke
claim: In the simulations the microgravity smoke contained larger particles than terrestrial smoke; when the microgravity size distribution was unimodal its mode diameter was 10 micrometers, roughly twice that of the terrestrial case.
quote: Microgravity smoke presented in this study contains larger particles than terrestrial smoke. When the microgravity PSD is bimodal, the larger mode contains particles with dp > 35 µm, while the terrestrial PSD contains effectively zero particles in this size range. Alternatively, the microgravity PSD can be uni- modal with a mode diameter of dp = 10 µm – roughly twice that of the terrestrial case.
source_title: Utilization of the SAME Data for Advanced Modeling and Simulation of Smoke Generation in Microgravity, NASA Grant NNX17AF08A Final Report, August 15, 2020 (PSI-115, Reports folder)

topic: settling removes the largest particles only on Earth
claim: In the Earth-gravity simulation, gravitational settling eliminated all particles with diameter above 35 micrometers downstream of the wake, and the 8 cm/s Earth-gravity case had a single size mode at 5 micrometers.
quote: Downstream of the wake vortices, gravitational settling elimi- nates all particles with diameter > 35 µm. Unlike the microgravity case, the 8 cm/s Earth gravity case is not bimodal, with a single local maximum at dp = 5 µm.
source_title: Utilization of the SAME Data for Advanced Modeling and Simulation of Smoke Generation in Microgravity, NASA Grant NNX17AF08A Final Report, August 15, 2020 (PSI-115, Reports folder)

topic: three mechanisms behind larger microgravity smoke
claim: The simulations point to three mechanisms that separate microgravity from Earth-gravity smoke: different recirculation geometries and volumes, particle settling removing large particles on Earth, and buoyant convection carrying condensable species toward cool surfaces.
quote: three primary mechanisms that differentiate the microgravity and Earth gravity smoke: (1) different re- circulation geometries and volumes modify the time-temperature-concentration history of the aerosol in regions of high temperature and high vapor mass fraction; (2) particle settling eliminates large particles from Earth gravity smoke, which reduces the maximum particle size and modifies aerosol development by changing coagulation and condensation rates of the remaining particles; (3) buoyant convection can transport condensible species toward relatively cool surfaces, increasing vapor-to-particle conversion.
source_title: Utilization of the SAME Data for Advanced Modeling and Simulation of Smoke Generation in Microgravity, NASA Grant NNX17AF08A Final Report, August 15, 2020 (PSI-115, Reports folder)

topic: the gravity effect depends on material and geometry
claim: The report cautions that each mechanism is highly material- and geometry-dependent; for example, settling is irrelevant if the condensing species forms particles too small to settle, and in such situations microgravity and Earth-gravity smoke are hypothesized to be more similar.
quote: each of these factors is also highly material- and geometry-dependent: (1) the wake dynamic becomes unimportant if nucleation occurs far downstream of the wake, or if there is a time dependent flow without a stable recirculation region; (2) particle settling is irrelevant if the condensing species forms particles that are too small to settle (the DBP considered in this work forms large particles); (3) if smoke is produced in an open environment, there may not be cool surfaces nearby to increase nucleation rates. In these situations, microgravity and Earth gravity smoke are hypothesized to be more similar.
source_title: Utilization of the SAME Data for Advanced Modeling and Simulation of Smoke Generation in Microgravity, NASA Grant NNX17AF08A Final Report, August 15, 2020 (PSI-115, Reports folder)

topic: recirculation behind the hot source keeps particles growing
claim: In the simulations the wake behind the heated vapor source holds large particle number densities because dividing streamlines prevent the particles from being convected away, and the particles keep growing as condensation consumes the available DBP vapor.
quote: The wake contains large particle number densities because dividing streamlines prevent the particles from being convected away, and the particles continue to grow as condensation consumes all available DBP vapor.
source_title: Utilization of the SAME Data for Advanced Modeling and Simulation of Smoke Generation in Microgravity, NASA Grant NNX17AF08A Final Report, August 15, 2020 (PSI-115, Reports folder)

topic: spacecraft detectors were designed from normal-gravity data
claim: Because no microgravity smoke data existed, all spacecraft smoke detectors in use at the time were designed on the basis of normal-gravity conditions.
quote: Owing to the absence of microgravity smoke data, all current spacecraft smoke detectors were designed based upon normal-g conditions.
source_title: Particle and Smoke Detection on ISS for Next Generation Smoke Detectors

topic: why smoke particles grow larger without buoyancy
claim: Removing buoyancy lowers the velocities in the hot zones of flames, which lengthens the residence time of smoke particles and so gives them more time to grow.
quote: The removal of buoyancy reduces the velocities in the high temperature zones in flames, increasing the residence time of smoke particles and consequently allowing longer growth time for the particles.
source_title: Particle and Smoke Detection on ISS for Next Generation Smoke Detectors

topic: smoke concentrates at the source and takes longer to reach detectors
claim: In low gravity buoyant flow is negligible, so particles concentrate at the smoke source, their residence time increases, and the transport time to smoke detectors increases.
quote: In low gravity, buoyant flow is negligible which causes particles to concentrate at the smoke source, increasing their residence time, and increasing the transport time to smoke detectors.
source_title: Spacecraft Fire Safety Research at NASA Glenn Research Center

topic: ionization and light-scattering detectors favour different sizes
claim: Of the two US systems, the Shuttle ionization detector is most sensitive (on a mass concentration basis) to smaller particulate, and the ISS light-scattering detector is most sensitive to particulate larger than 1 micron.
quote: The STS system uses an ionization detector coupled with a sampling pump and the ISS system is a forward light scattering detector operating in the near IR. These two systems have significantly different sensitivities with the ionization detector being most sensitive (on a mass concentration basis) to smaller particulate and the light scattering detector being most sensitive to particulate that is larger than 1 micron.
source_title: "Smoke": Characterization Of Smoke Particulate For Spacecraft Fire Detection

topic: false alarms are costly
claim: False alarms are extremely costly because the crew and the ground team must respond quickly to every alarm.
quote: At the same time, false alarms are extremely costly as the crew and the ground team must respond quickly to every alarm.
source_title: "Smoke": Characterization Of Smoke Particulate For Spacecraft Fire Detection

topic: how DAFT and SAME differ
claim: The two detection investigations asked different questions: DAFT examined the background aerosol particulate levels on the ISS, and SAME examined the particle-size distribution of smoke from spacecraft materials.
quote: The Dust Aerosol measurement Feasibility Test examined the background aerosol particulate levels on the ISS. The Smoke Aerosol Measurement Experiment (SAME) examined the particle-size distribution of the smoke from spacecraft materials.
source_title: A Researcher's Guide to: Combustion Science (NP-2015-10-034-JSC)

topic: Earth application: detectors for sealed environments
claim: PSI lists as an Earth benefit that smoke detectors developed from the SAME results can be useful in other extreme environments on Earth, such as submarines or underwater laboratories.
quote: The smoke detectors developed from the results of SAME can also be useful in other extreme environments on Earth, such as submarines or underwater laboratories.
source_title: Smoke and Aerosol Measurement Experiment (PSI record)

topic: Earth application: nuisance-free early warning for homes
claim: NASA states that knowing more about the behavior of smoke and particles in low gravity allows better nuisance-free early warning systems to be developed for both spacecraft and homes.
quote: By knowing more about the behavior of smoke and particles in low gravity, better nuisance-free early warning systems can be developed for both spacecraft and homes.
source_title: Smoke Particles Are Not All the 'SAME'

topic: Limiting oxygen index of methanol droplets
claim: The FLEX experiments show a limiting oxygen index for methanol in the diluent gases tested of around 12% to 13% oxygen by volume.
quote: The experiments also show that the limiting oxygen index for methanol in these diluent gases is around 12% to 13% oxygen by volume.
source_title: Methanol Droplet Combustion in Oxygen-Inert Environments in Microgravity

topic: Ignition at 13% oxygen
claim: At one atmosphere, methanol droplets ignited and burned for some time in 13% oxygen with the rest nitrogen.
quote: At one atmosphere pressure, ignition and some burning were observed for an oxygen concentration of 13% with the rest being nitrogen.
source_title: Methanol Droplet Extinction in Oxygen/Carbon-dioxide/Nitrogen Mixtures in Microgravity: Results from the International Space Station Experiments

topic: Burning at 12% oxygen (single PSI test record)
claim: PSI test table, FLEX test 86: a methanol droplet of 3.07 mm initial diameter in 0.12 oxygen / 0.87 nitrogen mole fraction at 770 mmHg has a recorded burn time of 9 s and a visible flame extinction diameter of 2.56 mm; the test end is recorded as Extinction.

topic: Small heptane droplet burned to completion at 14% oxygen (single PSI test record)
claim: PSI test table, FLEX test 69: a heptane droplet of 1.1 mm initial diameter in 0.14 oxygen / 0.84 nitrogen mole fraction at 767.1 mmHg is recorded with a visible flame extinction diameter of 0, a burn time of 1.3 s and test end Completion.

topic: Heptane at 13% oxygen: probably below the flammability limit
claim: In FLEX test 079 a free-floating heptane droplet in 0.13/0.85 O2/N2 at 1.0 atm gave only a very short, entirely transient burn; the report judges this atmosphere probably below the quasi-steady flammability limit. It also notes a vapor cloud that may indicate subsequent cool-flame burning and extinction.
quote: Figure 83.-Test FLEX-079. Free-floating heptane droplet burning in a 0.13/0.85 O2/N2, 1.0-atm ambient environment. This very short burn was entirely transient. The ambient environment was probably below the quasi-steady flammability limit. A small vapor cloud formed shortly after the visible flame extinguished, which may be indicative of cool flame burning and extinction following hot flame extinction.
source_title: Detailed Results from the Flame Extinguishment Experiment (FLEX) March 2009 to December 2011 (NASA/TP-2015-216046)

topic: Observed oxygen limits lower than expected
claim: The FLEX data report states that a principal objective was the limiting oxygen index, and that the observed LOI values for the fuels tested appear slightly lower than initially expected.
quote: A principle objective was to determine the limiting oxygen index (LOI), the oxygen percentage below which combustion would not occur. This objective reflected the FLEX focus on investigating fire safety in spacecraft. Observed LOI values for these fuels appear to be slightly lower than initially expected.
source_title: Detailed Results from the Flame Extinguishment Experiment (FLEX) March 2009 to December 2011 (NASA/TP-2015-216046)

topic: Oxygen limit lower in microgravity than in normal gravity
claim: The FLEX and FLEX-2 droplet experiments identified radiative and diffusive extinction limits for heptane and methanol droplets and a limiting oxygen index that is significantly lower than in normal gravity and lower than previously predicted.
quote: To date, these experiments have identified both the radiative and diffusive extinction limits for heptane and methanol droplets and identified an LOI that is both significantly lower than in normal gravity and lower than previously predicted and anticipated.
source_title: A Researcher's Guide to: Combustion Science (NP-2015-10-034-JSC)

topic: Ground standards for inert-gas suppressants lose margin in low gravity
claim: Research to date in FLEX has shown that the flammability limit is lower in reduced gravity, with the implication that terrestrial standards for inert gas suppressants do not offer the same margin of safety in low gravity as in normal gravity.
quote: The research to date has shown that the flammability limit is lower in reduced gravity. The implication is that terrestrial standards for inert gas suppressants in low gravity do not offer the same margin of safety as in normal gravity.
source_title: A Researcher's Guide to: Combustion Science (NP-2015-10-034-JSC)

topic: Methanol burned with 75% carbon dioxide present when oxygen stayed at 20%
claim: FLEX test point FLEX-145 lists a methanol droplet with initial diameter 3.38 mm at 1.0 atm in 20% O2 / 75% CO2 / 5% N2, and Dext = 1.66 at visible flame extinction; this excerpt prints no unit for Dext.
quote: Test Point FLEX-145 • 1.0 atm in 20% O2 / 75% CO2 / 5% N2 • Methanol droplet Do = 3.38 mm Dext = 1.66 (at visible flame extinction)

claim: PSI test table, FLEX test 18: a heptane droplet of 2.74 mm initial diameter in 0.21 oxygen / 0.09 nitrogen / 0.7 carbon dioxide mole fraction at 1553.8 mmHg has a recorded burn time of 8.1 s and a visible flame extinction diameter of 1.77 mm.

topic: Near-limit point: 15% oxygen with 50% carbon dioxide (single PSI test record)

topic: Heptane in 17% oxygen with 45% carbon dioxide: quick extinction, probably no or only brief cool flame
claim: In FLEX test 130 a fiber-supported heptane droplet translating at 3 mm/s in 0.17/0.38/0.45 O2/N2/CO2 at 0.7 atm burned only very briefly: the flame extinguished radiatively soon after translation began, no vapor cloud formed, and the report concludes there was probably no, or only very brief, cool flame burning.
quote: Figure 134.—Test FLEX–130. Fiber-supported heptane droplet translating 3 mm/s and burning in a 0.17/0.38/0.45 O2/N2/CO2, 0.7-atm ambient environment. This was a very short burn, and the flame extinguished radiatively very soon after translation began. No vapor cloud formed, and the vaporization rate was quite small after the visible flame extinguished. As a result, there was probably no, or only very brief, cool flame burning.
source_title: Detailed Results from the Flame Extinguishment Experiment (FLEX) March 2009 to December 2011 (NASA/TP-2015-216046)

topic: How FLEX measured the minimum carbon dioxide concentration
claim: In the FLEX CO2 tests, CO2 was added at constant pressure starting from the highest oxygen mole fraction until quasi-steady burning was no longer observed; the report treats that point as the LOI and as the minimum CO2 mole fraction required to extinguish or prevent the spread of a flame.
quote: These tests also began at the highest oxygen mole fraction ambient environment; then increasing amounts of CO2 were added while the ambient pressure was maintained constant. Testing concluded when quasi-steady burning was not observed, again the determination of the LOI. This also represented the minimum carbon dioxide mole fraction required to extinguish or prevent the spread of a flame.
source_title: Detailed Results from the Flame Extinguishment Experiment (FLEX) March 2009 to December 2011 (NASA/TP-2015-216046)

topic: Design goal of a total-flooding agent
claim: The FLEX test plan states that the LOI is a critical concept in fire safety and that the goal of the agent in a total flooding application is to reduce the oxygen concentration below the LOI.
quote: The LOI is a critical concept in fire safety, and also important in developing, refining and ultimately validating detailed chemical kinetic mechanisms. For fire safety, the goal of the agent in a total flooding application is to reduce the oxygen concentration below the LOI .
source_title: FLEX Test Plan, extracted from the Research Requirements Document for Droplet Flame Extinguishment in Microgravity (PSI-69, Science Documents)

topic: More agent needed in microgravity: cup-burner minimum extinction concentrations (background cited in the FLEX test plan)
claim: Table 2 of the FLEX test plan lists minimum extinction concentrations for cup burner flames from Takahashi et al. (2004): CO2 0.16 in 1-g and 0.19 in microgravity, He 0.27 and 0.31, N2 0.26 and 0.38. The plan says Takahashi et al. conducted normal gravity tests and microgravity simulations of the suppression of methane cup-burner flames.
quote: Table 2: Gaseous fire suppression agent efficacy, as measured by the M EC , for cup burner flames (Takahashi et al., 2004). Agent/Env. M EC , 1 − g M EC , µg CO2 0.16 0.19 He 0.27 0.31 N2 0.26 0.38 LOI = 0.209 (1 − M EC) (2) The M EC is a function of the fuel, agent and experimental geometry. Clearly, a more effective agent will have a lower M EC for a given fuel and fuel geometry. Takahashi et al. (2004) conducted normal gravity tests and microgravity simulations of the suppression of methane cup-burner flames using mixtures of various suppressants in standard air. The table below summarizes the findings for M EC in the two environments.
source_title: FLEX Test Plan, extracted from the Research Requirements Document for Droplet Flame Extinguishment in Microgravity (PSI-69, Science Documents)

topic: Carbon dioxide threshold higher in microgravity (background cited in the FLEX test plan)
claim: The FLEX test plan cites Katta et al. (2004): for a methane-air diffusion flame on a cup burner, a CO2 volume fraction greater than 19.1% is needed to destabilize the flame base in microgravity compared to 16.4% for a normal gravity flame.
quote: Katta et al. (2004) investigated the mechanism through which CO2 causes fire suppression using detailed numerical simulation and experiments in microgravity for a methane-air diffusion flame stabilized on a cup burner. Their results showed that a CO2 volume fraction greater than 19.1% is needed to destabilize the flame-base in microgravity compared to 16.4% for a normal gravity flame.
source_title: FLEX Test Plan, extracted from the Research Requirements Document for Droplet Flame Extinguishment in Microgravity (PSI-69, Science Documents)

topic: Carbon dioxide less effective than helium in microgravity flame spread tests (background cited in the FLEX test plan)
claim: The FLEX test plan cites Honda and Ronney (1998), who added inert diluents to air in microgravity tests of opposed-flow flame spread over thin solid fuels; their results seem to suggest that CO2 is less effective than He as a fire suppressant in microgravity in terms of the minimum O2 concentration that supports combustion.
quote: Honda and Ronney (1998) studied opposed-flow flame spread rates over thin solid fuels in microgravity by adding different inert diluents (He , N2 , Ar, CO2 and SF6 ) to the standard air atmosphere. Their experimental results seem to suggest that CO2 is less effective as a fire suppressant in microgravity than He in terms of the minimum O2 concentration that supports combustion.
source_title: FLEX Test Plan, extracted from the Research Requirements Document for Droplet Flame Extinguishment in Microgravity (PSI-69, Science Documents)

topic: Why carbon dioxide can behave differently without buoyancy
claim: The FLEX test plan explains that without buoyantly-driven convective flows, radiative losses can become a significant fraction of the heat loss from the reaction zone, and that when a thermally participating gas such as CO2 limits radiative exchange between flame and ambient, temperatures near the fuel source will increase.
quote: In the absence of buoyantly-driven convective flows, however, radiative losses from the flame can become a significant fraction of the total heat loss from the reaction zone. When radiative exchanges between the flame and the ambient are limited by the presence of a thermally participating gas, such as CO2 , temperatures in the proximity of the fuel source will increase.
source_title: FLEX Test Plan, extracted from the Research Requirements Document for Droplet Flame Extinguishment in Microgravity (PSI-69, Science Documents)

topic: Venting the cabin as an extinguishing strategy
claim: The MDCA-FLEX description notes that ambient pressure does not significantly influence droplet burning rate but does influence chemistry at sufficiently low values, that one strategy for extinguishing a fire is to isolate the habitat and vent the cabin to space, and that verified suppressant data at low pressures are therefore beneficial.
quote: Pressure: Ambient pressure does not significantly influence the droplet burning rate, but does influence chemistry at sufficiently low values. In addition, one strategy for extinguishing a fire is to isolate the habitat where it exists and vent the cabin to space. It is therefore beneficial to have verified suppressant data at low pressures.
source_title: Multi-User Droplet Combustion Apparatus - Flame Extinguishment Experiment (MDCA-FLEX fact sheet)

topic: Fuel keeps reacting after the visible flame is gone
claim: In FLEX, large alkane droplets burned briefly with a typical hot flame that extinguished when radiative loss lowered the flame temperature; after that the droplet continued to vaporize at the same rate for an extended period and then suddenly stopped at a finite size, with a large vapor cloud forming; this vaporization is supported by a lower-temperature cool flame that forms after visible flame extinction.
quote: Recent spaceflight experiments (FLEX) involving single alkane droplets burning in a quiescent ambient uncovered unexplained and unexpected behavior. For the large alkane droplets, after ignition the droplet burns for a short time with a typical hot flame. As expected, the hot flame extinguished when the radiative loss reduced the flame temperature below a critical value. Inexplicably after hot flame extinction, however, the droplet continued to vaporize at the same rate for an extended period and then suddenly stopped vaporizing at a finite droplet size. The plateau in vaporization occurred coincident with the formation of a large vapor cloud. This vaporization, we now know, is supported by a lower-temperature cool flame that forms after visible flame extinction.
source_title: A Researcher's Guide to: Combustion Science (NP-2015-10-034-JSC)

topic: Post-flame vaporization nearly as fast as burning (heptane in cabin air)
claim: In FLEX test 035 (free-floating heptane droplet, cabin air, 1.0 atm), after the visible flame extinguished the droplet vaporized very vigorously at a rate only slightly lower than the burning rate constant before extinction, then the rate plateaued as a very large vapor cloud formed; the report calls this indicative of cool flame burning and extinction.
quote: Figure 39.—Test FLEX−035. Free-floating heptane droplet in a cabin air (0.21/0.79 O2/N2), 1.0-atm ambient environment. The droplet remained in the High-Bit-Depth Multispectral (HiBMs) field of view (FOV) for the entire test including a long time after the visible flame extinguished. The flame oscillated before the visible flame extinguished, and this was apparent in both the Low Light Level Ultra-Violet (LLUV) and color camera. After the flame extinguished, the droplet vaporized very vigorously with droplet-diameter-squared versus time behavior that was nearly perfectly linear. The vaporization rate was only slightly lower than the burning rate constant before the flame extinguished. The droplet vaporization rate then plateaued coincident with the formation of a very large vapor cloud. This behavior is indicative of cool flame burning and extinction.
source_title: Detailed Results from the Flame Extinguishment Experiment (FLEX) March 2009 to December 2011 (NASA/TP-2015-216046)

topic: Cool flame temperature range
claim: The FLEX series showed that quasi-steady stable flames can surround a droplet in microgravity without a visible flame, at temperatures in the range of 700 to 900 K, unlike hot flames, whose temperature is higher than 1200 K.
quote: FLEX series of experiments showed for the first time that quasi-steady stable flames can be established surrounding a droplet in microgravity under certain conditions, without a visible flame at temperatures in the range of 700 to 900 K, unlike the hot flames where the flame temperature is higher than 1200 K.
source_title: Cool Flame Investigation (CFI) Science Final Report (PSI-39, Reports)

topic: The fire went out twice
claim: In FLEX, large (about 3 mm) heptane droplets showed dual modes of combustion and extinction: the fire went out twice, once with a visible flame and once without.
quote: In FLEX scientists observed for the first time large, about 3 mm, droplets of heptane fuel that had dual modes of combustion and extinction. The fire went out twice; once with a visible flame, once without.
source_title: ISS Passes the Torch of Flame Studies

topic: Cool flames last minutes in microgravity, a fraction of a second on Earth
claim: On Earth, cool flames can only be observed for a fraction of a second; in microgravity researchers observed them for a minute or two at a time.
quote: On Earth, cool flames can only be observed for a fraction of a second. In microgravity, however, researchers have been able to observe the phenomenon for a minute or two at a time.
source_title: Combustion Facility Celebrates Eight Years of Hot Science

topic: Why cool flames do not persist on Earth
claim: Cool flames are much weaker than hot flames, so on Earth the buoyant flow of oxygen drawn into the flame causes the flame to collapse and extinguish.
quote: Cool flames are much weaker than hot flames, so on Earth the oxygen being drawn into the flame, known as the buoyant flow, causes the flame to collapse and extinguish.
source_title: Combustion Facility Celebrates Eight Years of Hot Science

topic: Cool flames can re-ignite to hot flames
claim: The FLEX team concludes that these cool flames produce partially oxidized fuel and can potentially re-ignite to hot flames, posing fire safety concerns in spacecraft environments.
quote: These cool flames produce partially oxidized fuel and potentially re-ignite to hot flames posing fire safety concerns in spacecraft environments
source_title: Isolated Single Droplet Combustion: FLEX Experiments onboard the International Space Station

topic: Cool flame compared to smoldering; re-ignition seen with decane
claim: A 2013 FLEX team presentation states that in space a cool flame can persist after hot flame extinction and generate combustible vapor that can reignite, similar to smoldering combustion in solid fuels, and that recent results show re-ignition with decane.
quote: In space “cool flame” can persist after hot flame extinction and generate combustible vapor that can reignite (similar to smoldering combustion in solid fuels) • Recent results show re-ignition with decane
source_title: "Cool Flames" in Space, a Hot Prospect on Earth! (Nayagam, 2nd Annual ISS Research and Development Conference; PSI-69, Presentations)

topic: Model: adding carbon dioxide triggered the cool-flame mode
claim: In simulations of a 3.0 mm n-heptane droplet, which in ambient air did not show two-stage cool flame combustion, an increase in ambient CO2 concentration readily triggered the cool flame combustion; the authors add that any enhanced heat loss mechanism, not only radiative loss, can trigger it.
quote: To study the influence of radiative effects on the combustion characteristics, simulations were conducted for ambience containing increasing CO2 concentration since CO2 is a radiatively participating medium. An initial droplet diameter of 3.0 mm was so chosen as in ambient air it did not show a two stage “Cool Flame” combustion characteristics. The influence of CO2 concentration in the ambient is summarized in Figure 6. An increase 5 in the CO2 concentration in the ambient readily triggered the “Cool flame” combustion. The “Cool Flame” behavior can not only be triggered by radiative heat loss but rather any enhanced heat loss mechanism.
source_title: Isolated Alkane Droplet Combustion in Microgravity: "Cool Flames" (Farouk and Dryer, 8th U.S. National Combustion Meeting; PSI-69, Presentations)

topic: Cool flame followed radiative extinction with 15% carbon dioxide present
claim: Three free-floated n-heptane droplets at one atmosphere, in 21% O2 / 79% N2, 18% O2 / 82% N2 and 18% O2 / 67% N2 / 15% CO2 (initial diameters 3.91, 3.48 and 2.49 mm), all showed radiative extinction followed by cool flame combustion and a second-stage extinction leading to pure vaporization.
quote: Detailed results for n-heptane droplets burning in oxygen/carbon dioxide/nitrogen mixtures were presented earlier [3]. We summarize those results here for the sake of completeness. Figure 6 3 shows three typical free-floated cases, corresponding to ambient gas mixtures of 21% oxygen 79% nitrogen, 18% oxygen 82% nitrogen, and 18% oxygen 67% nitrogen 15% carbon dioxide, all by volume, at one atmospheric pressure. The initial diameters for these cases respectively were 3.91, 3.48, and 2.49 mm. All three cases exhibit radiative extinction followed by cool flame combustion and the second stage extinction leading to pure vaporization.
source_title: Cool-flame Extinction During N-Alkane Droplet Combustion in Microgravity

topic: Model: flash re-ignition after about 18 s of cool flame
claim: A two-dimensional simulation using a gaseous n-heptane source in zero gravity predicts that in air at <=2 mm/s, with fuel injection velocity 1 cm/s, a growing spherical flame radiatively extinguishes at about 1200 K, transitions to a roughly 700 K cool-flame regime, and after about 18 s undergoes flash re-ignition followed by extinction of the re-ignited flame.
quote: In a near-quiescent air environment (< or = 2 mm/s), with a sufficiently large fuel injection velocity (1 cm/s), a growing spherical diffusion flame extinguishes at ≈1200 K due to radiative heat losses. This is typically followed by a transition to the low-temperature (cool-flame) regime with a reaction zone (at ≈700 K) in close proximity to the fuel source. The 'cool flame' regime is formed due to the negative temperature coefficient in the low-temperature chemistry. After a relatively long period (≈18 s) of the cool flame regime, a flash re-ignition occurs, associated with flame-edge propagation and subsequent extinction of the re-ignited flame.
source_title: Combustion Characteristics in a Non-Premixed Cool-Flame Regime of n-Heptane in Microgravity

topic: Model: millimetre-per-second airflow changes whether the flame survives
claim: In the same simulation, a low-speed airstream of about 3 mm/s enhanced the diffusion flame upstream with local extinction downstream and steady pulsations at about 0.4 Hz, and at air velocities of 4 to 10 mm/s the locally extinguished flame became steady.
quote: In a low-speed (≈3 mm/s) airstream (which simulates the slight droplet movement), the diffusion flame is enhanced upstream and experiences a local extinction downstream at ≈1200 K, followed by steady flame pulsations (≈0.4 Hz). At higher air velocities (4-10 mm/s), the locally extinguished flame becomes steady state.
source_title: Combustion Characteristics in a Non-Premixed Cool-Flame Regime of n-Heptane in Microgravity

topic: Visible flame extinguished after 3 mm/s droplet translation stopped
claim: In FLEX test 064 a fiber-supported heptane droplet in 0.18/0.82 O2/N2 at 1.0 atm was translated at 3 mm/s for about 4 s: during translation the leading edge of the flame was bright and the trailing edge much dimmer; after translation stopped the flame extinguished and the droplet vaporized significantly, behavior the report calls indicative of cool flame burning and extinction.
quote: Figure 68.—Test FLEX−064. Fiber-supported heptane droplet translating 3 mm/s (for approximately 4 s) and burning in a 0.18/0.82 O2/N2, 1.0-atm ambient environment. The droplet had moderate transverse oscillations and remained within the High-Bit-Depth Multispectral (HiBMs) field of view (FOV) for the entire test. The flame grew and became dim blue. During translation, the leading edge of the flame was bright and the fiber glowed brightly. The trailing edge of the flame was much dimmer and the fiber did not glow. After the translation stopped, the flame extinguished and the droplet vaporized significantly. A small disruption very late in the droplet lifetime left a small residual droplet on the fiber. The behavior after the visible flame extinguished is indicative of cool flame burning and extinction.
source_title: Detailed Results from the Flame Extinguishment Experiment (FLEX) March 2009 to December 2011 (NASA/TP-2015-216046)

topic: Precursor tests: carbon dioxide at fixed 21% oxygen barely changed methanol extinction
claim: In precursor microgravity experiments (before the ISS runs) with 1.25 to 1.72 mm methanol droplets at one atmosphere and oxygen fixed at 21%, the extinction diameter grew with initial droplet diameter, while increasing the carbon dioxide concentration led only to a slight decrease in the extinction diameter.
quote: Diffusive extinction of methanol droplets with initial diameters between 1.25 mm and 1.72 mm, burning in a quiescent microgravity environment at one atmosphere pressure, was obtained experimentally for varying levels of ambient carbon-dioxide concentrations with a fixed oxygen concentration of 21% and a balance of nitrogen. These experiments serve as precursors to those which are beginning to be performed on the International Space Station and are motivated by the need to understand the effectiveness of carbon-dioxide as a fire suppressant in low-gravity environments. In these experiments, the flame standoff distance, droplet diameter, and flame radiation are measured as functions of time. The results show that the droplet extinction diameter depends on both the initial droplet diameter and the ambient concentration of carbon dioxide. Increasing the initial droplet diameter leads to an increased extinction diameter, while increasing the carbon-dioxide concentration leads to a slight decrease in the extinction diameter.
source_title: Methanol Droplet Extinction in Carbon-Dioxide-Enriched Environments in Microgravity

topic: An atmosphere that does not burn in normal gravity burned in microgravity
claim: Precursor tests described in the FLEX-2 science requirements: in 0.15 oxygen mole fraction (balance nitrogen) at 190 mmHg, a single droplet burned to completion in microgravity although that ambient was not flammable in normal gravity, where droplets of this size could not sustain a flame at this oxygen fraction at pressures up to 760 mmHg; the flame around a binary array extinguished about one second after the igniter withdrew.
quote: Figure 8 shows the burning behavior for a single droplet and a binary array (L ≈ 3 mm) in a 0.15 oxygen mole fraction (balance nitrogen), 190 mmHg ambient. There are several noteworthy features of the single droplet burning behavior. First, this ambient condition was not ﬂammable in normal gravity. In fact, in this ambient oxygen mole fraction, droplets of this size could not sustain a ﬂame in normal gravity at pressures up to 760 mmHg. Figure 8 also shows that while the single droplet burned to completion, the ﬂame surrounding the array extinguished approximately one second after the igniter withdrew.
source_title: Science Requirements Document: Fundamental Studies in Droplet Combustion and Flame Extinguishment in Microgravity (FLEX-2) (PSI-68, Science Documents)

topic: Paired-droplet extinction diameter exceeded the single-droplet value at 15% oxygen
claim: The FLEX-2 science requirements recount precursor observations over a range of droplet spacings and pressures: at oxygen mole fraction 0.15, the binary-array flame always extinguished at a finite droplet size larger than the single-droplet extinction diameter.
quote: The above trends were consistent over a range of inter-droplet spacings and ambient pressures. In the 0.15 oxygen mole fraction ambient, the ﬂame surrounding the binary array always extinguished at a ﬁnite droplet size that was larger than the single droplet extinction diameter.
source_title: Science Requirements Document: Fundamental Studies in Droplet Combustion and Flame Extinguishment in Microgravity (FLEX-2) (PSI-68, Science Documents)

topic: In helium-diluted oxygen the trend reverses: the pair burned longer
claim: The FLEX-2 requirements recount precursor oxygen/helium observations: the single-droplet flame extinguished quickly at about 1.4 mm while the binary-array flame burned longer to about 1.1 mm. The document states that this trend is opposite to the O2/N2 experiments and agrees with normal-gravity experiments.
quote: The ﬂame surrounding the single droplet extinguishes quickly after ignition (Dext ≈ 1.4 mm). The ﬂame surrounding the binary array, however, burns much longer, and the extinction droplet diameter is much smaller (Dext ≈ 1.1 mm). This extinction trend is opposite to that displayed in O2 /N2 experiments, but in agreement with the normal gravity experiments.
source_title: Science Requirements Document: Fundamental Studies in Droplet Combustion and Flame Extinguishment in Microgravity (FLEX-2) (PSI-68, Science Documents)

topic: Paired droplets produced a cool flame where single droplets had only a hot flame
claim: For n-decane droplets of similar size burning in 17% O2 / 83% N2 at 1 atm, single droplets showed only a hot flame while binary droplets showed a cool flame.
quote: N-decane droplets burning in 17-83% O2-N2 ambient at 1 atm o Similar size droplets: Single droplets only hot flame – Binary droplets cool flame
source_title: Aspects of Cool-Flame Supported Droplet Combustion in Microgravity (PSI-39, Presentations)

topic: Cameras saw nothing during the cool flame; radiometers did
claim: During the second, cool-flame stage of an n-decane droplet burn, neither the color camera nor the UV camera was sensitive enough to register any flame image, while both the broadband and narrowband radiometers registered continued radiative heat loss from the droplet, indicating active chemical heat release.
quote: The second-stage combustion termed "cool flame" zone starts immediately following hot-flame extinction. As in the hot-flame region the square of the droplet diameter decreases linearly with time in the cool-flame region, but at a slightly slower rate. Both the color camera and the UV-camera are not sensitive enough to register any flame images during this period. Both the broadband and narrowband radiometers, however, register continued radiative heat loss from the droplet indicating active chemical heat release. The end of "cool flame" combustion is clearly marked by the rapid drop in the narrowband radiometer output. Following cool flame extinction the droplet simply evaporates in the hot environment and the radiative loss measurements decay to zero values without any further abrupt changes.
source_title: Cool-flame Extinction During N-Alkane Droplet Combustion in Microgravity

topic: Burning rate in the invisible stage about four fifths of the visible stage
claim: Test R298 in the paper's n-octane series used a droplet with initial diameter 3.6 mm in O2:N2 = 0.21:0.79, without helium dilution. The reported hot/cool burning-rate constants were 0.48 and 0.38 mm2/s, respectively.
quote: Test R298 results shown in Fig. (2a) corresponds to a droplet with D0 = 3.6 mm burning in air (O2 :N2 = 0.21:0.79) with no helium dilution. Both hot-ﬂame and cool-ﬂame burning modes were found to exist with the respective burning rates of 0.48 and 0.38 mm2 /s.
source_title: Cool-flame Extinction During N-Alkane Droplet Combustion in Microgravity

topic: Lower oxygen brought earlier hot-flame and cool-flame extinction
claim: For n-decane droplets at 0.5 atm in oxygen/nitrogen mixtures, reducing the ambient oxygen concentration led to earlier hot and cool flame extinctions.
quote: In general it can be summarized based on the results presented in Fig. 1 that reducing the ambient oxygen concentration leads to earlier hot and cool ﬂame extinctions.
source_title: Cool-flame Extinction During N-Alkane Droplet Combustion in Microgravity

topic: Higher oxygen removed radiative self-extinction
claim: When the oxygen concentration was sufficiently high, radiative extinction was avoided and visible flame extinction occurred at a much smaller droplet size, either by micro-explosion of the droplet or by diffusive extinction.
quote: When the oxygen concentration is sufﬁciently high radiative extinction is avoided and visible ﬂame extinction occurs at a much smaller droplet size either by micro-explosion of the droplet or by diffusive extinction.
source_title: Cool-flame Extinction During N-Alkane Droplet Combustion in Microgravity

topic: 75% helium: hot flame died in a fraction of a second, brief cool flame followed
claim: In test R707 of the paper's n-octane series, at 75% helium dilution and initial diameter 2.49 mm, the hot flame died within a fraction of a second and a short cool flame followed. The entire process was transient and quasi-steady burning was not achieved.
quote: When helium dilution was increased to 75% by volume in test R707 for D0 of 2.49 mm first stage burning is almost eliminated (see, Fig. (2d)). The hot flame that formed during the ignition dies within a fraction of a second and the cool flame burning commences immediately which also ends quickly leaving the droplet to evaporate. The high thermal conductivity of helium leads to large heat loss from the flame zone and as a consequence the flame temperature rapidly decreases leading to cool flame extinction. The entire process was transient and quasi- steady burning was not achieved.
source_title: Cool-flame Extinction During N-Alkane Droplet Combustion in Microgravity

topic: Post-visible-flame diameter regression exceeded the pure-evaporation comparison
claim: For an n-octane droplet with initial diameter 3.61 mm, the paper reports a decrease in burning rate at visible-flame extinction, while the post-extinction rate remained above the pure-evaporation comparison.
quote: Figures 9a, 9d and 9e show such a decrease for n-octane with Do = 3.61 mm at about 1.0 s/mm2. At larger times the octane burning rate is much lower, though the post-extinction burning rate is still higher than the rate of pure evaporation for n-octane as shown by the green data in Fig. 9a.
source_title: Effect of Varying the Initial Diameter of n-Octane and n-Decane Droplets over a Wide Range on the Spherically Symmetric Combustion Process: International Space Station and Ground-based Experiments (PSI-69, Presentations)

topic: Larger droplets appeared dimmer; less soot was inferred
claim: For initial diameters above 1.5 mm the flames appeared less luminous, which the authors interpreted as less sooty, and burning slowed as initial diameter increased. They conjecture a competition between radiative losses and residence-time effects.
quote: For Do > 1.5 mm the droplet flames appeared less luminous and therefore less sooty, yet the droplets continued to burn progressively slower as Do increased. This effect is conjectured to be the result of increased radiative losses that would tend to reduce sooting that outweigh the longer residence times of the larger droplets that would tend to increase sooting.

topic: Fuel mixture at elevated pressure: very weak visible flame, high burning rate

quote: Recent experiments involving large, bi-component fuel (n-decane and hexanol, 50/50 by volume) droplets at elevated pressures show that the visible, hot flame becomes extremely weak while the burning rate remains relatively high, suggesting the possibility of simultaneous presence of "cool" and "hot" flames of roughly equal importance. The radiant output from these bi-component droplets is relatively high and cannot be accounted for only by the presence of a visible hot-flame.

quote: No new anomalies or surprises were observed during the CFI experiments. However, as the ambient pressure is increased above 2 atm, multiple reignition cycles were observed, where first the hot flame extinguishes due to radiative heat loss followed by cool flame, and then reignition to a hot-flame followed by a cool flame, with this cycle repeating several times until the fuel droplet is completely consumed.

topic: Model: hot, warm and cool flame temperatures at elevated pressure
claim: The abstract reports simulations of isolated n-alkane droplets at elevated pressure in helium-substituted air. It predicts roughly 1500 K hot, 970 K warm and 765 K cool stages, with all three first appearing near 20% helium substitution and their duration strongly dependent on substitution from 20% to 60%. Above 60%, hot-flame extinction is followed only by the lower-temperature cool stage.
quote: Transient, isolated n-alkane droplet combustion is simulated at elevated pressure for helium-diluent substituted-air mixtures. We report the presence of unique quasi-steady, three-stage burning behavior of large sphero-symmetric n-alkane droplets at these elevated pressures and helium substituted ambient fractions. Upon initiation of reaction, hot-flame diffusive burning of large droplets is initiated that radiatively extinguishes to establish cool flame burning conditions in nitrogen/oxygen "air" at atmospheric and elevated pressures. However, at elevated pressure and moderate helium substitution for nitrogen ( X He > 20%), the initiated cool flame burning proceeds through two distinct, quasi-steady-state, cool flame burning conditions. The classical "Hot flame " ( ∼1500 K) radiatively extinguishes into a "Warm flame " burning mode at a moderate maximum reaction zone temperature ( ∼ 970 K), followed by a transition to a lower temperature ( ∼765 K), quasi-steady "Cool flame " burning condition. The reaction zone ("flame") temperatures are associated with distinctly different yields in intermediate reaction products within the reaction zones and surrounding near-field, and the flame-standoff ratios characterizing each burning mode progressively decrease. The presence of all three stages first appears with helium substitution near 20%, and the duration of each stage is observed to be strongly dependent on helium substitutions level between 20-60%. For helium substitution greater than 60%, the hot flame extinction is followed by only the lower temperature cool flame burning mode.
source_title: Three Stage Cool Flame Droplet Burning Behavior of n-Alkane Droplets at Elevated Pressure Conditions: Hot, Warm and Cool Flame
