quote: Figure 18 reveals that smoke points of nonbuoyant coflowing flames decrease with increasing burner diameter. This behavior also can be attributed to effects of residence time, as fuel velocity is proportional to d–2 when fuel mass flow rate is constant.
source_title: Smoke Point in Co-flow Experiment (SPICE): Laminar Smoke Point Properties of Non-buoyant Round-Jet Diffusion Flames, Final Report (PSI-107 Reports)

topic: flame tip temperature at the smoke point
claim: The SPICE 30-day report cites earlier work finding that a buoyant flame stops burning out its smoke when its tip cools to about 1300 K, while a non-buoyant (microgravity) flame tip reaches 1000 K at its smoke point.
quote: Kent and Wagner [21] found that smoke burn out in the oxidative region of the flame ceases when the tip of a buoyant diffusion flame cools to approximately 1300 K. Urban et al. [22] found that the tip of a nonbuoyant (microgravity) flame reaches 1000 K at its smoke point.
source_title: Smoke Point In Coflow Experiment "SPICE", Microgravity Science Glovebox, Increment 19-20 (30 Day Report) (PSI-107 Reports)

topic: cause of flame-tip cooling
claim: The SPICE 30-day report states that the tip temperature drop is attributed mainly to heat conduction in buoyant flames and largely to radiative quenching in non-buoyant flames.
quote: In buoyant flames this decrease in temperature is attributed primarily to heat conduction, while in nonbuoyant flames it is attributed largely to radiative quenching [23].
source_title: Smoke Point In Coflow Experiment "SPICE", Microgravity Science Glovebox, Increment 19-20 (30 Day Report) (PSI-107 Reports)

topic: radiative loss at the smoke point
claim: The SPICE final report lists, as one proposed criterion, that the smoke point occurs at a radiative loss fraction of 0.2 – 0.4 for normal-gravity flames and 0.4 – 0.6 for microgravity flames.
quote: The second is that smoke point occurs when radiative loss fraction reaches 0.2 - 0.4 for normal-gravity flames12-16 or 0.4 - 0.6 for microgravity flames.
source_title: Smoke Point in Co-flow Experiment (SPICE): Laminar Smoke Point Properties of Non-buoyant Round-Jet Diffusion Flames, Final Report (PSI-107 Reports)

topic: open-tipped smoking flames
claim: The SPICE final report says open-tipped flames are common in microgravity when smoke points are far exceeded, with flame extinguishment along the centerline and soot escaping in an annular shell.
quote: Open-tipped flames are common in microgravity when smoke points are far exceeded4 and are associated with flame extinguishment along the centerline and soot that escapes in an annular shell.
source_title: Smoke Point in Co-flow Experiment (SPICE): Laminar Smoke Point Properties of Non-buoyant Round-Jet Diffusion Flames, Final Report (PSI-107 Reports)

topic: how the smoke point looks
claim: In SPICE some smoke points, particularly for propane and ethylene, were identified by gradual dimming, reddening and rounding of the luminous flame tip.
quote: Some smoke points (particularly for propane and ethylene) were identified by the onset of gradual dimming, reddening, and rounding of the luminous flame tip. Conversely, the brightest flames (particularly for propylene and propylene mixtures) normally did not display significant dimming and reddening near their tips, except when much longer than their smoke points. For these flames, smoke points were identified by the rapid transition to open-tipped flames.
source_title: Smoke Point in Co-flow Experiment (SPICE): Laminar Smoke Point Properties of Non-buoyant Round-Jet Diffusion Flames, Final Report (PSI-107 Reports)

topic: soot path in non-buoyant flames
claim: The SPICE final report states that in non-buoyant flames most soot first forms near the cool core of the flame and is drawn directly toward the flame sheet, a process it calls completely different from buoyant flames.
quote: The soot formation process for nonbuoyant flames is completely different: most of the soot initially forms near the cool core of the flame, where φ is close to 2, and is drawn directly toward the flame sheet.
source_title: Smoke Point in Co-flow Experiment (SPICE): Laminar Smoke Point Properties of Non-buoyant Round-Jet Diffusion Flames, Final Report (PSI-107 Reports)

topic: radiation-dominated smoke point
claim: The SPICE final report states that results from the Laminar Soot Processes experiment showed that removing buoyancy can make the smoke point dominated by radiative heat losses at low flame velocity, with the flame extinguishing at its tip and letting soot escape.
quote: Results from an MSL-1 combustion project, the Laminar Soot Processes (LSP), revealed that the smoke height phenomenon in microgravity can be substantially different form that seen in normal gravity. The removal of buoyancy induced acceleration can cause the smoke point phenomenon to be dominated by radiative heat losses for conditions of low overall flame velocity. Under these conditions the flame extinguishes at the flame tip allowing soot to be emitted. In spite of this effect, it is still possible to have flames that either emit soot along all stream lines or do not emit soot anywhere, for conditions where radiation losses do not dominate.
source_title: Smoke Point in Co-flow Experiment (SPICE): Laminar Smoke Point Properties of Non-buoyant Round-Jet Diffusion Flames, Final Report (PSI-107 Reports)

topic: propane sooting in microgravity
claim: The SPICE final report abstract says the measurements allow estimates of pseudo threshold soot indices for microgravity diffusion flames and indicate an unusually high sooting propensity for propane in microgravity.
quote: The measurements allow estimates of pseudo threshold soot indices (TSI) for microgravity diffusion flames, indicating an unusually high sooting propensity for propane in microgravity.
source_title: Smoke Point in Co-flow Experiment (SPICE): Laminar Smoke Point Properties of Non-buoyant Round-Jet Diffusion Flames, Final Report (PSI-107 Reports)

topic: 2012 retest of the propane anomaly
claim: The preliminary SPICE findings in the 30-day report included in the SLICE final report say the smoke points were consistent with SPICE-1, the potential propane anomaly was not observed, and the trends agreed with 1g although quantitative values were very different.
quote: Thus far, the SPICE results show that the smoke points for these conditions are consistent with those from SPICE-1. The potential anomalous result seen in SPICE- 1 for propane was not observed and the smoke point trends are consistent with 1g conditions although the quantitative values are very different.
source_title: SLICE Final Report (2017), Structure & Liftoff In Combustion Experiment (PSI-106 Raw Data/Legacy)

topic: methane did not reach a smoke point in 2009
claim: In the 2009 SPICE tests smoke points were attempted with methane but could not be obtained before the flames reached the copper plate at the end of the duct.
quote: Smoke points were attempted with methane, but could not be obtained before the flames impinged on the copper plate at the end of the duct.
source_title: Smoke Point in Co-flow Experiment (SPICE): Laminar Smoke Point Properties of Non-buoyant Round-Jet Diffusion Flames, Final Report (PSI-107 Reports)

topic: time to steady flame
claim: SPICE flames generally reached steady conditions within 5 s of ignition or of a change in fuel or air flow rate.
quote: The flames generally reached steady conditions within 5 s of ignition or a change in flow rate of fuel or air.
source_title: Smoke Point in Co-flow Experiment (SPICE): Laminar Smoke Point Properties of Non-buoyant Round-Jet Diffusion Flames, Final Report (PSI-107 Reports)

topic: soot clogs the outlet screen
claim: The only significant SPICE anomaly was soot accumulating in the outlet screen, which changed the flow in the duct; a crew member fixed it by vacuuming the screen.
quote: SPICE operated very successfully with the only significant anomaly being the accumulation of soot in the outlet screen which changed the flow behavior in the duct. This was corrected by a crew member using the vacuum to clean the outlet screen on June 15.
source_title: Smoke Point In Coflow Experiment "SPICE", Microgravity Science Glovebox, Increment 19-20 (30 Day Report) (PSI-107 Reports)

topic: toxic gas from smoking flames
claim: The SPICE final report states that carbon monoxide emitted by smoking flames is the major cause of death in fires.
quote: Carbon monoxide emitted by smoking flames is the major cause of death in fires.
source_title: Smoke Point in Co-flow Experiment (SPICE): Laminar Smoke Point Properties of Non-buoyant Round-Jet Diffusion Flames, Final Report (PSI-107 Reports)

topic: why soot matters for fire spread
claim: The SPICE fact sheet says previous experiments show that soot dominates the heat emitted from flames in normal-gravity and microgravity fires, and that controlling this heat emission is critical for preventing fire spread on Earth and in space.
quote: Previous experiments show that soot dominates the heat emitted from flames in normal gravity and microgravity fires. Control of this heat emission is critical for prevention of the spread of fires on Earth and in space for the design of efficient combustion systems (jet engines and power generation boilers).
source_title: Smoke Point in Co-flow Experiment (SPICE) fact sheet

topic: limits of Earth-based material screening
claim: The SPICE fact sheet says current NASA spacecraft materials selection uses a simplified test method that sorts materials by their behavior on Earth without real consideration of microgravity effects.
quote: Current NASA spacecraft materials selection is based upon a simpliﬁed test method that segregates material based upon behavior on Earth without real consideration of microgravity effects.
source_title: Smoke Point in Co-flow Experiment (SPICE) fact sheet

topic: normal-gravity comparison of co-flow effect
claim: The SPICE thesis reports that in normal Earth gravity co-flow velocity had mixed effects: smoke points increased with co-flow velocity for burner diameters of 0.41, 0.76 and 1.6 mm, while for an unconfined co-flow burner of 13.7 mm diameter the smoke point length decreased with increasing co-flow velocity for ethylene and propylene and increased for propane.
quote: In normal earth gravity coflow velocity exhibited mixed effects. For burner diameters of 0.41, 0.76, and 1.6 mm, smoke points increased with increases of coflow velocity. For an unconfined coflow burner with a burner diameter of 13.7 mm smoke point length decreased with increasing coflow velocity for ethylene and propylene, while increasing for propane flames.
source_title: Smoke Points of Microgravity and Normal Gravity Coflow Diffusion Flames, K. T. Dotson, M.S. thesis (PSI-107 Reports)

topic: co-flow and burner size cannot be ignored
claim: The SPICE thesis concludes that the smoke point depends on the choice of co-flow velocity and burner diameter and that these factors cannot be assumed negligible.
quote: It has shown that the smoke point depends on choice of coflow velocity and burner diameter; these factors cannot be assumed away as negligible.
source_title: Smoke Points of Microgravity and Normal Gravity Coflow Diffusion Flames, K. T. Dotson, M.S. thesis (PSI-107 Reports)

topic: flames need forced airflow in microgravity
claim: The SLICE final report states that microgravity flames tend to quench without buoyant convection, which normally brings air to a flame, and that glovebox combustion experiments have therefore typically used fans to provide forced convection.
quote: Microgravity flames tend to quench in the absence of buoyant convection, which normally transports air to flames, so the glovebox combustion experiments have typically incorporated fans to provide forced convection since that start.
source_title: SLICE Final Report (2017), Structure & Liftoff In Combustion Experiment (PSI-106 Raw Data/Legacy)

topic: dilute flames stay attached in microgravity
claim: The preliminary SLICE findings say microgravity flames were generally wider and less likely to lift off than their 1g counterparts, and more highly diluted flames could be stabilized in microgravity.
quote: Due to the lack of buoyancy force, the microgravity (0g) flames are generally wider and less likely to lift off than their 1 g counterparts, and flames with higher dilution levels can be stabilized in microgravity.
source_title: SLICE Final Report (2017), Structure & Liftoff In Combustion Experiment (PSI-106 Raw Data/Legacy)

topic: diluted flame: lifted in 1g, attached in 0g
claim: For a pair of diluted flames shown in the SLICE report, the 1g flame was lifted while its 0g counterpart was attached and even formed a small soot cone.
quote: For the diluted flames, the 1g flame is lifted while its 0g counterpart is attached, and a small soot cone is even formed in the 0g flame.
source_title: SLICE Final Report (2017), Structure & Liftoff In Combustion Experiment (PSI-106 Raw Data/Legacy)

topic: soot temperature and amount, 1g versus 0g
claim: For the sooty-flame pair in the preliminary SLICE report, soot pyrometry gave a 1g temperature about 200 K higher than the 0g value and a soot volume fraction about an order of magnitude smaller.
quote: The temperature of the 1g flame is about 200 K higher than that of the 0 g flame since there is less radiative loss. The soot volume fraction of the 1g flame is about an order of magnitude smaller than that of the 0g flame.
source_title: SLICE Final Report (2017), Structure & Liftoff In Combustion Experiment (PSI-106 Raw Data/Legacy)

topic: soot increase factor in microgravity
claim: In the SLICE soot study the microgravity flames were sootier than the normal-gravity flames by a factor of approximately 4 to 8 in peak soot volume fraction.
quote: From the experiments, the microgravity flames were found to be sootier than normal gravity flames by a factor of approximately 4 to 8 in terms of the peak soot volume fraction (based on the uncertainty of the soot dispersion exponent and temperature measurements).

topic: longer residence time, more soot
claim: A 30-day report in the SLICE final report states that soot residence time is greatly enhanced in microgravity, leading to lower soot temperatures and greater soot volume fractions.
quote: The soot residence time is also greatly enhanced in microgravity, which leads to lower soot temperatures and greater soot volume fractions.

topic: soot moves to the flame wings
claim: In SLICE the soot distribution tended to shift from the centerline of the flame in normal gravity to the wings in microgravity.
quote: The soot distribution tends to shift from the centerline of the flame to the wings from normal gravity to microgravity.
source_title: An Experimental and Computational Study on Soot Formation in a Coflow Jet Flame Under Microgravity and Normal Gravity

topic: lift-off velocities and stability
claim: A status note in the SLICE final report says the microgravity flames lifted at significantly greater velocities than the normal-gravity flames but were much less stable once lifted.
quote: The microgravity flames have lifted at significantly greater velocities than the normal-gravity flames, but upon lifting have been much less stable.
source_title: SLICE Final Report (2017), Structure & Liftoff In Combustion Experiment (PSI-106 Raw Data/Legacy)

topic: blowout near the lift-off limit
claim: In SLICE, as the flow was slowly increased toward the lift-off limit the flame detached from the burner, in some cases stabilizing above it but often blowing out.
quote: Generally, the flow was slowly increased as the flame approached the liftoff limit where it detaches from the burner and in some cases stabilizes above the burner but often blows out (i.e., extinguishes) as in this example.
source_title: SLICE Final Report (2017), Structure & Liftoff In Combustion Experiment (PSI-106 Raw Data/Legacy)

topic: co-flow lowers the lift-off fuel velocity
claim: A preliminary SLICE lift-off limit plot for methane shows the flame lifting at lower fuel velocities when the co-flow velocity is increased.
quote: A preliminary example of the flame liftoff limit for methane is shown below. As can be seen, the flame lifts at lower fuel velocities when the coflow velocity is increased.
source_title: SLICE Final Report (2017), Structure & Liftoff In Combustion Experiment (PSI-106 Raw Data/Legacy)

topic: unexpected soot from diluted methane
claim: In SLICE, soot appeared in 70% methane flames, a dilution not expected to reach smoking conditions; the note attributes it to longer residence times from reduced velocities in the near absence of buoyant convection.
quote: It was interesting to see the soot in the 70% methane flames, as that dilution wasn’t expected to approach or reach smoking conditions. Yet with the near absence of buoyant convection in microgravity, the reduced velocities lead to longer residence times and enhanced soot production.
source_title: SLICE Final Report (2017), Structure & Liftoff In Combustion Experiment (PSI-106 Raw Data/Legacy)

topic: soot release collapsed the airflow
claim: After SLICE tests run above the smoke point with soot streaming from the flame, the reference air velocity at maximum fan voltage fell to one fifth of its previous value, from ~43 cm/s to ~9 cm/s.
quote: The fan calibration at the end of this day’s session revealed a dramatic drop in the coflow where Stocker had guided Petit through test conditions that exceeded the smoke point, i.e., where soot was streaming out of the flame. In contrast, the SPICE procedure was to reach and identify the smoke point and then reduce the flow to avoid the soot release. With the fan at the maximum voltage during the calibration, the reference velocity dropped to one fifth of what it had been at the end of the previous session (on March 19), i.e., from ~43 cm/s to ~9 cm/s.
source_title: SLICE Final Report (2017), Structure & Liftoff In Combustion Experiment (PSI-106 Raw Data/Legacy)

topic: known flow degradation from soot
claim: The SLICE report describes a general decline in air velocity consistent with soot accumulation, while noting fluctuations and measurement uncertainty.
quote: Furthermore, fluctuations can be seen in the rest of the plot, suggesting uncertainty regardless of the GMT 040 results, although the general trend was decreasing air velocity with time which is reasonable given the known degradation of the flow with the accumulation of soot.
source_title: SLICE Final Report (2017), Structure & Liftoff In Combustion Experiment (PSI-106 Raw Data/Legacy)

topic: co-flow raises peak CH* concentration

topic: only one atmosphere tested for gas-jet flames in space

topic: tilted lifted flames point to uneven duct flow

topic: smoke particle size, microgravity versus Earth
claim: In the PSI-115 simulations without recirculation, the mode particle diameter of microgravity smoke was about 10 µm, roughly twice that of terrestrial smoke.
quote: Without recirculation, the mode particle diameter in microgravity is ∼ 10 µm, or approximately twice that of terrestrial smoke.
source_title: Utilization of the SAME Data for Advanced Modeling and Simulation of Smoke Generation in Microgravity, NASA Grant NNX17AF08A Final Report (PSI-115 Reports)

topic: very large particles survive without settling
claim: In the PSI-115 simulations, when the microgravity particle size distribution was bimodal its larger mode held particles above 35 µm, a size range in which the terrestrial distribution had effectively none.
quote: Microgravity smoke presented in this study contains larger particles than terrestrial smoke. When the microgravity PSD is bimodal, the larger mode contains particles with dp > 35 µm, while the terrestrial PSD contains effectively zero particles in this size range.
source_title: Utilization of the SAME Data for Advanced Modeling and Simulation of Smoke Generation in Microgravity, NASA Grant NNX17AF08A Final Report (PSI-115 Reports)

topic: recirculation zones grow the largest particles
claim: In the PSI-115 simulations a bimodal particle size distribution appeared in microgravity when prominent recirculation occurred behind the hot vapor source.
quote: A bimodal particle size distribution results in microgravity when prominent recirculation occurs behind the hot vapor source.
source_title: Utilization of the SAME Data for Advanced Modeling and Simulation of Smoke Generation in Microgravity, NASA Grant NNX17AF08A Final Report (PSI-115 Reports)

topic: measured size ratio cited from earlier work
claim: The PSI-115 final report cites measurements suggesting microgravity smoke particles are 2 to 8 times larger than terrestrial smoke particles.
quote: Measurements suggest microgravity smoke particles to be 2 − 8 times larger than terrestrial smoke particles (Urban et al., 2005).
source_title: Utilization of the SAME Data for Advanced Modeling and Simulation of Smoke Generation in Microgravity, NASA Grant NNX17AF08A Final Report (PSI-115 Reports)

topic: Earth-calibrated detectors may misread
claim: The PSI-115 final report states that smoke detection systems developed and calibrated for terrestrial use may not perform correctly in microgravity because of inappropriate particle size sensitivities.
quote: Understanding gravitational effects is of practical interest because it assists in the design of mission-critical smoke detection systems for use in microgravity environments, including the Interna- tional Space Station (Mulholland et al., 2015); systems developed and calibrated for terrestrial use may not perform correctly in microgravity because of inappropriate particle size sensitivities (Urban et al., 2005).
source_title: Utilization of the SAME Data for Advanced Modeling and Simulation of Smoke Generation in Microgravity, NASA Grant NNX17AF08A Final Report (PSI-115 Reports)

topic: large particles persist in cabin air
claim: The PSI-115 final report cites measurements that large particles persist in microgravity, with mass concentrations of particles larger than 100 µm at ten times those of a nominal terrestrial environment.
quote: Moreover, large particles (not only smoke particles) persist in microgravity, with mass concentrations of particles with diameter > 100 μm measured at ten-times that of a nominal terrestrial environment (Liu et al., 1991).
source_title: Utilization of the SAME Data for Advanced Modeling and Simulation of Smoke Generation in Microgravity, NASA Grant NNX17AF08A Final Report (PSI-115 Reports)

topic: three mechanisms behind the size difference
claim: The PSI-115 final report names three mechanisms that differentiate microgravity and Earth-gravity smoke: different recirculation geometries, particle settling that removes large particles on Earth, and buoyant convection carrying condensable species toward cool surfaces.
quote: Results exhibit three primary mechanisms that differentiate the microgravity and Earth gravity smoke: (1) different re- circulation geometries and volumes modify the time-temperature-concentration history of the aerosol in regions of high temperature and high vapor mass fraction; (2) particle settling eliminates large particles from Earth gravity smoke, which reduces the maximum particle size and modifies aerosol development by changing coagulation and condensation rates of the remaining particles; (3) buoyant convection can transport condensible species toward relatively cool surfaces, increasing vapor-to-particle conversion. Each of these factors tend to increase the size of particles in microgravity relative to Earth gravity. How- ever, each of these factors is also highly material- and geometry-dependent: (1) the wake dynamic becomes unimportant if nucleation occurs far downstream of the wake, or if there is a time dependent flow without a stable recirculation region; (2) particle settling is irrelevant if the condensing species forms particles that are too small to settle (the DBP considered in this work forms large particles); (3) if smoke is produced in an open environment, there may not be cool surfaces nearby to increase nucleation rates. In these situations, microgravity and Earth gravity smoke are hypothesized to be more similar.
source_title: Utilization of the SAME Data for Advanced Modeling and Simulation of Smoke Generation in Microgravity, NASA Grant NNX17AF08A Final Report (PSI-115 Reports)

topic: when the gravity effect may vanish
claim: The PSI-115 final report says each of these factors is also highly material- and geometry-dependent: the wake dynamic becomes unimportant if nucleation occurs far downstream of the wake or the flow has no stable recirculation region, and particle settling is irrelevant if the condensing species forms particles too small to settle.
quote: How- ever, each of these factors is also highly material- and geometry-dependent: (1) the wake dynamic becomes unimportant if nucleation occurs far downstream of the wake, or if there is a time dependent flow without a stable recirculation region; (2) particle settling is irrelevant if the condensing species forms particles that are too small to settle (the DBP considered in this work forms large particles); (3) if smoke is produced in an open environment, there may not be cool surfaces nearby to increase nucleation rates. In these situations, microgravity and Earth gravity smoke are hypothesized to be more similar.
source_title: Utilization of the SAME Data for Advanced Modeling and Simulation of Smoke Generation in Microgravity, NASA Grant NNX17AF08A Final Report (PSI-115 Reports)

topic: hot flame turns into a cool flame

topic: temperature at the hot-to-cool transition

topic: cool flame temperatures

source_title: Extinction characteristics of isolated n-alkane fuel droplets during low temperature cool flame droplet burning in air, slides, T. Farouk and F. Dryer (PSI-117 Presentations)

topic: re-ignition with pressure

topic: burning regimes against pressure

topic: repeated hot-cool cycling

topic: cool flame without any hot flame
claim: The PSI-117 extinction slides state that sufficiently constraining the initiation energy can lead to single-stage sustained cool flame burning.
quote: Sufficiently constraining initiation energy can lead to single stage sustained cool flame burning.
source_title: Extinction characteristics of isolated n-alkane fuel droplets during low temperature cool flame droplet burning in air, slides, T. Farouk and F. Dryer (PSI-117 Presentations)

topic: helium dilution and a third burning stage
claim: The PSI-117 seminar slides state that introducing helium increases the burning rate and that at higher helium concentration a third-stage quasi-steady burn is observed.

source_title: Cool Flames in Space, NASA Physical Sciences Informatics (PSI) Seminar slides, T. Farouk (PSI-117 Presentations)

topic: cool flame extinction diameter against pressure
claim: The PSI-117 extinction slides say the modeled cool-flame extinction diameter decreases with increasing pressure and is absent at 3 atm because the droplet burns to completion following warm-flame combustion.

source_title: Extinction characteristics of isolated n-alkane fuel droplets during low temperature cool flame droplet burning in air, slides, T. Farouk and F. Dryer (PSI-117 Presentations)

topic: heavier fuels hold cool flames better
claim: The PSI-117 extinction slides state that cool flame extinction properties are significantly affected by the molecular weight of the n-alkane.
quote: Cool flame extinction properties are significantly affected by the n-alkane molecular weight, and the chain length of the n-alkane has significant effect on the cool flame reactivity - larger n- alkane exhibited more robust cool flame (i.e., higher temperature) and hence smaller extinction diameters.
source_title: Extinction characteristics of isolated n-alkane fuel droplets during low temperature cool flame droplet burning in air, slides, T. Farouk and F. Dryer (PSI-117 Presentations)

topic: model validated on FLEX
claim: The PSI-117 seminar summary says the cool-flame models were validated against FLEX data and then used to explore other scenarios.
quote: Models were validated against the FLEX data and then utilized to explore other scenarios
source_title: Cool Flames in Space, NASA Physical Sciences Informatics (PSI) Seminar slides, T. Farouk (PSI-117 Presentations)

topic: warm flame links cool and hot flames
claim: The PSI-142 record states that the warm flame has a double reaction zone structure and plays a critical role in the transition between cool flames and hot flames.
quote: The results showed that the warm flame has a double reaction zone structure and plays a critical role in the transition between cool flames and hot flames.
source_title: PSI record PSI-142: Quantitative Studies of Cool Flame Transitions at Radiation / Stretch Extinction Using Counterflow Flames

topic: pressure widens cool and warm flame limits
claim: The PSI-142 record states that at elevated pressures the flammable region of warm flames and cool flames expands, because low- and intermediate-temperature reactivity increases with pressure.
quote: At elevated pressures, it was found that the flammable region of warm flames and cool flames expands due to the increase in low-temperature and intermediate-temperature reactivity with pressure.
source_title: PSI record PSI-142: Quantitative Studies of Cool Flame Transitions at Radiation / Stretch Extinction Using Counterflow Flames

topic: why warm flames matter in microgravity
claim: The PSI-142 record says understanding the warm diffusion flame is particularly relevant to microgravity environments because long residence times are possible there.
quote: Obtaining a fundamental understanding of the warm diffusion flame is particularly relevant to combustion in highly turbulent flow fields and in microgravity environments, owing to the possibility of long residence times.
source_title: PSI record PSI-142: Quantitative Studies of Cool Flame Transitions at Radiation / Stretch Extinction Using Counterflow Flames

topic: factors hypothesised to control the cool flame transition
claim: The PSI-142 record hypothesizes that oxygen concentration, dilution, pressure, diffusion and convection transport processes affect the cool flame transition.
quote: The investigation hypothesizes that factors such as oxygen concentration, dilution, pressure, diffusion, and convection transport processes affect the cool flame transition.
source_title: PSI record PSI-142: Quantitative Studies of Cool Flame Transitions at Radiation / Stretch Extinction Using Counterflow Flames

topic: what the data set contains
claim: The PSI-142 record describes three numerical schemes for comparing oxygen effects on cool-flame extinction: n-heptane/air spark-assisted propagation, freely propagating DME flames, and elevated-pressure DME/air burning limits.
quote: Using the experimental conditions of FLEX flight, a comparative studies of the oxygen concentration effects on the extinction limits of cool flames was conducted using three different numerical modeling schemes, (a) spark-assisted flame propagation of a n-heptane/air mixture, (b) one dimensional freely-propagating dimethyl ether (DME) flames using an arc-length continuation method and (c) simulated cool flame regimes and burning limits at elevated pressure (up to 20\u202fatm) using DME/air mixtures.
source_title: PSI record PSI-142: Quantitative Studies of Cool Flame Transitions at Radiation / Stretch Extinction Using Counterflow Flames

topic: flame spread rate against oxygen and pressure
claim: The SSCE leading-edge flame spread rate determined from the film was 0.092 cm/s at 35% oxygen and 1.0 atm, 0.150 cm/s at 1.5 atm, and 0.358, 0.454 and 0.547 cm/s at 50% oxygen for 1.0, 1.5 and 2.0 atm (the scanned text prints "1.0" as "l.0").
quote: The nominal leading-edge spread rate determined from the film for the 35% oxygen/l.0 atm experiment here is 0.092 cm/s, while at 1.5 atm it is 0.150 cm/s, and at 50% oxygen, for 1.0, 1.5, and 2.0 atm it is 0.358, 0.454, and 0.547 cm/s, respectively.
source_title: The Solid Surface Combustion Experiment Aboard the USML-1 Mission, Joint L+1 Science Review for USML-1 and USMP-1 (PSI-108 Reports)

topic: trend of spread rate with oxygen and pressure
claim: Across the five SSCE thin-fuel experiments, flame spread rate increased with increasing ambient oxygen content and pressure, and flame brightness and visible soot radiation increased with spread rate.
quote: Experimental results from the five experiments indicate that flame spread rate increases with increasing ambient oxygen content and pressure. The brightness of the flame and the visible soot radiation also increase with increasing spread rate.
source_title: The Solid Surface Combustion Experiment Aboard the USML-1 Mission, Joint L+1 Science Review for USML-1 and USMP-1 (PSI-108 Reports)

topic: flame nearly invisible at 35% oxygen
claim: In the SSCE films, flame brightness ranged from nearly undetectable in the 35% oxygen case to near saturation at 50% oxygen; at 35% oxygen the flame image from the top was not detectable on film.
quote: The apparent brightness of the flames varies from nearly undetectable in this 35% oxygen case to near saturation, indicating enhanced soot production both with increasing atmospheric oxygen content and pressure, particularly at 50% oxygen. For 35% oxygen a flame image from the top is not detectable on film, but the 1 Hz strobe 87 lightin thechamber allows the progress of the apparent pyrolysis front across the sample to be seen.
source_title: The Solid Surface Combustion Experiment Aboard the USML-1 Mission, Joint L+1 Science Review for USML-1 and USMP-1 (PSI-108 Reports)

topic: fuel left behind the flame
claim: In the SSCE test at 35% oxygen the fuel was not entirely consumed as the flame passed, unlike at 35% oxygen in normal gravity, which the report says suggests pyrolysis products may be available far behind the flame leading edge.
quote: In the top view, there is evidence that the fuel was not entirely consumed as the flame passed, as it would have been at 35% oxygen in normal gravity. This observation suggests that pyrolysis products may be available far behind the flame leading edge.
source_title: The Solid Surface Combustion Experiment Aboard the USML-1 Mission, Joint L+1 Science Review for USML-1 and USMP-1 (PSI-108 Reports)

topic: flame size at 35% oxygen
claim: In the SSCE USML-1 test at 35% oxygen the visible flame was symmetrical about its midpoint and, after the ignition transient, steady with a maximum visible height of 0.5 cm and a length of 1.4 cm.
quote: For the USML-1 experiment at 35% oxygen, the shape of the visible flame is symmetrical about the midpoint of its length, and, after the ignition transient, becomes steady with a maximum visible height of 0.5 cm and a length of 1.4 cm.
source_title: The Solid Surface Combustion Experiment Aboard the USML-1 Mission, Joint L+1 Science Review for USML-1 and USMP-1 (PSI-108 Reports)

topic: radiation matters in low-flow microgravity flames
claim: The SSCE report states that buoyancy-induced flows are generally strong enough to suppress radiative effects, which prove to be important in the low-flow environments obtained in microgravity.
quote: Buoyancy induced flows are generally strong enough to suppress radiative effects, which prove to be important in the low-flow environments that is obtained in microgravity.
source_title: The Solid Surface Combustion Experiment Aboard the USML-1 Mission, Joint L+1 Science Review for USML-1 and USMP-1 (PSI-108 Reports)

topic: blue to orange with faster spread
claim: The SSCE report concludes that flame brightness increases as spread rate increases with atmospheric conditions, and that flame color changes from blue to orange, indicating increased soot production.
quote: The brightness of the flames increases as the spread rate increases with atmospheric conditions, and the color of the flame changes from blue to orange, indicating increased soot production.
source_title: The Solid Surface Combustion Experiment Aboard the USML-1 Mission, Joint L+1 Science Review for USML-1 and USMP-1 (PSI-108 Reports)

topic: surface-tension flows replace buoyant flows in liquids
claim: The STDCE paper introduction, citing Ostrach (1982), says buoyancy usually overshadows thermocapillary flow on Earth except in small configurations, whereas thermocapillarity becomes important in reduced gravity.
quote: In a terrestrial environment such flows are usually overshadowed by buoyancy-driven flows, except in configurations of small dimension (less than several ram). In the reduced gravity environment of space, however, buoyancy is greatly reduced and thermocapillarity becomes an important driving force for fluid motion (Ostrach, 1982).
source_title: Surface Tension Driven Convection Experiment (STDCE), Joint L+1 Science Review for USML-1 and USMP-1 (PSI-108 Reports)

topic: combustion link stated by PSI
claim: The PSI-108 record says the non-intrusive measurement techniques developed for STDCE, such as infrared imaging and particle image velocimetry, are now widely used on Earth, including in the study of combustion processes.
quote: The development and refinement of non-intrusive measurement techniques, such as infrared imaging and particle image velocimetry, for the STDCE have expanded the toolkit for studying fluid flows in various settings. These techniques are now widely employed in research and industrial applications on Earth, including the study of combustion processes, crystal growth, and microfluidics.
source_title: PSI record PSI-108: Surface Tension Driven Convection Experiment-1

topic: flame spread rate, large thin fabric, concurrent flow
claim: The 40.6 cm x 94 cm cotton-fiberglass (SIBAL) sheet burning in air at 20 cm/s concurrent flow spread at an average 1.8 mm/s with an estimated average flame power of 1200 +/- 300 W.
quote: SIBAL fabric (40.6 cm x 94 cm) burning in air at 20 cm/s concurrent flow Average flame spread rate is 1.8 mm/s; estimated average flame power is 1200 +/- 300 W
source_title: Results of Large-Scale Spacecraft Flammability Tests

topic: steady flame size in concurrent flow
claim: In the concurrent-flow test the flame size stayed constrained after the ignition transient, which does not happen in 1-g.
quote: For the concurrent flame spread test, the flame size remained constrained after the ignition transient, which is not the case in 1-g.
source_title: Results of Large-Scale Spacecraft Flammability Tests

topic: earth comparison: upward flame accelerates
claim: On Earth an upward-spreading flame on a sample of this size accelerates and grows; the Saffire result was qualitatively different.
quote: These results were qualitatively different from those on earth where an upward-spreading flame on a sample of this size accelerates and grows.
source_title: Results of Large-Scale Spacecraft Flammability Tests

topic: flame length plateau, concurrent vs opposed
claim: On the 40.6-cm-wide sample the concurrent flame length reached a plateau of around 40 mm; the opposed-flow flame was shorter at 24 mm.
quote: For the concurrent flame, the length reaches a plateau value of around 40 mm, while the opposed-flow flame is a bit shorter at 24 mm.
source_title: Results of Large-Scale Spacecraft Flammability Tests

topic: flame spread direction: concurrent vs opposed rate
claim: Average spread rate was 1.8 mm/s with the flow (concurrent) and 1.3 mm/s against it (opposed).
quote: The average concurrent-flow flame spread rate is 1.8 mm/s. The opposed-flow flame average spread rate 1.3 mm/s.
source_title: Results of Large-Scale Spacecraft Flammability Tests

topic: ventilation stop: thin fabric in air
claim: After burning for about 7 minutes, the flame on the large fabric sample went out immediately when the air flow was shut off.
quote: The flame burned the entire allotted test time of about 7 min. at which point the air flow was shut off and the flame immediately extinguished
source_title: Results of Large-Scale Spacecraft Flammability Tests

topic: smoldering after the flame has passed
claim: After the flame passed, exothermic smolder spots that kept burning leftover fuel were visible on the fabric.
quote: After the flame had passed, exothermic surface smolder spots burning some of the leftover fuel were visible
source_title: Results of Large-Scale Spacecraft Flammability Tests

topic: enclosure (duct) size effect on spread
claim: Compared with earlier microgravity tests in smaller tunnels, the flame in the larger tunnel spread more slowly even on a wider sample.
quote: Compared to previous microgravity work in smaller tunnels, the flame in the larger tunnel spread more slowly, even for a wider sample.
source_title: Results of Large-Scale Spacecraft Flammability Tests

topic: why small tunnels spread faster
claim: The slower spread in the larger tunnel is attributed to flow acceleration from hot-gas expansion in the smaller tunnels.
quote: This is attributed to the effect of flow acceleration in the smaller tunnels as a result of hot gas expansion.
source_title: Results of Large-Scale Spacecraft Flammability Tests

topic: flame fluctuation after ignition
claim: The flame length first fluctuated at about 1.4 Hz and became more stable at about 90 s.
quote: Initially the flame length fluctuated at about 1.4 Hz before finally becoming more stable at about 90 s
source_title: Results of Large-Scale Spacecraft Flammability Tests

topic: test record: oxygen and burn time (PSI table)
claim: PSI lists Saffire-I sample S1 as SIBAL fabric burned in concurrent flow at 20 cm/s air flow, 21.5 - 21.7 percent O2, for 420 s.
source_title: PSI-98 Experimental table SAFFIRE-1 (CSV)

topic: silicone: flammability in microgravity vs 1-g
claim: Silicone looked less flammable in microgravity than in normal gravity, at least at the flow speeds tested.
quote: Flammability of silicone in microgravity appears to be reduced compared to normal gravity, at least for the flow speeds tested.
source_title: Results of Large-Scale Spacecraft Flammability Tests

topic: silicone: none of four samples burned
claim: None of the silicone samples burned: when the igniter was switched off a tiny gas-phase flame remained, did not spread, and quickly went out.
quote: Results were convincing although rather anticlimactic as none of the silicone samples burned. When the igniter was powered off, a tiny gas phase flame remained but did not spread and quickly extinguished.
source_title: Results of Large-Scale Spacecraft Flammability Tests

topic: silicone 0.27 mm: 1-g complete burn vs microgravity none (PSI table)
claim: PSI table row for sample 2-1 (silicone, 0.27 mm): microgravity burn length about 0, while the 1-g burn was complete and acceleratory.

topic: silicone: 1-g flammability by thickness
claim: In normal-gravity upward tests the 0.61-mm silicone burned on average 7.6 cm of the available 30 cm before going out.
quote: The 0.61-mm thickness burned on average 7.6 cm of the available 30 cm before extinguishing
source_title: Results of Large-Scale Spacecraft Flammability Tests

topic: Nomex not ignited by a pilot flame in cabin air
claim: The PMMA starter gave an average flame power of 460 W (printed as 460 + 50 W) and, despite this heating load, the Nomex fabric was not ignited.
quote: The average flame power from the PMMA (assuming complete conversion of the fuel) was 460 + 50 W. Despite this significant heating load, the fabric was not ignited.
source_title: Results of Large-Scale Spacecraft Flammability Tests

topic: Nomex oxygen threshold on Earth
claim: On Earth, Nomex HT90-40 burns only when the oxygen concentration is raised to around 24 to 25%.
quote: On Earth, it will only burn if the oxygen concentration is increased to around 24 to 25%.
source_title: Results of Large-Scale Spacecraft Flammability Tests

topic: Nomex heat damage without ignition
claim: The first 1 cm of the Nomex fabric was significantly damaged, the first 5 cm completely blackened, and the rest had a black streak down its center.
quote: The first 1-cm of the fabric was significantly damaged, the first 5-cm was completely blackened, and the remainder had a black streak down its center.
source_title: Results of Large-Scale Spacecraft Flammability Tests

topic: sample width effect on spread rate
claim: At 20 cm/s the 5-cm-wide fabric sample spread marginally faster than the 40.6-cm-wide one: 2.1 versus 1.8 mm/s.
quote: The flame spread rate for the 5-cm-wide sample is marginally faster compared to the spread rate for the 40.6-cm-wide sample for the same flow speed of 20 cm/s (2.1 compared to 1.8 mm/s).

topic: thin fabric burn and spread rate (PSI table)

topic: thick PMMA: flame anchored, slow regression (PSI table note)
claim: On the thick PMMA samples the flames stayed anchored at the base of the sample, which regressed very slowly (0.01 to 0.04 mm/s).
quote: Note 4 The flames remain anchored at the base of the sample which has a very slow regression rate (0.01 to 0.04 mm/s)
source_title: PSI-99 Experimental table SAFFIRE-2 (CSV)

topic: thick PMMA flame length limit
claim: The two 5-cm-wide two-sided PMMA samples reached flame lengths of 8.0 cm (grooved) and 9.5 cm (flat).
quote: For Saffire II, the two PMMA 5 cm wide, two-sided samples grew to flame lengths of 8.0 cm for the grooved sample and 9.5 for the flat sample.
source_title: Fire Safety Implications of Preliminary Results from Saffire IV and V Experiments on Large Scale Spacecraft Fires

topic: average flame power of small samples

quote: Average flame power: Saffire 1: 1200 +/- 300 W Saffire 2: (SIBAL fabric) 200 +/- 50 W Saffire 2: (Thick PMMA) 600 +/- 100 W
source_title: Results of Large-Scale Spacecraft Flammability Tests

topic: reduced pressure as a ground stand-in for microgravity
claim: Reducing pressure slowed flame spread over the PMMA surface, approaching the spread seen in microgravity.
quote: Results show that reductions of pressure slow down the flame spread over the PMMA surface approaching that in microgravity.
source_title: Buoyancy Effects on Concurrent Flame Spread Over Thick PMMA

topic: limit of the reduced-pressure method
claim: Pressure would have to be reduced to the order of 20 kPa to simulate microgravity conditions, and some simplifications used in the analysis may not apply there.
quote: This is important since it would be necessary to reduce the pressure to values of the order of 20 kPa to simulate microgravity conditions and some of the simplifications used in the analysis may not be applicable to these environments.
source_title: Buoyancy Effects on Concurrent Flame Spread Over Thick PMMA

topic: dim blue flames at low pressure
claim: As pressure was reduced the flame weakened, giving dimmer blue flames at the lowest pressures.

source_title: Buoyancy Effects on Concurrent Flame Spread Over Thick PMMA

topic: reduced pressure for Moon or Mars gravity
claim: The authors state that concurrent spread over thick solids at Moon or Mars gravity can be simulated by reducing pressure so the mixed-flow gas velocity matches that at reduced gravity.
quote: Also, it is worth noting that at different gravity levels, such as on the Moon or Mars, the concurrent flame spread can be simulated for thick solids with a flame spread formulation as in Eq. (8) by reducing the pressure so that the mixed flow gas velocity remains the same than that at reduced gravity.
source_title: Buoyancy Effects on Concurrent Flame Spread Over Thick PMMA

topic: silicone ground test: removing forced flow
claim: In ground flammability tests run in anticipation of Saffire, silicone samples burning in the upward configuration under forced flow self-extinguished after the forced flow was removed.
quote: Samples in upward configuration burning under forced flow self extinguish after forced flow is removed
source_title: Buoyant Effects on the Flammability of Silicone Samples Planned for the Spacecraft Fire Experiment (Saffire)

topic: opposed spread rate at higher flow (table row)

topic: flame speed scales with air flow velocity
claim: The authors state that the flame speed is proportional to the air flow velocity.

source_title: Saffire: A Novel Approach to Study of Spacecraft Fire Safety Using Un-Manned Spacecraft

topic: steady spread on a large thin charring surface
claim: Flame spread over a large thin charring surface in low gravity showed that steady flame spread is possible, unlike in normal gravity.

topic: duct size sensitivity of concurrent spread

topic: re-growth when airflow is restored

topic: soot blocked the outlet screen

source_title: Fire Safety Implications of Preliminary Results from Saffire IV and V Experiments on Large Scale Spacecraft Fires

topic: deflagration from accumulated fuel vapor

topic: why fuel vapor accumulates in low gravity
claim: In normal gravity buoyancy tends to move hot vapors away from the source; in low gravity hot fuel vapors can accumulate more easily.
quote: Unlike in normal gravity where buoyancy tends to move hot vapors away from the source, in low gravity hot fuel vapors can more easily accumulate.
source_title: Fire Safety Implications of Preliminary Results from Saffire IV and V Experiments on Large Scale Spacecraft Fires

topic: speed of the deflagration

The right image is 267 ms later and the flame has filled the entire region below the sample and has induced a stronger flame above the sample.
source_title: Fire Safety Implications of Preliminary Results from Saffire IV and V Experiments on Large Scale Spacecraft Fires

topic: duct height effect on thin-fuel spread rate

topic: thick PMMA maximum flame length across atmospheres (table row)

topic: NASA-STD-6001 Test 1 and low-gravity behavior
claim: Passing the normal-gravity upward flammability test cannot be taken to mean a material will not burn under those conditions in low gravity.
quote: The test is quite successful at identifying highly flammable materials; however, the test cannot be assumed to indicate that a material will not burn under those conditions in low gravity.
source_title: Fire Safety Implications of Preliminary Results from Saffire IV and V Experiments on Large Scale Spacecraft Fires

topic: model of the vehicle response
claim: A Fire Dynamics Simulator model of Cygnus during Saffire-IV predicted the CO2 data reasonably, over-predicting in some cases, possibly because of uncertainty in the free air volume.
quote: The model did a reasonable job of predicting the CO2 data, while over-predicting in some cases. This could be due to a wide range of reasons, with one prevalent reason being the uncertainty in the vehicle free air volume.
source_title: Model Development of Large-Scale Spacecraft Fires During the Saffire-IV Experiments

topic: ventilation stop: thin cotton re-ignited after 70 s
claim: With the fan off for 70 seconds, the cotton flame grew back when flow resumed and burned another 150 seconds until the material was consumed.
quote: At approximately 280 seconds, the fan was turned off and remained off for 70 seconds. Despite this long interval, the flame grew back when the flow was turned on again and continued to burn for another 150 seconds until the material was consumed.
source_title: Fire Safety Implications of Preliminary Results from Saffire IV and V Experiments on Large Scale Spacecraft Fires

topic: what survives with the flow off: flamelets and embers
claim: About 10 s after the flow was turned off, both surviving small flamelets and glowing char embers were present.
quote: As seen in the image in Figure 3, there were both surviving flamelets and glowing char embers at the moment imaging stopped (~ 10 s after the flow was turned off).
source_title: Fire Safety Implications of Preliminary Results from Saffire IV and V Experiments on Large Scale Spacecraft Fires

topic: likely cause of re-ignition
claim: The authors judge it likely that survival of a flamelet, at the edge of unburned fuel, led to the reignition.
quote: However, since the embers are typically isolated in a larger area of charred material and the flamelets are typically at the edge of unburned fuel, it is likely that survival of a flamelet led to the reignition.
source_title: Fire Safety Implications of Preliminary Results from Saffire IV and V Experiments on Large Scale Spacecraft Fires

topic: low flow then stop gave immediate extinction
claim: On Saffire V-3, after an extended 300 second interval at reduced air flow (5 cm/s), the flame extinguished quickly when the flow was turned off.
quote: After an extended (300 second) interval at reduced air flow (5 cm/s), the flame extinguished quickly when the flow was turned off.
source_title: Fire Safety Implications of Preliminary Results from Saffire IV and V Experiments on Large Scale Spacecraft Fires

topic: reduced flow as a strategy: caution
claim: Reduced air flow can extinguish faster than zero flow through convective cooling, but as a strategy it carries other risks given uncertain configurations and flow rates in a spacecraft.
quote: Furthermore, using reduced air flow rather than going to zero air flow can lead to more rapid extinction due to the convective cooling. However, as an extinguishment strategy, this would carry other risks given the uncertainty of configurations and flow rates in a spacecraft.
source_title: Fire Safety Implications of Preliminary Results from Saffire IV and V Experiments on Large Scale Spacecraft Fires

topic: extinction under quiescent conditions is not assured
claim: Extinction cannot be assumed to occur quickly under quiescent conditions; thin materials, higher oxygen concentrations and heating of the solid fuel can all support extended burning.
quote: These results indicate that extinction of the fire cannot be assumed to occur quickly under quiescent conditions. Thin materials, higher oxygen concentrations and heating of the solid fuel can all support extended burning.
source_title: Fire Safety Implications of Preliminary Results from Saffire IV and V Experiments on Large Scale Spacecraft Fires

topic: deflagration at first ignition
claim: When sample V-4 first ignited in 20 cm/s flow, ignition began on the underside and within 100 ms the flame had expanded to fill the field of view.
quote: In this case, the ambient gas flow was 20 cm/s and ignition first occurred on the underside of the sample. Within 100 ms, the flame had expanded to fill the field of view.
source_title: Fire Safety Implications of Preliminary Results from Saffire IV and V Experiments on Large Scale Spacecraft Fires

topic: flow obstructions and low flow let vapor build up
claim: Reduced air flow and complex flow obstructions can let fuel vapor accumulate into a readily ignited mixture that can produce a strong deflagration.
quote: suggests that reduced air flow and complex flow obstructions can allow the accumulation of fuel vapor, thereby creating a readily-ignited mixture that can produce a strong deflagration.
source_title: Fire Safety Implications of Preliminary Results from Saffire IV and V Experiments on Large Scale Spacecraft Fires

topic: thick PMMA flame length in enriched oxygen
claim: The one-sided PMMA flame in 25.4% oxygen grew to 11 cm after 450 seconds.
quote: In Saffire V-3, the one-sided PMMA sample flame (in 25.4% oxygen) grew to 11 cm after 450 seconds.
source_title: Fire Safety Implications of Preliminary Results from Saffire IV and V Experiments on Large Scale Spacecraft Fires

topic: flames reach a limiting length, unlike 1-g
claim: In all these cases (the Saffire II, IV-2 and V-3 PMMA flames, compared with the thin samples) the flame length reached an upper limit, contrary to similar 1-g tests that did not reach a steady length.
quote: In all these cases the flame length reached an upper limit contrary to similar 1-g tests that did not reach a steady length.
source_title: Fire Safety Implications of Preliminary Results from Saffire IV and V Experiments on Large Scale Spacecraft Fires

topic: oxygen shadow of an upstream flame
claim: Once a flame reached its limiting size, flames downstream were inhibited or extinguished by the oxygen "shadow" of the upstream flame.
quote: Once a flame achieved its limiting size, downstream flames were inhibited or extinguished by the oxygen "shadow" of the upstream flame.
source_title: Fire Safety Implications of Preliminary Results from Saffire IV and V Experiments on Large Scale Spacecraft Fires

topic: flame jumped a gap to a warmed surface
claim: In one case a flame jumped a 4.5 cm gap and ignited a previously warmed PMMA surface.
quote: In one case, a flame was seen to jump a 4.5 cm gap to ignite a previously warmed PMMA surface.
source_title: Fire Safety Implications of Preliminary Results from Saffire IV and V Experiments on Large Scale Spacecraft Fires

topic: thick fuels: spread direction in low gravity
claim: Flames on thick fuels do not grow or spread concurrently in low gravity and depend on surface regression to advance; spread is more likely in opposed flow.
quote: As discussed above, flames on thick fuels will not grow or spread concurrently in low gravity and instead depend on surface regression to move the flame forward; instead, spread is more likely to be seen in opposed (downward) spread.
source_title: Fire Safety Implications of Preliminary Results from Saffire IV and V Experiments on Large Scale Spacecraft Fires

topic: surface ribs set the effective thickness
claim: Although the V-4 sample was 10 mm thick, the dimension that mattered for flame spread was the width of the ribs.
quote: Although the Saffire V-4 sample was 10 mm thick, the relevant dimension for flame spread was the width of the ribs.
source_title: Fire Safety Implications of Preliminary Results from Saffire IV and V Experiments on Large Scale Spacecraft Fires

topic: rib width and opposed spread rate
claim: In opposed flow at 761 hPa and 26.9 vol % oxygen, flames propagated along the rib edges at up to 0.88 mm/s on the 1 mm wide rib.
quote: It was found that the flames ignited downstream propagated forward along the rib edges surprisingly fast with up to 0.88 mm/s (1 mm rib width).
source_title: Opposed Flame Spreading Along a Structured PMMA Sample in Exploration Atmosphere Under Microgravity

topic: wider ribs spread slower
claim: The wider the rib, the slower the flame propagation.
quote: Also, it was observed that the wider the rib, the slower the propagation.
source_title: Opposed Flame Spreading Along a Structured PMMA Sample in Exploration Atmosphere Under Microgravity

topic: shutting down air circulation as primary control measure
claim: Because any active firefighting measure disturbs the stable stratification, the authors suggest considering a shutdown of air circulation as the primary control measure.
quote: Since any active firefighting measure also forces a disturbance of the stable stratification, it is obvious to alternatively consider a shutdown of the air circulation as the primary control measure.
source_title: Opposed Flame Spreading Along a Structured PMMA Sample in Exploration Atmosphere Under Microgravity

topic: reduce flow rather than cut it, to avoid flashover
claim: From the Saffire IV deflagration, the authors draw the lesson that actively cooling still-burning material by reducing the flow, rather than shutting it down completely, may better avoid flashover effects.
quote: that actively cooling the still burning material by reducing the flow rather than completely shutting it down may be a better way to avoid flashover effects.
source_title: Opposed Flame Spreading Along a Structured PMMA Sample in Exploration Atmosphere Under Microgravity

topic: most ignitable condition is low flow
claim: The authors judge the most ignitable condition to be low flow rates, since higher flow velocity delays or deters ignition through surface heat losses.
quote: The most ignitable condition is likely to be at low flow rates since as the flow velocity increases, ignition becomes delayed or deterred due to heat losses from the surface of the fuel the adjacent flow.
source_title: Fire Safety Implications of Preliminary Results from Saffire IV and V Experiments on Large Scale Spacecraft Fires

topic: elevated oxygen: more energetic flames
claim: The project manager reported that elevated oxygen levels gave more energetic flames, which would have a larger impact on the vehicle.
quote: "The elevated oxygen levels show more energetic flames, which would have a larger impact on the vehicle,"
source_title: Saffire Ignites New Discoveries in Space

topic: cotton fire: heat and gas increase (table row)
claim: Table row for V-2 (cotton jersey): burn duration 200 s, average heat release 2,800 W (560 kJ total, from fuel consumption), maximum 46 C at the flow-unit outlet and 23 C at the far-field unit or nearest location, CO2 up 2360 ppm (1.26 mmHg), CO up 83 ppm.
source_title: Preliminary Results from the Saffire VI Experiment

topic: vehicle model: heat transfer to cargo
claim: A convective heat transfer coefficient of 150 W/m2-K, calibrated on the Saffire V cotton burn, gave an excellent prediction for both Saffire V PMMA burn events.
quote: for the Saffire V cotton burn in previous work was determined to be 150 W/m2-K and gave and excellent prediction for both Saffire V PMMA burn events.
source_title: Vehicle Modeling During the Burning of Thermally Thick Samples in the Saffire V Experiments

topic: feasibility of predicting habitability impact
claim: The Saffire V modelling results demonstrate the feasibility of predicting the impact of a fire on the habitability of an orbiting spacecraft.
quote: These results demonstrate the feasibility of predicting the impact of a fire on the habitability of an orbiting spacecraft.
source_title: Vehicle Modeling During the Burning of Thermally Thick Samples in the Saffire V Experiments

topic: fire size and where the temperature rose
claim: Fires of 1.5 to 3.2 kW were tested in spacecraft with 17 to 19 cubic meters of free air; temperature rose significantly only very near the fire.
quote: Practical scale fires ranging from 1.5 to 3.2 kW were tested in unmanned spacecraft with free air volumes of 17 to 19 cubic meters. Despite these fires, the temperature only increased significantly very near to the fire itself.
source_title: Preliminary Results from the Saffire VI Experiment

topic: CO and CO2 exceeded exposure limits
claim: CO and CO2 rose significantly: the PMMA tests exceeded the 1-hour carbon dioxide limit and the 24-hour carbon monoxide limit.
quote: the ambient concentrations of carbon monoxide and carbon dioxide rose significantly with the PMMA tests exceeding the 1-hour carbon dioxide limit and the 24-hour carbon monoxide limit.
source_title: Preliminary Results from the Saffire VI Experiment

topic: exposure limits used as reference
claim: The reference limits are a 1-hour CO SMAC of 425 ppm, a 24-hour CO SMAC of 100 ppm, and a 1-hour average CO2 partial pressure of no more than 3 mm Hg.
quote: For CO the 1-hour SMAC is 425 ppm, and the 24-hour SMAC is 100 ppm. For CO2, which is a metabolic product that is prevalent in crewed spacecraft, NASA-STD-3001 [11] establishes the limit based on the partial pressure to no more than 3 mm Hg for a 1-hour average.
source_title: Heat and Smoke Emission from Tests on the Saffire VI Experiment

topic: PMMA fires: gas increase (table rows)
claim: Table rows: VI-3 (2-sided PMMA) burned 780 s with 3080 W peak heat release, CO2 up 8539 ppm (3.51 mmHg) and CO up 308 ppm at the far-field unit; VI-4 (1-sided PMMA) burned 1200 s with 1507 W peak, CO2 up 8117 ppm (3.37 mmHg) and CO up 320 ppm.
source_title: Preliminary Results from the Saffire VI Experiment

topic: alarm timing summary
claim: Smoke was readily detected by an ionization detector and a light scattering system, but a typical alarm threshold was reached only at 981 seconds, when most of the hazardous gas release had occurred.
quote: The smoke from the fire event was readily detected by an ionization detector and a light scattering system but a typical alarm threshold was only achieved at 981 seconds. By this time most of the hazardous gas release had occurred.
source_title: Preliminary Results from the Saffire VI Experiment

topic: smoke and gas, not heat, are the main hazard
claim: The human hazard from a spacecraft fire is very similar to terrestrial fires: heat is not the principal hazard; smoke and gaseous products are a much greater concern.
quote: Collectively these results demonstrate that the human hazard from a fire in a spacecraft is very similar to terrestrial fires where the heat from the fire is not the principal hazard and rather the smoke and gaseous products are a much greater concern.
source_title: Preliminary Results from the Saffire VI Experiment

topic: partial gravity is not covered
claim: The authors state further work is needed to extend these results to the partial gravity expected on the Moon and Mars.
quote: Further work will be needed to extend these results to the partial gravity environment expected on future mission to the moon and Mars.
source_title: Preliminary Results from the Saffire VI Experiment

topic: thick PMMA: flame anchored, linear growth rate
claim: The flames stayed anchored at the leading edge; the PMMA samples showed several minutes of very linear flame growth with slopes from 0.22 to 0.38 mm/s.
quote: Unlike 1-g upward burning of thick materials such as PMMA, the flames did not spread but remained anchored at the leading edge and only spread as the material regressed. The PMMA samples all showed intervals of very linear flame growth for periods of several minutes. The slopes were generally similar ranging from 0.22 to 0.38 mm/s.
source_title: Heat and Smoke Emission from Tests on the Saffire VI Experiment

topic: no acceleration even at high oxygen
claim: The linear growth rate suggests that even in high oxygen conditions low-gravity flame spread and growth will not be acceleratory.
quote: This linear growth rate is an important finding as it suggests that even in high oxygen conditions, low-gravity flame spread and growth will not be acceleratory.
source_title: Heat and Smoke Emission from Tests on the Saffire VI Experiment

topic: oxygen raises growth rate despite lower pressure
claim: For the 2-sided samples the growth rate rose 73% for an oxygen increase of 0.08 mol fraction, despite a 45% pressure decrease.
quote: The growth rate trends for the 2-sided samples show a 73% increase in the spread rate from an oxygen concentration increase of 0.08 mol fraction despite the overall pressure decrease of 45%.
source_title: Heat and Smoke Emission from Tests on the Saffire VI Experiment

topic: thin fabric spread rate across atmospheres (table row)
claim: Table row of thin-fuel flame spread rates: 3.6 mm/s (IV-1 SIBAL, 980 mbar, 0.23 O2), 3.4 mm/s (V-2 cotton, 741 mbar, 0.28 O2), 4.05 mm/s (VI-2 SIBAL, 541 mbar, 0.31 O2).
quote: Flame spread rate (mm/s) NA NA NA NA 3.6 3.4 4.05
source_title: Heat and Smoke Emission from Tests on the Saffire VI Experiment

topic: one-sided panels plateau; back-side heat loss
claim: The 2-sided samples were still growing at about 500 s, while the 1-sided samples began to plateau around 380 s (Saffire V) and 420 s (Saffire VI).
quote: The 2-sided samples are still growing at the end of the test (around 500 seconds) while the 1- sided samples begin to plateau around 380 s for SAFFIRE V and 420 s for SAFFIRE VI.
source_title: Heat and Smoke Emission from Tests on the Saffire VI Experiment

topic: two-sided burn as conservative bound
claim: 2-sided burn results can be used as a conservative upper-bound estimate of the growth rate for 1-sided applications.
quote: 2-sided burn results can be used as a conservative upper-bound estimate of the growth rate for 1-sided applications.
source_title: Heat and Smoke Emission from Tests on the Saffire VI Experiment

topic: heat release versus cabin temperature
claim: The peak heat release rate hit 3 kW, which is substantial for a small spacecraft, yet the temperature rise at the far-field unit was only 0.5 C.
quote: The peak HRR hit 3 kW which is substantial for a small spacecraft. However, as seen in Table 1, the temperature rise at the FFD was only 0.5 °C.
source_title: Heat and Smoke Emission from Tests on the Saffire VI Experiment

topic: detection threshold of 2 mg/m3 was not low enough
claim: For this spacecraft configuration a 2 mg/m3 detection threshold did not detect the fires before some cases exceeded the 24-hour SMAC for CO, though only one case approached the 1-hour SMAC.
quote: For this configuration spacecraft, a 2 mg/m3 detection threshold was not low enough to detect the fires before some cases exceeded the 24-hour SMAC for CO, however it only approached the 1-hour SMAC for one case.
source_title: Heat and Smoke Emission from Tests on the Saffire VI Experiment

quote: Time to alarm (s) [aerosol = 2 mg/m3] 1083 1117 1037 1603 92 146 201

topic: CO at the moment of alarm (table row)
claim: Table row of CO increase at the time of alarm: 63.2, 28.1, 105 and 283 ppm for the PMMA tests (IV-2, V-3, VI-3, VI-4) and 7.9, 11.9 and 57.1 ppm for the thin fuels (IV-1, V-2, VI-2).
quote: CO increase (ppm) at alarm 63.2 28.1 105 283 7.9 11.9 57.1
source_title: Heat and Smoke Emission from Tests on the Saffire VI Experiment

topic: detection here was a best case
claim: Because most of the flow went straight from the flow unit to the far-field unit without extensive mixing, detection in this test is likely quicker than in many spacecraft.
quote: Consequently, the detection scenario tested here is likely to be quicker than in many spacecraft.
source_title: Heat and Smoke Emission from Tests on the Saffire VI Experiment

topic: dim blue leading edge of the flame
claim: In the camera images the trailing edge of the flame was very bright (soot) while the leading edge could be dim blue.
quote: In general, the trailing edge was very bright (soot) while the leading edge could be dim blue.
source_title: Heat and Smoke Emission from Tests on the Saffire VI Experiment

topic: low-flow interval to cool before stopping flow
claim: The 5 cm/s low-flow interval was used to cool the sample and ensure extinguishment when flow was stopped, avoiding the issues seen in Saffire IV-2.
quote: The primary purpose of this low-flow interval was to cool the sample material and ensure extinguishment upon flow termination, thereby avoiding the issues seen in SAFFIRE IV-2 [6].
source_title: Heat and Smoke Emission from Tests on the Saffire VI Experiment

topic: Nomex did not ignite
claim: The Nomex fabric sample on Saffire VI did not ignite.
quote: The Nomex sample did not ignite and so it will not be included in this paper.
source_title: Preliminary Results from the Saffire VI Experiment

topic: heat release method for modelling
claim: Heat release was calculated from oxygen consumption using 13.1 kJ per gram of oxygen consumed.
quote: the heat release is estimated for a wide range of combustibles to be 13.1 kJ per gram of oxygen consumed.
source_title: Preliminary Results from the Saffire VI Experiment

topic: acid gas (HCl): stopping ventilation keeps it airborne (model)
claim: In a model validated by data collected during the Saffire campaign, a simulation with the Environmental Control and Life Support System shut off once HCl reached 5 ppm at the far-field unit showed HCl staying in the atmosphere considerably longer.
quote: An additional simulation where the Environmental Control and Life Support System (ECLSS) was shut off once the FFD reached 5 ppm of HCl showed that HCl stayed in the atmosphere considerably longer.
source_title: Spacecraft Fire Safety Predictions using Verified Saffire Model

topic: acid gas (HCl) removed rapidly with flow on (model and release)
claim: The model predicted rapid removal of HCl from the atmosphere, which compared well with far-field data from the Saffire VI release of a bottle of 5% HCl.
quote: The model prediction showed that the HCl was removed from the atmosphere rapidly. This compared well against the FFD data in the Saffire VI campaign event where a bottle of 5% HCl was released into the vehicle.
source_title: Spacecraft Fire Safety Predictions using Verified Saffire Model

topic: lithium-ion battery fire would heat more of the vehicle (model)
claim: A simulated lithium-ion battery fire used a heat addition rate considerably higher than the Saffire solid-fuel burns and produced a non-trivial temperature increase in more locations within the vehicle.
quote: This simulation used a heat addition rate that is considerably higher than what was determined from the burning of solid fuels in the Saffire campaign and hence produced a non-trivial temperature increase in more locations within the vehicle.
source_title: Spacecraft Fire Safety Predictions using Verified Saffire Model

topic: vehicle model validated across burns
claim: A model with a cargo heat transfer coefficient of 150 W/m2-K, calibrated on the Saffire V cotton burn, gave adequate cabin temperature predictions for three Saffire VI simulations.
quote: In previous work, an effective convective heat transfer coefficient of 150 W/m2-K for the cargo in the standoffs that was calibrated at RS3 for the Saffire V cotton burn was used for the three simulations in this work and provided adequate temperature predictions in the cabin.
source_title: Vehicle Modeling During the Burn Events in the Saffire VI Experiments

topic: number of runs and materials
claim: Saffire-VI made 19 experiment runs with adjusted air conditions, igniting plexiglass, cotton, Nomex and Solid Inflammability Boundary at Low-Speed fabrics.
quote: During the 19 Saffire-VI experiment runs, the NASA team and counterparts at Northrop Grumman made various adjustments to air conditions. They then ignited a flame on materials such as plexiglass, cotton, Nomex, and Solid Inflammability Boundary at Low-Speed fabrics.
source_title: Flame Burns Out on NASA's Long-Running Spacecraft Fire Experiment

topic: smoke does not rise to a ceiling detector

quote: In microgravity, no buoyancy → plume does not rise to ceiling
source_title: Evaluation of Combustion Products from Large-Scale Spacecraft Fires during the Saffire-IV and Saffire-V Experiments

topic: longer times to alarm in microgravity

source_title: The Combustion Product Monitor instrument for the spacecraft fire safety demonstration project

topic: gas monitoring as early warning
claim: Monitoring these gases can give early warning of combustion events and can help make post-fire cleanup safe.

topic: airflow sensitivity of microgravity flames
claim: In BASS, microgravity flames were especially sensitive to air flow speed in the range 0 to 5 cm/s.
quote: Microgravity flames were found to be especially sensitive to air flow speed in the range 0 to 5 cms.
source_title: Thickness and Fuel Preheating Effects on Material Flammability in Microgravity from the BASS Experiment

topic: speed of flame response to airflow changes
claim: The gas phase responds much faster than the solid, so the flame responds to a change in flow speed with almost no delay.
quote: The gas phase response is much faster compared to the solid and so as the flow speed is changed, the flame responds with almost no delay.
source_title: Thickness and Fuel Preheating Effects on Material Flammability in Microgravity from the BASS Experiment

topic: dim blue flames at very low flow
claim: At the lowest flow speeds examined (less than 1 cm/s) all the flames tended to become dim blue and very stable, and because heat loss is small at these low convective rates they can burn for a long time.
quote: At the lowest speeds examined (less than 1 cms) all the flames tended to become dim blue and very stable. However, heat loss at these very low convective rates is small so the flames can burn for a long time.
source_title: Thickness and Fuel Preheating Effects on Material Flammability in Microgravity from the BASS Experiment

topic: flame strengthens with time at moderate flow
claim: At moderate flow speeds (between about 1 and 5 cm/s) the flame keeps heating the solid fuel, which raises fuel temperature and vaporization rate and gives a stronger, more luminous flame as time progresses.
quote: At moderate flow speeds (between about 1 and 5 cms) the flame continually heats the solid fuel resulting in an increasing fuel temperature, higher rate of fuel vaporization, and a stronger, more luminous flame as time progresses.
source_title: Thickness and Fuel Preheating Effects on Material Flammability in Microgravity from the BASS Experiment

topic: small flames burn for minutes undetected
claim: Even the smallest flames on acrylic slabs, the only ones that appeared to be hurt by conductive heat loss into the solid, burned for over 5 minutes before self-extinguishing; the authors note a tiny flame might be undetected for a long time.
quote: Only the smallest flames burning acrylic slabs appeared to be adversely influenced by solid conductive heat loss, but even these burned for over 5 minutes before self-extinguishing. This has implications for spacecraft fire safety since a tiny flame might be undetected for a long time.
source_title: Thickness and Fuel Preheating Effects on Material Flammability in Microgravity from the BASS Experiment

topic: flare-up when airflow increases
claim: A small flame is not particularly hazardous while it stays small, but it might flare up if air convection is suddenly increased or if it spreads into another fuel source.
quote: While the small flame is not particularly hazardous if it remains small, the danger is that it might flare up if the air convection is suddenly increased or if the flame spreads into another fuel source.
source_title: Thickness and Fuel Preheating Effects on Material Flammability in Microgravity from the BASS Experiment

topic: flame goes out when airflow is shut off (thin acrylic)
