quote: Top view image montage for a 1-cm wide flat acrylic sample burning in air at low flow speed (around 9 cm/s). Images progress from left to right then top to bottom (1.3 seconds between images). The air flow direction is from right to left. The flame is about 1 cm in size and can persist for a very long time at this low air flow speed. The flame goes out only in the last two frames when the air flow is completely shut off.
source_title: Thickness and Fuel Preheating Effects on Material Flammability in Microgravity from the BASS Experiment

topic: nitrogen jet fails on a warm thick solid
claim: On a PMMA sample (15-mm initial diameter, 17% O2/N2, 1 atm, flow under 1 cm/s) a nitrogen jet imposed near the end of the burn failed to extinguish the flame while the solid was very warm; the flame went out after flow reductions, when the flow speed was zero.
quote: Flow of less than 1 cm/s. Near the end of the burn, a jet of nitrogen is imposed but it fails to extinguish the flame. (Solid is very warm.) Finally after a series of flow reductions, the flame goes out when the flow speed is zero. Fuel: PMMA; 15-mm initial diameter; 17% O2/N2; 1 atm; Time between images: 1.3 sec
source_title: Thickness and Fuel Preheating Effects on Material Flammability in Microgravity from the BASS Experiment

topic: heat stored in thick solids defeats the nitrogen jet
claim: Thicker solids can store a great deal of heat even with only a small flame, and as a result extinction with the nitrogen jet was not possible for the given flow rate.
quote: Thicker solids can store a great deal of heat even with only a small flame. One result is that extinction with the nitrogen jet was not possible for the given flow rate.
source_title: Thickness and Fuel Preheating Effects on Material Flammability in Microgravity from the BASS Experiment

topic: nitrogen can strengthen a flame
claim: The Researcher's Guide reports that early BASS results demonstrated nitrogen applied to the flame can strengthen it, through entrainment of oxygen by the suppressant stream.
quote: Depending on the geometry of the flame and the characteristics of the extinguisher (distance from flame, dispersion angle), it is possible that the suppressant stream will be ineffective or might actually make the flame worse through the entrainment of oxygen. Early results have demonstrated that nitrogen applied to the flame can actually strengthen it because of this effect.
source_title: A Researcher's Guide to: Combustion Science (NP-2015-10-034-JSC)

topic: where to aim the suppressant
claim: For a fire burning in microgravity the best point to apply suppressant may not be immediately apparent, especially for a partially obstructed flame or a wake-stabilized flame.
quote: For a fire burning in microgravity, the best point of application of suppressant may not be immediately apparent, especially for a partially obstructed flame or a wake-stabilized flame.
source_title: Burning and Suppression of Solids (BASS) fact sheet: BASS, BASS-II, BASS-M

topic: concurrent versus opposed spread rate on fabric
claim: In the BASS cotton-fiberglass fabric tests, concurrent and opposed spread at about 10 cm/s were 2.55 mm/s versus 1.21 mm/s.
quote: Concurrent and Opposed Spread at ~ 10 cm/s 2.55 mm/s versus 1.21 mm/s
source_title: Flammability Aspects of Fabric in Opposed and Concurrent Air Flow in Microgravity (PSI-26 presentation file)

topic: opposed-flow spread peaks at intermediate flow
claim: In opposed flow the fabric flame quickly reached steady spread at each flow speed, and spread rate was fastest at an intermediate flow speed.
quote: For the opposed flow configuration, the flame quickly reached steady spread for each flow speed, and the spread rate was fastest at an intermediate value of flow speed.
source_title: Flammability Aspects of Fabric in Opposed and Concurrent Air Flow in Microgravity (PSI-26 presentation file)

topic: material burns in microgravity that self-extinguishes on Earth
claim: The BASS fabric tests show enhanced flammability in microgravity for the opposed-flow geometry: in normal-gravity air a flame self-extinguishes in that geometry (downward flame spread).
quote: These tests show the enhanced flammability in microgravity for this geometry, since, in normal gravity air, a flame self-extinguishes in the opposed flow geometry (downward flame spread).
source_title: Flammability Aspects of Fabric in Opposed and Concurrent Air Flow in Microgravity (PSI-26 presentation file)

topic: concurrent-flow spread grows linearly with flow
claim: In concurrent flow a limiting flame length and steady spread rate were obtained only at low flow speeds, and under those conditions spread rate increased linearly with flow.
quote: For the concurrent flow configuration, a limiting length and steady spread rate were obtained only in low flow speeds. For these conditions, flame spread rate increased linearly with increasing flow.
source_title: Flammability Aspects of Fabric in Opposed and Concurrent Air Flow in Microgravity (PSI-26 presentation file)

topic: quenching of a concurrent-flow flame near 1 cm/s
claim: Decreasing the concurrent flow speed to a very low value (around 1 cm/s) produced quenching extinction of the fabric flame.
quote: decreasing concurrent flow speed to a very low value (around 1 cm/s), quenching extinction was observed.
source_title: Flammability Aspects of Fabric in Opposed and Concurrent Air Flow in Microgravity (PSI-26 presentation file)

topic: Ultem and Nomex HT90-40 did not burn in ISS air
claim: Ultem and Nomex HT90-40 samples did not burn in ISS atmosphere at 21% to 22% O2 with flow speeds around 15 cm/s.
quote: Ultem and Nomex HT90-40 samples did not burn on ISS atmosphere 21% to 22% O2 Flow speeds around 15 cm/s
source_title: Thickness and Fuel Preheating Effects on Material Flammability in Microgravity from the BASS Experiment

topic: Nomex III burned at 22% O2
claim: A 2-cm wide Nomex III sample did burn: it propagated almost completely in concurrent flow at 15 cm/s on ISS, the flame shrinking in width until it extinguished within 1 cm of the end of the sample.
quote: Nomex-III sample did burn NOMEX – III, 22% O2, 1 atm 14 cm/s (0g) 2 cm wide sample At 1g ULOI, but narrower sample Nomex III sample residue after nearly complete concurrent propagation at 15 cm/s on ISS. Flame was shrinking in width until it extinguished within 1 cm of the end of the sample
source_title: Thickness and Fuel Preheating Effects on Material Flammability in Microgravity from the BASS Experiment

topic: candle flame goes out when flow is turned off
claim: A paraffin wax candle in a ceramic tube burning at 17% oxygen and less than 1 cm/s flow went out rapidly when the flow was turned off.
quote: Image sequence of a burning paraffin wax candle within a ceramic tube at 17% oxygen and less than 1 cm/s flow. Images are about 9 sec. apart and the flow direction is up. The test is concluded when the flow is turned off and the flame rapidly goes out.
source_title: Burning and Suppression of Solids (BASS): An Overview of Recent ISS Results (PSI-26 presentation file)

topic: steady flame in microgravity versus no downward spread in 1 g
claim: With 10 cm/s opposed flow in 0 g the fabric flame had steady size and spread, while in 1 g the flame does not propagate downward.
quote: Comparison of 0-g and 1-g Opposed Flow Flames 0-g with flow (10 cm/s) 1-g Steady flame size and spread Flame does not propagate downward
source_title: Flammability Aspects of Fabric in Opposed and Concurrent Air Flow in Microgravity (PSI-26 presentation file)

topic: low-flow flames flare up when airflow rises
claim: BASS-II flames were quite sensitive to air flow speed between 0 and 5 cm/s; they could be sustained below 1 cm/s, where they became dim blue and stable, and could flare up quickly with a sudden increase in air flow speed.
quote: The flames are quite sensitive to air flow speed in the range 0 to 5 cms. They can be sustained at very low flow speeds of less than 1 cms, when they become dim blue and stable. In this state they are not particularly dangerous from a fire safety perspective, but they can flare up quickly with a sudden increase in air flow speed.
source_title: Combustion of Solids in Microgravity: Results from the BASS-II Experiment

topic: flow cut-off extinguishes a thin PMMA flame within 2 s
claim: A flame spreading steadily at 2.2 mm/s over a 100-micrometer PMMA film extinguished within 2 s after the flow was abruptly cut off.
quote: In the first test, a steady flame was established over a 100-μm sample. After the flame propagated across half the sample length at a steady spread rate of 2.2 mm/s, the flow was abruptly cut off and the flame was observed to extinguish within 2 s
source_title: Burning and Suppression of Solids-II (BASS-II) Summary Report, NASA/TM-20210011385

topic: extinction flow velocity for thin PMMA films
claim: For thin PMMA films the opposed-flow extinction velocities were about 1 cm/s for 100, 200 and 300 micrometer thickness and about 1.5 cm/s for 400 micrometers.
quote: When tests are repeated with samples of different thicknesses, the extinction velocities are found to be about 1 cm/s for 100, 200, and 300 μm and about 1.5 cm/s for 400 μm.
source_title: Burning and Suppression of Solids-II (BASS-II) Summary Report, NASA/TM-20210011385

topic: extinction velocity rises as oxygen falls
claim: At about 16 percent O2 the extinction velocities were about 2.6 cm/s (100 micrometer film) and about 4 cm/s (200 micrometer film); the report concludes the extinction velocity increases significantly as O2 is reduced and is independent of fuel thickness.
quote: Tests were also conducted at a lower O2 level of about 16 percent for two different thicknesses and the extinction velocities were found to be about 2.6 cm/s for 100 μm and about 4 cm/s for 200 μm. It should be mentioned that the width of the sample was different, 20 mm for the 100-μm sample and 10 mm for the 200-μm sample. Even though there is insufficient data at the lower O2 level, it is clear that the extinction velocity significantly increases as the O2 level is reduced and is independent of the fuel thickness.
source_title: Burning and Suppression of Solids-II (BASS-II) Summary Report, NASA/TM-20210011385

topic: flame turns fully blue and vanishes before radiative extinction
claim: As the opposed flow was gradually reduced, the thin-film flame shrank, lost its orange color and became completely blue.
quote: As the flow speed is gradually reduced from about t = 27 s, the flame size starts shrinking and the orange color disappears and the flame becomes completely blue, most possibly because of the temperature drop brought about by radiative losses, which is enhanced by the increased residence time at low flow velocity.
source_title: Burning and Suppression of Solids-II (BASS-II) Summary Report, NASA/TM-20210011385

topic: quenching flow speed for cotton-fiberglass fabric
claim: For the SIBAL cotton-fiberglass fabric in concurrent flow, quenching speeds were between 1 and 5 cm/s, higher in lower-oxygen atmospheres.
quote: The quenching speeds were found to be between 1 and 5 cm/s with higher speed in lower oxygen atmosphere.
source_title: Concurrent Flame Growth, Spread and Extinction over Composite Fabric Samples in Low Speed Purely Forced Flow in Microgravity

topic: no ignition of the fabric at 16.4% O2
claim: Two 2.2-cm-wide SIBAL fabric tests at 16.4% O2, at 10 cm/s and at 5 cm/s, are recorded as no ignition.
quote: GMT175-T9 2.2 10 16.4 No ignition GMT175-T10 2.2 5 16.4 No ignition
source_title: Concurrent Flame Growth, Spread and Extinction over Composite Fabric Samples in Low Speed Purely Forced Flow in Microgravity

topic: dim blue flames hard to see on video
claim: When flow speed and oxygen concentration were low the fabric flame became very dim blue and was difficult to see in the side video camera.
quote: When flow speed and oxygen concentration were low, the flame became very dim blue and was difficult to see in the side video camera.
source_title: Concurrent Flame Growth, Spread and Extinction over Composite Fabric Samples in Low Speed Purely Forced Flow in Microgravity

topic: narrower samples, lower flow and lower oxygen slow the spread
claim: Flames spread more slowly across the narrower fabric samples, at lower flow velocities and at lower oxygen percentages.
quote: Flames spread more slowly across the narrower samples, at lower flow velocities and at lower oxygen percentages.
source_title: Concurrent Flame Growth, Spread and Extinction over Composite Fabric Samples in Low Speed Purely Forced Flow in Microgravity

topic: smoldering spots left behind the flame
claim: Top-view images showed bright spots behind the flame base after the flame passed, from smoldering of a small amount of fuel not completely consumed by the flaming combustion.
quote: In the top-view images, we can find bright spots behind the flame base when the flame passes. The spots come from the smoldering of a small amount of fuel that is not complete consumed by the flaming combustion.
source_title: Concurrent Flame Growth, Spread and Extinction over Composite Fabric Samples in Low Speed Purely Forced Flow in Microgravity

topic: negative oxygen margin of safety for PMMA rods
claim: The 1-g blowoff limit for the 1/4-inch PMMA rod is at 16% oxygen, while BASS-II obtained steady spreading at 13.6% oxygen: a negative oxygen margin of safety of 2.4% O2, so normal-gravity flammability limits should be de-rated by at least that much.
quote: The 1g blowoff for the ¼” rod is at 16% oxygen, whereas we obtained steady spreading at 13.6% oxygen in BASS-II. Thus the material has a negative Oxygen Margin of Safety of 2.4% O2, and the normal gravity flammability limits should be de-rated by at least that much.
source_title: Combustion of Solids in Microgravity: Results from the BASS-II Experiment

topic: extrapolating the blowoff line to zero stretch
claim: The authors suggest linearly extrapolating blowoff data to zero stretch rate as a conservative estimate of the minimum oxygen concentration at which the material burns; the y-intercept of their fit was 13.3% O2 against a minimum test point of 13.6% O2.
quote: The linear blowoff boundary has interesting implications in that it may be possible to linearly extrapolate blowoff data down to zero stretch rate and use that oxygen value as a conservative estimate of the minimum oxygen concentration where the material will burn. This will allow us to de-rate materials based on normal gravity flammability tests to ensure the material will not burn in space. Using the y-intercept of the linear fit (13.3 % O2 in the Figure 4 fit, versus the minimum test point of 13.6 % O2) would add a slight level of conservatism.
source_title: Microgravity Flammability of PMMA Rods in Concurrent Flow

topic: after blowoff the flame cannot move back upstream at low oxygen
claim: Once the flame was blown downstream of the stagnation region it could not propagate back upstream at the low oxygen levels tested (16.1% O2 and lower); in the opposed-flow rod tests flame spread was not observed below 16.4% O2.
quote: so it seems that once the flame is blown downstream of the stagnation region, the flame is unable to propagate upstream for the low oxygen levels tested (16.1% O2 and lower). This is consistent with tests for opposed flow flame spread rods that were also done as part of BASS-II [18], where flame spread was not observed below 16.4 % O2.
source_title: Microgravity Flammability of PMMA Rods in Concurrent Flow

topic: near-limit flames burn for tens of minutes
claim: Quench test burns on PMMA rods lasted up to 28 minutes.
quote: Quench test burns lasted up to 28 minutes.
source_title: Microgravity Flammability of PMMA Rods in Concurrent Flow

topic: materials have burned at or below the Test 1 limits
claim: Materials have sustained burning in microgravity at or below the flammability limits measured with the NASA-STD-6001 Test 1 protocol.
quote: Materials have sustained burning in microgravity at or below the flammability limits measured with the Test 1 protocol.
source_title: Microgravity Flammability of PMMA Rods in Concurrent Flow

topic: ignition takes much longer near the oxygen limit
claim: In the concurrent rod tests ignition delay rose significantly as the minimum limiting O2 concentration was approached, ignition limits sat at higher O2 than flammability limits, and the delay could be almost 10 times the NASA-STD-6001 standard igniter on time.
quote: Ignition delay time increased significantly as the minimum limiting O2 concentration is approached. Ignition limits are found to be at higher O2 concentrations than the flammability limits due to the added heat loss to the initially cold fuel rod present at ignition. The ignition delay time can be up to almost 10 times longer than the NASA STD–6001 standard igniter on time.
source_title: Burning and Suppression of Solids-II (BASS-II) Summary Report, NASA/TM-20210011385

topic: flame oscillates at about 1 Hz before quenching
claim: Just before quenching the rod flame shrank to a hemispherical blue shape, and pre-quenching oscillations at 1.1 Hz were observed with a radiometer.
quote: The flame shrinks to a hemispherical blue shape just before quenching. Prequenching extinction oscillations at 1.1 Hz are observed with a radiometer and are similar to previously reported quiescent candle flame oscillations in microgravity.
source_title: Burning and Suppression of Solids-II (BASS-II) Summary Report, NASA/TM-20210011385

topic: drop tower blowoff limits match the long-duration ISS limits
claim: Blowoff extinction limits from the ISS rod experiments agree well with limits from 5.18-s drop tests in the Zero Gravity Research Facility.
quote: Blowoff extinction limits from the ISS experiments agree well with Zero Gravity Research Facility 5.18-s drop test limits.
source_title: Burning and Suppression of Solids-II (BASS-II) Summary Report, NASA/TM-20210011385

topic: carbon monoxide rises near the oxygen limit
claim: In the concurrent rod tests CO production increased significantly at low O2 levels, and so did the CO to CO2 ratio.
quote: CO production also increases significantly at low O2 levels. The CO to CO2 ratio increases as well at low O2 concentrations.
source_title: Burning and Suppression of Solids-II (BASS-II) Summary Report, NASA/TM-20210011385

topic: flame spread at lower oxygen in microgravity than in 1 g (opposed-flow rods)
claim: For black PMMA rods in opposed flow, flame spread was observed in microgravity at O2 concentrations as low as 17.5 percent, while in normal gravity it was not observed below 19 percent.
quote: The most important result of the comparison is that of the minimum O2 concentration for flame spread in normal and microgravity. While in microgravity, flame spread was observed at O2 concentrations as low as 17.5 percent, in normal gravity, flame spread was not observed below 19 percent.
source_title: Burning and Suppression of Solids-II (BASS-II) Summary Report, NASA/TM-20210011385

topic: lowest opposed-flow velocity that sustained spread on PMMA rods
claim: Sustained flame spread was not observed for opposed-flow velocities below approximately 4 mm/s for the 6.35 mm and 9.525 mm diameter black PMMA rods.
quote: Sustained flame spread for the conditions tested was not observed for opposed-flow velocities below approximately 4 mm/s for the 0.00635- and 0.009525-m- diameter rods.
source_title: Burning and Suppression of Solids-II (BASS-II) Summary Report, NASA/TM-20210011385

topic: flame appearance versus flow on PMMA rods
claim: At very low flow velocities the rod flames appeared very small, blue, faint and open at their downstream ends; as flow rose toward 20 mm/s and above they became much more luminous, with bright yellow flames.
quote: Visually it was observed that at very low flow velocities the flames appear to be very small, blue, faint, and open at their downstream ends. As the flow velocity rises towards 20 mm/s and above, the flames become much more luminous, with bright yellow flames, and a closed downstream tip.
source_title: Burning and Suppression of Solids-II (BASS-II) Summary Report, NASA/TM-20210011385

topic: hot material keeps releasing fuel vapor after extinction
claim: After extinction the hot PMMA can keep producing fuel for some time until it cools, and premixed flame oscillations along the rod persist much longer in microgravity than in normal gravity; the report says suppression efforts should be maintained until the burning material has cooled and stopped emitting vapors.
quote: After extinction, the hot material can continue to produce fuel for some time until it cools. Premixed flame oscillations along the rod have been observed for the concurrent rod geometry that persist much longer in microgravity than in normal gravity due to the lower rate of convective cooling of the rod. This suggests that spacecraft fire suppression efforts should be maintained until the burning material has cooled and stopped emitting vapors.
source_title: Burning and Suppression of Solids-II (BASS-II) Summary Report, NASA/TM-20210011385

topic: burning droplets ejected from melting fuel
claim: A candle wick in opposed flow ejected a droplet of wax upstream; the report says this typifies the flame spread hazard of melting plastics in microgravity, where burning droplets can be ejected and possibly ignite other materials if melt viscosity is low enough.
quote: The ejected wax droplet shown in Figure 3.1(b) typifies the flame spread hazard associated with melting plastics in microgravity. If the melt viscosity is low enough, burning droplets can be ejected and possibly ignite other materials.
source_title: Burning and Suppression of Solids-II (BASS-II) Summary Report, NASA/TM-20210011385

topic: Nomex samples did not ignite
claim: The three Nomex samples tested in BASS-II did not ignite.
quote: The three Nomex® samples did not ignite, which is an excellent result for fire safety aboard the ISS.
source_title: Burning and Suppression of Solids-II (BASS-II) Summary Report, NASA/TM-20210011385

topic: microgravity flames are inefficient: high CO to CO2 ratio
claim: CO to CO2 ratios for the BASS-II fires were an order of magnitude higher than for efficient flue gases.
quote: The CO to CO2 ratios for these fires are an order of magnitude higher than for efficient flue gases, indicating that these flames are not efficient.
source_title: Burning and Suppression of Solids-II (BASS-II) Summary Report, NASA/TM-20210011385

topic: CO yield of concurrent-flow rod flames
claim: Concurrent-flow PMMA rod flames produced on average 550 ppm of CO for every 1 percent of CO2.
quote: Figure 1.4 shows that the concurrent rods produced on average 550 ppm of CO for every 1 percent of CO2.
source_title: Burning and Suppression of Solids-II (BASS-II) Summary Report, NASA/TM-20210011385

topic: a small fire is diluted below CO limits in a large module
claim: Combustion products from a fire of the scale of a BASS-II test would be diluted quickly: within the U.S. Lab (106 m3) CO would only be 1.5 ppm, below the long-term SMAC of 10 ppm and the 1-hour SMAC of 55 ppm.
quote: Since the ISS is quite large, the combustion products from a fire of the scale of a BASS–II test would quickly be diluted, so that even within just the U.S. Lab (106-m3 pressurized volume), the CO levels in the lab would only be 1.5 ppm, well below spacecraft maximum allowable concentration (SMAC) values for even long-term exposure (10 ppm), let alone the 1 hour SMAC of 55 ppm
source_title: Burning and Suppression of Solids-II (BASS-II) Summary Report, NASA/TM-20210011385

topic: heat release rate of small solid-fuel flames
claim: Most BASS-II tests had heat release rates well below 100 W, from oxygen consumption with 13.1 kJ per gram of O2.
quote: We calculated the heat release rates during each test from the O2 consumption and burn times, using the constant 13.1 kJ of heat released per gram of O2 consumed. The results showed that most of the tests had heat release rates well below 100 W.
source_title: Burning and Suppression of Solids-II (BASS-II) Summary Report, NASA/TM-20210011385

topic: a 100 W flame damaged hardware during a long burn
claim: The one long opposed-flow thick slab test that released close to 100 W caused damage to the lower downstream corner of the front window.
quote: The one long opposed thick slab test that caused the lower downstream corner of the front window damage released close to 100 W.
source_title: Burning and Suppression of Solids-II (BASS-II) Summary Report, NASA/TM-20210011385

topic: flames were under-ventilated and left soot, CO and unburned fuel
claim: In general the BASS-II flames were under-ventilated and did not burn all of the vaporized fuel: some ended up as soot, some as CO and some as unburned hydrocarbons.
quote: So, in general, the flames were under- ventilated and did not burn all of the vaporized fuel. Some fuel ended up as soot, some as CO, and some as unburned hydrocarbons.
source_title: Burning and Suppression of Solids-II (BASS-II) Summary Report, NASA/TM-20210011385

topic: thick PMMA stops spreading across the surface near 19% O2
claim: As O2 was reduced to approximately 19 percent, flames could no longer spread across the surface of two-sided PMMA slabs and instead completely consumed the fuel from the trailing edge.
quote: As O2 concentrations were reduced to approximately 19 percent however, the flames could no longer spread across the surface of the two-sided fuel, but rather completely consumed the fuel from the trailing edge.
source_title: Burning and Suppression of Solids-II (BASS-II) Summary Report, NASA/TM-20210011385

topic: backing a fuel with a heat sink weakens the flame
claim: One-sided PMMA samples burned more slowly than two-sided samples and needed a higher opposed-flow rate to keep burning.
quote: As shown in Figure 5.9, the one-sided samples burned more slowly than the two-sided samples, and also needed a higher opposed-flow rate to keep burning.
source_title: Burning and Suppression of Solids-II (BASS-II) Summary Report, NASA/TM-20210011385

topic: spread rate over a thick PMMA slab
claim: BASS-II test M20, a 5-mm-thick, 2.2-cm-wide two-sided PMMA slab in 10 cm/s opposed flow, had a spread rate of 0.012 mm/s (initial O2 18 vol%, final 17.4 vol%).
source_title: Burning and Suppression of Solids-II (BASS-II) Summary Report, NASA/TM-20210011385

topic: thicker fuel spreads slower
claim: The greater the fuel thickness, the longer the flame takes to spread and the lower the spread rate.
quote: The greater the thickness of the fuel, the greater is the time taken for the flame to spread and so the lower is the spread rate.
source_title: Burning and Suppression of Solids-II (BASS-II) Summary Report, NASA/TM-20210011385

topic: fire model over-predicts spread rate
claim: The numerical model predicted much higher spread rates than those obtained in the experiment.
quote: The model currently predicts much higher spread rates than those obtained in the experiment.
source_title: Burning and Suppression of Solids-II (BASS-II) Summary Report, NASA/TM-20210011385

topic: opposed-flow spread on PMMA rods is faster in microgravity than in 1 g
claim: The summary report states that opposed-flow flame spread on cylindrical PMMA rods is appreciably faster in microgravity than in 1 g, and that decreasing rod diameter increases spread rate in both.
quote: Decreasing the rod diameter increases the flame spread rate in both 1g and microgravity environments, as shown in Figure 4.3. It is also apparent that flame spread in microgravity is appreciably faster than in 1g for cylindrical rods of PMMA.
source_title: Burning and Suppression of Solids-II (BASS-II) Summary Report, NASA/TM-20210011385

topic: where the flammability boundary has its minimum
claim: For PMMA rods the minimum in the flammability boundary is at low speed, on the order of diffusive flows.
quote: The minimum in the flammability boundary is at low speed, on the order of diffusive flows.
source_title: Combustion of Solids in Microgravity: Results from the BASS-II Experiment

topic: no ignition of a PMMA rod at 13.6% O2 (PSI table)
claim: The PSI experimental table records test O12 on a 3/8-inch clear PMMA rod as "no ign at any flow" at a calibrated initial O2 of 13.6% by volume.
source_title: PSI-25 Experimental table BASS-II (CSV)

topic: ground blowoff limits correlate with the flight limits
claim: Normal-gravity blowoff limits for PMMA rods in upward stagnation flow compare favorably with the BASS-II results when buoyant stretch is included and the flow is corrected for blockage; the normal-gravity blowoff boundary is linear, with oxygen concentration proportional to flow speed.
quote: These blowoff limits compare favorably with the BASS-II results when the buoyant stretch is included and the flow is corrected by considering the blockage factor of the fuel. From these results, the normal gravity blowoff boundary for this axisymmetric rod geometry is determined to be linear, with oxygen concentration directly proportional to flow speed.
source_title: Correlation of Normal Gravity Mixed Convection Blowoff Limits with Microgravity Forced Flow Blowoff Limits

topic: background: lower oxygen limit in low or partial gravity
claim: The 2015 Researcher's Guide, in its Solid-Fuel Combustion/Material Flammability section, says that in the low-flow conditions of microgravity or partial gravity, some materials are flammable at lower oxygen concentrations than in normal gravity.
quote: In the low-flow conditions of microgravity or partial gravity, some materials are flammable at lower oxygen concentrations than in normal gravity (Figure 8).
source_title: A Researcher's Guide to: Combustion Science (NP-2015-10-034-JSC)

topic: background: easier ignition in low gravity
claim: The 2015 Researcher's Guide, in its Solid-Fuel Combustion/Material Flammability section, says that materials are easier to ignite in low gravity because natural convective cooling of the fuel surface is reduced.
quote: Materials are easier to ignite in low gravity because of reduced natural convective cooling from the fuel surface.
source_title: A Researcher's Guide to: Combustion Science (NP-2015-10-034-JSC)

topic: background: flames can spread into the oncoming airflow
claim: The 2015 Researcher's Guide, in its Solid-Fuel Combustion/Material Flammability section, says that once established, flames in low-speed airflows may preferentially spread into the oncoming airflow depending on flow speed, opposite to what occurs in normal gravity.
quote: Once established, flames in low-speed airflows may preferentially spread into the oncoming airflow (Figure 9) depending on the flow speed. This is opposite to the effect that occurs in normal gravity.
source_title: A Researcher's Guide to: Combustion Science (NP-2015-10-034-JSC)

topic: background: external radiant heat raises flammability
claim: The 2015 Researcher's Guide, in its Solid-Fuel Combustion/Material Flammability section, says that surface radiative heat loss reduces flammability, but an external radiative heat flux can cause materials to ignite and spread faster.
quote: Surface radiative heat loss reduces the flammability, but an external radiative heat flux can cause materials to ignite and spread faster.
source_title: A Researcher's Guide to: Combustion Science (NP-2015-10-034-JSC)

topic: two ways a thick-fuel flame goes out: quenching and blowoff
claim: On 4-cm PMMA spheres, quenching at low velocity was seen as the flame tip shrinking upstream, and blowoff as a hole forming in the flame at the forward stagnation point.
quote: Quenching at low velocity is observed with the flame tip shrinking upstream and blowoff is observed when a hole forms in the flame at the forward flow stagnation point.
source_title: Extinction of Solid Diffusion Flame in Microgravity: Details of Quenching and Blowoff Processes

topic: quenching limit at low flow
claim: GEL case 1 (quenching, sample inside the duct): at 4.83 cm/s flow the flame went out at 14.21% O2 and 1.04 atm.
source_title: Extinction of Solid Diffusion Flame in Microgravity: Details of Quenching and Blowoff Processes

topic: blowoff limit at high flow
claim: GEL case 2 (blowoff, sample inside the duct): at 34.28 cm/s flow the flame blew off at 14.99% O2 and 1.06 atm.
source_title: Extinction of Solid Diffusion Flame in Microgravity: Details of Quenching and Blowoff Processes

topic: lowest oxygen limit at intermediate flow
claim: GEL case 3 (intermediate flow, sample inside the duct): at 11.50 cm/s the flame went out at 13.54% O2, the lowest extinction oxygen among the five reported cases.
quote: 1 1409B quenching inside duct 4.83 128.8 3.63 14.21 1.04 0.36 2 1408A blowoff inside duct 34.28 914.1 25.71 14.99 1.06 0.95 3 1402C intermediate Inside duct 11.50 306.7 8.63 13.54 1.07 0.37 4 1409C quenching duct exit 0.44 11.7 0.33 20.77 1.03 0.17 5 1410C blowoff duct exit 49.68 1324.8 37.26 14.37 1.07 not recorded
source_title: Extinction of Solid Diffusion Flame in Microgravity: Details of Quenching and Blowoff Processes

topic: near-still air: quenching at about 21% oxygen
claim: GEL case 4 (quenching, sample at the duct exit): at 0.44 cm/s flow the flame quenched at 20.77% O2 and 1.03 atm.
source_title: Extinction of Solid Diffusion Flame in Microgravity: Details of Quenching and Blowoff Processes

topic: pulsating flame persists about 15 minutes in near-still, oxygen-rich gas
claim: At very low flow velocity (about 0.4 cm/s) and elevated oxygen, self-sustained cyclic flame tip pulsations were observed for about 15 minutes.
quote: In the first, at very low flow velocity (~ 0.4 cm/s) and elevated oxygen, self-sustained flame tip cyclic pulsations are observed for a lengthy period (~15 minutes).
source_title: Extinction of Solid Diffusion Flame in Microgravity: Details of Quenching and Blowoff Processes

topic: after local blowoff the flame re-anchors on the side of the object
claim: At 50 cm/s the diffusion flame stabilized at the shoulder of the sphere after local stagnation-point blowoff, and as oxygen kept falling spinning flamelets formed.
quote: In the second case with a higher flow velocity (50 cm/s), the diffusion flame is stabilized at the shoulder of the spherical sample after local stagnation point blowoff. With steady decrease in ambient oxygen due to depletion, spinning flamelets are formed.
source_title: Extinction of Solid Diffusion Flame in Microgravity: Details of Quenching and Blowoff Processes

topic: extinction is not smooth: the flame pulsates
claim: Quenching was not quasistatic: the flame tip pulsated periodically downstream and shrank upstream, ending each cycle smaller.
quote: However, these processes are not quasistatic. The quenching motion involves periodic flame tip pulsating toward downstream and shrinking upstream with a continually decreasing flame size at the end of each cycle.
source_title: Extinction of Solid Diffusion Flame in Microgravity: Details of Quenching and Blowoff Processes

topic: flight observations agree with model trends
claim: NASA reports that SoFIE-GEL observations agree with trends predicted by the models.
quote: SoFIE-GEL analyzes how the temperature of a fuel affects material flammability. Researchers report that experiment observations agree with trends predicted by the models.
source_title: Studying Combustion and Fire Safety

topic: flame turns bluer as oxygen falls, then goes out
claim: A SoFIE-GEL image sequence shows the flame turning bluer as ambient oxygen concentration is reduced, and eventually extinguishing.
quote: This sequence of images from the SoFIE-GEL investigation shows a flame as the ambient oxygen concentration is reduced, turning the flame bluer and eventually extinguishing it.
source_title: NASA, SpaceX's 27th Resupply Mission Returns Science Samples for Study

topic: model: flammability boundary depends on heat soaked into the solid
claim: In the GEL stagnation-point model the classical U-shaped flammability boundary (oxygen versus stretch rate) becomes a series of U-shaped boundaries as a function of the excess conductive heat loss into the solid, each with a blowoff branch and a radiative quenching branch.
quote: The classical U-shaped flammability boundary in the oxygen vs. stretch rate plot now becomes a series of U-shaped boundaries as a function of Ψ. For a given oxygen ambient, extinction boundary is a function of Ψ. The boundary consists of a blowoff branch and a radiative quenching branch.
source_title: Extinction of the Stagnation Point Diffusion Flame: Effect of Conductive Heat Loss into Solid Interior

topic: model: radiation loss on the quenching branch
claim: In the GEL model radiative heat loss is important on the quenching branch, explaining up to 46% of the total heat generation from combustion.
quote: Radiative heat loss is important on the quenching branch. It explains up to 46% of the total heat generation from combustion.
source_title: Extinction of the Stagnation Point Diffusion Flame: Effect of Conductive Heat Loss into Solid Interior

topic: drop tower: heat loss into a thick sphere grows with stretch rate
claim: Drop tower tests in support of GEL on a 4-cm-diameter PMMA sphere (17% oxygen by volume, 2 to 25 cm/s concurrent flow) found that conductive heat loss into the solid increases with stretch rate.
quote: Within the test range (17% Oxygen by volume, 2 – 25 cm/s concurrent flow), the conductive heat loss increases with the stretch rate.
source_title: Extinction of the Stagnation Point Diffusion Flame: Effect of Conductive Heat Loss into Solid Interior

topic: model: piloted ignition is earlier in 0 g than in 1 g
claim: In the MIST numerical simulation of piloted ignition of PMMA, ignition occurred significantly earlier at 0 g than at 1 g (596 s compared with 774 s).
quote: Furthermore, ignition occurs significantly earlier at 0-g than at 1-g conditions (596 s compared to 774 s).
source_title: Material Ignition and Suppression Test (MIST) in Space Exploration Atmospheres, Summary of Research

topic: low-gravity aircraft tests: shorter ignition times at low flow
claim: The Researcher's Guide, describing the SoFIE investigation "External Heat Flux Effects on the Ignitability and Suppression of Materials in Microgravity", reports that at airflow velocities below those induced by buoyancy, ignition times are significantly lower than in normal-gravity buoyant flows, because reduced surface heat loss matters more than reduced oxygen transport.
quote: At airflow velocities below those induced by buoyancy, ignition times reach values that are significantly lower than those observed in normal-gravity buoyant flows. The reduction of the ignition times indicates that, under these low-flow conditions, the ignition process is affected more by the reduction in surface heat loss than by the corresponding oxygen transport reduction.
source_title: A Researcher's Guide to: Combustion Science (NP-2015-10-034-JSC)

topic: model: critical heat flux for ignition may be half the 1-g value
claim: The Researcher's Guide reports that a theoretical ignition-time model showed the critical heat flux for ignition in microgravity can be as low as half the value measured in normal gravity.
quote: By developing a theoretical model for the ignition time, it was also shown that the critical heat flux for ignition in microgravity can be as short as half the value measured in normal gravity.
source_title: A Researcher's Guide to: Combustion Science (NP-2015-10-034-JSC)

topic: ground test: a re-ignited sample behaves differently
claim: In MIST ground tests on cast PMMA, mass loss before ignition and time to ignition were statistically different between ignition of virgin samples and re-ignition of the same samples after cooling.
quote: It is seen that the mass loss before ignition as well as the time to ignition are statistically different between ignition of virgin samples and re-ignition of the same samples after cooling.
source_title: Material Ignition and Suppression Test (MIST) in Space Exploration Atmospheres, Summary of Research

topic: ground test: ignition time falls steeply with heat flux
claim: MIST laboratory data for cast PMMA seem to indicate an exponential decay in time to ignition with rising heat flux, and a minimum time to ignition for the test geometry.
quote: As can be seen in Figure 7, the data seems to indicate an exponential decay in time to ignition with rising heat flux as well as a minimum time to ignition for the given geometrical constraints of the experiment.
source_title: Material Ignition and Suppression Test (MIST) in Space Exploration Atmospheres, Summary of Research

topic: ground test: mass loss rate at ignition is roughly constant
claim: Across a broad range of incident heat fluxes at ambient atmospheric conditions, MIST laboratory tests on cast PMMA show an apparently constant mass loss at ignition.
quote: Additionally, Figure 8 indicates that across a broad range of incident heat fluxes, at ambient atmospheric conditions, that there is an apparently constant mass loss at ignition.
source_title: Material Ignition and Suppression Test (MIST) in Space Exploration Atmospheres, Summary of Research

topic: model: ignition in microgravity is unsteady
claim: In the MIST simulation the microgravity reaction was quenched multiple times, jumping from the pilot location onto the surface and back, before it anchored on the solid surface and propagated toward the leading edge.
quote: A distinct feature was observed in the microgravity flame: the reaction was quenched multiple times, jumping from the pilot location onto the surface and back, until it anchored on the solid surface and propagated uniformly towards the leading edge.
source_title: Material Ignition and Suppression Test (MIST) in Space Exploration Atmospheres, Summary of Research

topic: no test method yet for exploration atmospheres
claim: The 2015 Researcher's Guide states that there is currently no testing methodology specifically designed to determine the fire hazard of materials in space exploration atmospheres (SEA), and that microgravity experiments will be used to validate a model meant to predict the fire behavior of combustible materials in SEA.
quote: Microgravity experiments will be used to validate the model, which in turn will be used to predict the fire behavior of different combustible materials in SEA. Currently, there exists no testing methodology specifically designed to determine the fire hazard of materials under those conditions.
source_title: A Researcher's Guide to: Combustion Science (NP-2015-10-034-JSC)

topic: a 1-g narrow channel reproduces microgravity spread for thin PMMA
claim: At 1 atm the San Diego State narrow channel apparatus reproduced microgravity flame spread for thin PMMA sheets as well as for thin cellulose fuels.
quote: This comparison confirms that at 1 atm pressure, the SDSU NCA successfully simulates microgravity for not only thin cellulose fuels, but also for thin PMMA sheets as well.
source_title: Opposed-Flow Flame Spread in a Narrow Channel Apparatus over Thin PMMA Sheets

topic: narrow-channel flames go out sooner than true microgravity flames
claim: Near the low-velocity extinction end the narrow channel flames lose more heat to the nearby window and bottom plate and tend to go out sooner than true microgravity flames.
quote: The NCA flames suffer more heat loss due to the proximity of the quartz window and the bottom plate, so that those flames tend to go out sooner than the true microgravity flames which do not have this loss mechanism.
source_title: Opposed-Flow Flame Spread in a Narrow Channel Apparatus over Thin PMMA Sheets

topic: spread rate peaks at an intermediate flow at 21% O2 but not at 30%
claim: For thin PMMA in the narrow channel at 21% oxygen, spread rate rises, plateaus and then drops with relative velocity, so there is a velocity that maximizes spread; at 30% oxygen the drop after the plateau no longer appeared within the velocities tested.
quote: At 21 percent oxygen concentration it is noticed that the flame spread rate raises, plateaus, and then begins to drop once again, so that there is an optimal relative velocity that maximizes the flame spread rate. As oxygen concentration is raised to 30 percent it is noticeable that the drop immediately following the plateau no longer exists within the velocities tested here.
source_title: Opposed-Flow Flame Spread in a Narrow Channel Apparatus over Thin PMMA Sheets

topic: dim blue flame at 21% O2 and low flow, bright at 30% O2
claim: With 75 micrometer PMMA at 1 atm, the flame at 21% O2 and 7 cm/s opposed flow was very dim blue, compared with the flame at 30% O2 and 30 cm/s.
quote: Figure 5: Flame comparison. Tests are with 75 µm PMMA at 1 atm pressure. Left: 30% O2 concentration and 30 cm/s opposed flow velocity. Right: 21% O2 concentration and 7 cm/s opposed flow velocity (flame is very dim blue)
source_title: Opposed-Flow Flame Spread in a Narrow Channel Apparatus over Thin PMMA Sheets

topic: higher oxygen gives brighter, longer flames
claim: In the narrow channel tests higher oxygen percentages caused brighter, yellow and longer flames.
quote: As with opposed flow velocity, the oxygen percentage caused the same effects. The higher oxygen percentages caused brighter, yellow, and longer flames.
source_title: Opposed-Flow Flame Spread in a Narrow Channel Apparatus over Thin PMMA Sheets

topic: gap height of the ground apparatus is not settled
claim: Gap heights of 18 mm and 6 mm were found unfit for the narrow channel apparatus, and the gap that best balances buoyancy suppression against heat loss to the plates was still unclear.
quote: While gap height experiments have shown 18 mm and 6 mm gaps to be unfit for the SDSU NCA, it is unclear what gap height produces the best compromise in buoyancy suppression and heat loss to the top and bottom plates of the NCA.
source_title: Opposed-Flow Flame Spread in a Narrow Channel Apparatus over Thin PMMA Sheets

topic: heat conducted ahead of the flame must be modeled
claim: Infrared measurements on 3 mm PMMA in the narrow channel (5 mm gap, 15 cm/s mean opposed flow) show nontrivial forward heat conduction ahead of the flame, which must be included in computational models.
quote: Test conditions of a 5 mm gap, mean opposed flow velocity of 15 cm/s, and fuel thickness of 3 mm are used.PMMA is selected as the fuel due to repeatability of test results, ease of computational modeling, and known combustion mechanics. Using specific lens and bandpass filter combinations the PMMA can be imaged as effectively opaque. The spectral emissivity for PMMA was calculated and incorporated into the calibration of the camera.Surface temperatures from the IR camera are compared to results from thermocouples embedded in the surface of the fuel. The IR camera results show that nontrivial forward conduction occurs during tests, and therefore must be included in computational models of the process.
source_title: Infrared Measurements of Forward Heat Conduction during Simulated Microgravity Flame Spread in the Narrow Channel Apparatus

topic: why the standard test differs from spacecraft conditions
claim: Flames in NASA-STD-6001 Test 1 are buoyantly driven, so Test 1 cannot be run in a simulated microgravity atmosphere; the narrow channel suppresses buoyancy to do that.
quote: The buoyant suppression achieved with a NCA allows for tests to be conducted in a simulated microgravity atmosphere-a characteristic that Test 1 lacks since flames present in Test 1 are buoyantly driven.
source_title: Opposed-Flow Flame Spread in a Narrow Channel Apparatus over Thin PMMA Sheets

topic: thin acrylic burning at high oxygen and half an atmosphere
claim: NASA reports that during SoFIE-RTDFS a sheet of clear acrylic plastic burned at higher oxygen levels and half the standard pressure of Earth’s atmosphere.
quote: During the Residence Time Driven Flame Spread (SOFIE-RTDFS) investigation at the International Space Station, this sheet of clear acrylic plastic burns at higher oxygen levels and half the standard pressure of Earth’s atmosphere.
source_title: Ahead of Crew Return, NASA's Crew-9 Concludes Science Mission

topic: model: no steady spread above a critical fuel thickness
claim: Theoretical modeling behind RTDFS, an experiment on flame propagation over solid fuels in microgravity, predicts that steady flame spread over solid fuels cannot be sustained, even in a high oxygen environment, if the fuel exceeds a critical thickness.
quote: Theoretical modeling predicts that steady flame spread over solid fuels cannot be sustained, even in a high oxygen environment if the fuel exceeds a critical thickness.
source_title: Solid Fuel Ignition and Extinction (SoFIE)

topic: thicker thin-fuels spread slower in still air because radiation loss grows
claim: In a quiescent microgravity environment flame spread rate over thin fuels decreases with fuel thickness, both from added thermal mass and because the relative importance of radiative losses increases in direct proportion to fuel thickness.
quote: Flame spread rate over thin fuels in a quiescent microgravity environment decreases with fuel thickness not only because of increased thermal mass but also because the relative importance of radiative losses, as quantified by a non-dimensional radiation number, increases in direct proportion of fuel thickness.
source_title: Solid Fuel Ignition and Extinction (SoFIE)

topic: critical flow for radiative extinction does not depend on thickness
claim: The RTDFS tests run in BASS-II vindicated the theoretical and computational finding that the critical opposed-flow velocity for radiative extinction in microgravity is independent of fuel thickness.
quote: RTDFS vindicated the theoretical and computational findings that the critical opposed-flow velocity at which radiative extinction occurs in a microgravity environment is independent of fuel thickness
source_title: Burning and Suppression of Solids-II (BASS-II) Summary Report, NASA/TM-20210011385

topic: in microgravity spread slows as opposed flow falls, to extinction
claim: In the microgravity regime, where opposing flow can be very mild or absent, spread rate over thin fuels decreases as the opposed flow is reduced, and under certain conditions this leads to flame extinguishment at a low enough flow velocity.
quote: While spread rate over thin fuels is independent of the opposing flow velocity in the thermal regime, in the microgravity regime, where the opposing flow can be very mild or even completely absent in the absence of buoyancy-induced flow, the spread rate is known to decrease as the opposed flow is reduced. Under certain conditions, this can lead to flame extinguishment at a low enough flow velocity.
source_title: Burning and Suppression of Solids-II (BASS-II) Summary Report, NASA/TM-20210011385

topic: radiative quenching below about 2 cm/s (project slide)
claim: A 2019 SoFIE project slide for RTDFS shows computed (model) flames over a thin PMMA sheet, with radiative quenching when flow velocity goes below 2 cm/s.
quote: Left: radiative quenching when flow velocity goes below 2 cm/s.
source_title: Solid Fuel Ignition and Extinction (SoFIE) Project on ISS

topic: goal: a thickness, flow or oxygen level that makes a material inherently fire safe
claim: The Researcher's Guide says the planned work on "Thermal and Species Field Effects on Material Flammability" can lead to specifying a critical fuel thickness, a critical forced velocity or a critical oxygen level that makes a material inherently fire safe in microgravity, where radiative heat transfer dominates.
quote: The significance of this portion of the work is that it will establish quantitative criteria, based on fundamentals, which determine the flammability of materials in microgravity where radiative heat transfer dominates because of high-residence time created by a lack of buoyancy-induced or forced flow. This can lead to the specification of a critical fuel thickness, a critical forced velocity, or a critical oxygen level that makes a material inherently fire safe.
source_title: A Researcher's Guide to: Combustion Science (NP-2015-10-034-JSC)

topic: flames sustained at lower oxygen in 0 g, lunar g and Martian g
claim: The SoFIE project slides for SMuRF state that in reduced gravity (0 g, lunar g, Martian g) a flame can be sustained at lower O2.
quote: In reduced gravity (0g, Lunar g, Martian g), a flame can be sustained at lower O2.
source_title: Solid Fuel Ignition and Extinction (SoFIE) Project on ISS

topic: 1-g screening flames go out by blowoff
claim: The SoFIE project slides for SMuRF state that in the 1-g screening tests flames extinguish by blowoff.
quote: In the 1-g screening tests, flames extinguish by blowoff.
source_title: Solid Fuel Ignition and Extinction (SoFIE) Project on ISS

topic: negative oxygen margin of safety for PMMA rods (2019 value)
claim: The 2019 SoFIE project slides give a negative oxygen margin of safety of 1.4% O2 for PMMA rods, to be used to de-rate materials.
quote: Negative Oxygen Margin of Safety to de-rate materials. PMMA rods: NOMS = 1.4% O2
source_title: Solid Fuel Ignition and Extinction (SoFIE) Project on ISS

topic: few thin materials are rated at the exploration atmosphere
claim: The SoFIE project slides state that few thin fuel sheet materials are rated even in 1 g at 34% O2 and 8.2 psia, the exploration atmosphere.
quote: Thin fuel sheets: few materials rated even in 1g at 34% O2, 8.2 psia (exploration atmosphere).
source_title: Solid Fuel Ignition and Extinction (SoFIE) Project on ISS

topic: drop tower results question Test 1
claim: The Researcher's Guide says drop-tower results suggest the current NASA-STD-6001 Test 1 might not be conservative, and that this work would give an increased margin of safety based on a slightly modified Test 1 protocol.
quote: It will also provide an increased margin of safety for materials flammability based upon a slightly modified NASA Test 1 protocol, since recent drop-tower results suggest that the current Test 1 might not be conservative.
source_title: A Researcher's Guide to: Combustion Science (NP-2015-10-034-JSC)

topic: a ground test method to estimate low-gravity oxygen limits
claim: A new normal-gravity upward flame spread test method extrapolates the linear blowoff boundary to the zero stretch limit to resolve microgravity flammability limits.
quote: We describe a new normal gravity 'upward flame spread test' method which extrapolates the linear blowoff boundary to the zero stretch limit in order to resolve microgravity flammability limits
source_title: Correlation of Normal Gravity Mixed Convection Blowoff Limits with Microgravity Forced Flow Blowoff Limits

topic: iss_fire_response
claim: Raise the alarm. Any crew member may.
quote: The crew may also initiate the alarm if they see or smell evidence of a combustion event.
source_title: Evolution of Hardware and Philosophy of Emergency Response Actions on the International Space Station and Future Spacecrafts

topic: iss_fire_response
claim: Gather at a clean point and keep measuring the air.
quote: They will constantly monitor air quality using hand-held combustion product analyzers to ensure their gathering point remains a safe haven with a clean atmosphere.
source_title: Evolution of Hardware and Philosophy of Emergency Response Actions on the International Space Station and Future Spacecrafts

topic: iss_fire_response
claim: Fans, gas introduction and oxygen generation stay off.
quote: Intramodular and intermodular fans are deactivated, gas introduction is terminated, oxygen generation systems are deactivated, and location specific fans are deactivated
source_title: Evolution of Hardware and Philosophy of Emergency Response Actions on the International Space Station and Future Spacecrafts

topic: iss_fire_response
claim: Remove power at the alarm location.
quote: If a location specific fire alarm is triggered, then power in that area is removed.
source_title: Evolution of Hardware and Philosophy of Emergency Response Actions on the International Space Station and Future Spacecrafts

topic: iss_fire_response
claim: Put on breathing masks before investigating; use the combustion-product analyzer to locate the event.
quote: Upon identifying the locations to investigate, crew will don breathing masks, to be described in section 3.2.4. Utilizing their combustion product analyzer and probe (section 3.2.5) to identify the location of the event, crew will proceed to unpower the equipment behind the panel, thus attacking the Ignition Source (Heat) leg of the fire triangle.
source_title: Evolution of Hardware and Philosophy of Emergency Response Actions on the International Space Station and Future Spacecrafts

topic: iss_fire_response
claim: Unpower the equipment behind the panel.
quote: crew will proceed to unpower the equipment behind the panel, thus attacking the Ignition Source (Heat) leg of the fire triangle.
source_title: Evolution of Hardware and Philosophy of Emergency Response Actions on the International Space Station and Future Spacecrafts

topic: iss_fire_response
claim: Use the extinguisher if unpowering fails.
quote: If that does not extinguish the fire, they will utilize a fire extinguisher
source_title: Evolution of Hardware and Philosophy of Emergency Response Actions on the International Space Station and Future Spacecrafts

topic: iss_fire_response
claim: Partial, then full powerdown; leave the module.
quote: If the fire extinguisher fails to stop the event, crew will proceed to a partial powerdown of the entire module they are located in, followed by a full powerdown and evacuation of the module.
source_title: Evolution of Hardware and Philosophy of Emergency Response Actions on the International Space Station and Future Spacecrafts

topic: iss_fire_response
claim: If the crew feels uncomfortable continuing, they may choose to isolate an isolatable module and stop further response.
quote: It should be noted, with crew safety being the top priority, if at any point crew does not feel comfortable proceeding forward through the procedures, it is their prerogative to isolate the module and stand down on any further fire response steps.
source_title: Evolution of Hardware and Philosophy of Emergency Response Actions on the International Space Station and Future Spacecrafts
